title: Strip slash-command markup from titles
description:
42 conversations (1.4%) show garbage as their result header — harness-injected markup
reaching the title verbatim instead of the prose the user actually typed. Examples:
`find-skills` from a slash-command expansion, a sentence about whichever file happened to be
focused in the editor, and bracketed interruption notices the harness writes as though the
user had typed them.

Both importer paths are affected and they need different rules, because the two tools inject
differently: Claude Code wraps machinery in pseudo-XML tags, Codex writes bare slash-command
lines and `[$name](path)` skill links.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. `cs index`
2. `cs search` with a blank query to list recent conversations, or search for `find-skills`.
3. Scan the grouped result headers. 42 of them are markup rather than prose — a
   slash-command expansion, an `ide_opened_file` sentence, or `[Request interrupted by user]`.

Blocks the eval set (chat-search-6eb.9): a result header that shows machinery makes
"is this the conversation I meant" unanswerable, so relevance judgements would be scored
against a title the ranking never saw.
acceptance_criteria: No conversation title on either the claude-code or codex path contains harness-injected markup. A turn that is entirely markup yields no title and the next user message gets the job. <command-args> keeps its body when the sibling <command-name> is a custom command and yields nothing when it is /model or /fast. Bare bracketed harness notices never title a conversation. Codex bare slash-command lines are rejected while real paths (/Users/x, /usr/local/bin) and prose containing a slash are not. All 42 affected conversations render real prose. Synthetic tests only.
close_reason: Verified against a fresh full-corpus index: 0 conversation titles contain pseudo-XML markup, ide_* blocks, bracketed harness notices, or bare slash commands. Both importer paths covered by synthetic tests.

title: ymd() renders dates in UTC, so evening-local conversations show tomorrow date
description:
A session at 2026-07-18 21:00 PDT prints as 2026-07-19. Every grouped result line is
affected, and a wrong date makes "is this the one I meant" unanswerable.

Not a rare edge: `ymd()` renders in UTC, so on Pacific time every conversation after 17:00
local shows tomorrow's date — roughly seven hours of every day, and the evening is when a
lot of this corpus was written.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Find a conversation whose `ended_at` is an evening local time — 2026-07-18 21:00 PDT is
   2026-07-19 04:00 UTC.
2. `cs index`, then `cs search` for it.
3. The grouped result header reads 2026-07-19. It should read 2026-07-18.
design:
DECIDED: take chrono, convert to local at the parse boundary, keep storage as epoch millis.

Rationale from fast-resume (the category leader, already benchmarked against): it depends on chrono 0.4 and uses Local exclusively — Utc appears nowhere in its src/. Adapters convert at parse time (adapters/shared.rs parse_datetime returns DateTime<Local> via with_timezone(&Local), with a naive-local fallback for offset-less formats), then reduce to f64 epoch seconds for storage. Local-ness is a render/bucket concern, never a storage one — which matches ended_at already being epoch millis here.

Rejected: reading TZ or /etc/localtime for a fixed offset. Correct for ymd() today, wrong the moment date arithmetic appears. fast-resume's next_day_start_seconds uses checked_add_days(Days::new(1)) — civil-day arithmetic — and its test proves a next-day boundary is 82,800s across spring-forward and 90,000s across fall-back, neither of which a fixed offset can express. chat-search-6eb.11 (Query DSL) would want exactly this for after:/before:/yesterday filters.

Testing note: fast-resume keeps chrono-tz as a DEV-dependency only, to pin a zone (Europe/Paris) so DST behaviour is deterministic in tests. Production reads the system zone. Worth copying.

The old localtime_r advisory does not apply — chrono 0.4 has not pulled in time 0.1 by default for years.
acceptance_criteria: Dates render as the local civil date: a conversation at 2026-07-18 21:00 PDT prints 2026-07-18. Storage stays epoch millis — local-ness is a render concern, never a storage one. A test pins the behaviour against a fixed zone via chrono-tz as a dev-dependency only, so it is deterministic in CI regardless of the runner's zone. The rule lives in exactly one place, landing as part of chat-search-me9.12 rather than separately, so ymd() in the binary and the strflocaltime call in the cs-fzf jq both go away.
close_reason: Landed as part of me9.12. cs-core/src/time.rs owns the rule; DST behaviour pinned with chrono-tz as a dev-dependency; Group.ended_date rendered in cs-core so no client re-derives it.

title: ChatGPT reaches the index only via --chatgpt-export
description:
69% of the corpus vanishes silently if the flag is omitted. An eval run without it measures
the wrong index and nothing says so.

The ChatGPT export is the only source not read through `ArchiveReader` — `crates/cs/src/query.rs:63-79`
reads it straight from a directory handed in on the command line, which is why it is the one
source that can be forgotten.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. `cs index` with no flags.
2. `cs search` for a phrase you know is in a ChatGPT conversation.
3. Zero hits. The run reports success and its per-source table simply has no
   `chatgpt-export` row — nothing states that 2,011 conversations were not considered.
4. `cs index --chatgpt-export ~/dev/sandbox/chat-history/data/`, search again, and the same
   phrase is found.
acceptance_criteria: ChatGPT conversations are indexed on a default run with no extra flags, or the run refuses to proceed and says what is missing.
close_reason: chatgpt-export is now an ordinary mirror source in config.toml and the --chatgpt-export flag is gone; a bare 'cs index' reaches all 2,011 ChatGPT conversations. Also closes the silent half of the acceptance: a configured source the archive holds nothing for now gets a report row stating why (bundle-not-implemented vs nothing-archived) instead of being skipped invisibly — opencode now shows as skipped rather than absent.

title: A rebuild is invisible to clients, and its partial answers look like complete ones
description:
Measured by chat-search-me9.22 (poc/swift RESULTS.md §4), querying a scratch index every 250 ms while cs index rewrote it.

Rebuilding over an existing index, from the client's side:

  t=0.0s        818 conversations — complete
  t=1.8-4.4s    exit 1, 'index records no importer version, so it predates this schema'
  t=4.7-8.0s    exit 0, 489 conversations
  t=8.5-9.3s    exit 0, 678 conversations
  after         818 conversations

So there are two distinct failures, and the second is worse than the first.

1. For ~2.6s the index reports as MISSING, not as rebuilding. The prose says 'predates this schema', which is wrong and points the user at the very command that is already running.

2. For ~5s after that, queries succeed and return silently incomplete answers. Nothing in the response says the index is partial. A user searching mid-rebuild is told 'nothing matched' about a conversation that is indexed and will be found thirty seconds later, and there is no signal any client could use to say otherwise.

ADR 14's stated consequence is that clients must treat 'no index yet' and 'index being rebuilt' as first-class states rather than transport errors. This is the measurement of what happens when they try: the contract does not carry the distinction, so they cannot.
design:
The client cannot fix this. It sees exit 0 and a well-formed body; there is nothing to branch on. It has to be answered on the cs side, and the options differ in cost:

A. A build marker in the index. Set a row when a build starts and clear it when it commits; cs search reads it and reports 'rebuilding' in the JSON body (a field, not an error — the results are real, just incomplete). Cheap, and it makes both failures reportable through one mechanism.

B. Build into a temporary file and rename over the target. An atomic swap means a reader sees either the whole old index or the whole new one and never a half-built one. This is the stronger fix — it removes the partial-answer window rather than labelling it — and it fits ADR 1's disposable index exactly, since the index is already rebuilt from scratch. Costs peak disk of two indexes, ~660 MB at today's size.

B looks right and A is not redundant with it: even with an atomic swap, 'there is no index yet' is still a state worth naming properly rather than reporting as a schema-age error.

Also, separately: cs search creates an empty database file at a --db path that does not exist, so a typo'd path silently becomes a new empty index rather than an error.
acceptance_criteria: A client can tell 'no index yet', 'rebuilding', and 'this answer is complete' apart from the JSON contract alone, without matching on English prose. No window exists in which a query returns exit 0 and a silently partial result set.
notes: branch: worktree-me9-28-index-swap (worktree .claude/worktrees/me9-28-index-swap, 5 commits off main)
close_reason:
Both failures gone. cs index now builds through cs_core::IndexBuild — the whole index assembled in index.db.building and renamed over the target — so a reader sees the whole old index or the whole new one, never a partial one. Re-ran chat-search-me9.22's experiment on the real corpus (3,097 conversations, 334 MB): a query every 250 ms across a 17 s rebuild returned 51 conversations at every poll with index_state=rebuilding, against 2.6 s of exit 1 plus 5 s of exit 0 over 489 of 818 before. The swap costs 257-367 ms of a 14-26 s rebuild.

Four states now travel as names, not prose: no_index and building as {"error":{"code","message"}} on stdout beside the nonzero exit, ready and rebuilding as index_state on a successful cs search --json (both shapes) and on cs status --json. A build holds a lock on index.db.building.lock for its lifetime, so a ^C mid-rebuild leaves litter that reads as ready rather than as a build that never ends, and a second cs index is refused instead of interleaved. Readers open read-only, which is what stops a mistyped --db becoming a new empty index. Also fixed at the source: an empty archive built an index with no importer_version row, which read as 'predates this schema'.

Not done, and filed: chat-search-me9.35 (the TUI holds one connection per session, so a swap never reaches it). Noted on chat-search-me9.29, which keeps the rest of the error contract: index_corrupt vs index_stale, config_missing, compact --json, and whether cs show --json should carry index_state (its body is a Transcript serialized whole, so that one is a shape decision).

Gate green: cargo build --workspace --all-targets with no warnings, cargo test --workspace 517 passed. MSRV moved 1.85 -> 1.89 for std::fs::File::try_lock. branch: worktree-me9-28-index-swap

title: Should the fts tables carry a prefix index? It is most of what a broad keystroke costs
description:
fts5 answers a prefix term by scanning its term index for every term with that prefix and merging their doclists, and it redoes that on every query. On the 180k-message corpus that is the dominant cost of a broad typeahead keystroke, measured two independent ways while doing chat-search-6eb.30:

- Ranking (search_grouped, limit 50, nested 0): `pro` 29.4 ms, `the` 59.3 ms, against `commit` 5.2 ms and `borrow` 0.5 ms. Same shape chat-search-6eb.29 measured as `rus` 1193 ms / `rust` 25 ms.
- Marking one row through the corpus index: `the` exact 54.6 us/row against `the`* 5427 us/row — 100x, on the same rows, differing only in the star.

A prefix index (`prefix='2 3 4'` on the CREATE VIRTUAL TABLE) turns those into ordinary single-term doclist lookups for the configured lengths. Prefixes longer than the longest configured length fall back to the scan, so the choice of lengths is the whole decision.

## What has to be decided

Which prefix lengths, if any, against how much index growth. Each configured length is another full posting list over the corpus; the index is 315 MB today. Nobody has priced it — that measurement is the first task if this is taken up.

## Why it is filed as a decision

It changes the index schema and needs an IMPORTER_VERSION bump and a reindex, and ADR 6's 'revisit when' now names it. It is also the only remaining lever on the two queries chat-search-6eb.30 could not get under the 30 ms keystroke budget, because after that change the marking is 6-12 ms of them and the ranking is the other 29-59 ms.
design: Measure first, decide second. The sequence: build the index with prefix='2 3', with prefix='2 3 4', and without; record file size and rebuild time for each; re-run the search_grouped numbers in chat-search-6eb.29 and the per-row marking numbers in highlight::spans_for against all three. If a prefix index makes the index route cheap for prefix terms too, highlight::spans_for's two-branch rule collapses back to one branch, which is a second reason to want it.
acceptance_criteria: Either the fts tables declare a prefix index, with the size cost measured and recorded in ADR 6 and IMPORTER_VERSION bumped — or the option is measured, rejected, and the rejection written down so it is not re-litigated.
notes:
branch: worktree-bead-6eb38-prefix-index

MEASURED 2026-08-01, release, 181k messages / 317 MB index, TUI settings (limit 50).
Three full rebuilds: no prefix, prefix='2 3', prefix='2 3 4'. Full numbers in ADR 6.

Cost: index 317 -> 373 MB ('2 3') -> 400 MB ('2 3 4'); fts postings 41 -> 96 -> 123 MB,
i.e. one full posting list per configured length. Rebuild ~10.4 s -> ~15.4 s (+48%,
medians of three interleaved rounds; interleaved because the machine was loaded).

Buy, ranking (search_grouped, nested 0, typeahead): the 59.9 -> 50.4 ms, pro 30.2 ->
26.9, rus 19.9 -> 18.8. End to end at nested 3: the 71.6 -> 62.1, pro 38.3 -> 35.5.
Both stay over the 30 ms budget. Cold first touch in a fresh process does not improve
at all: pro 637 -> 747 ms, the 487 -> 538 ms, slightly worse for the bigger file.

WHY THE PREMISE WAS WRONG. the* ranks in 59.9 ms and the exact ranks in 48.9 ms, so
the prefix expansion is only the 11 ms gap. Probed directly in sqlite3: the doclist
merge for "the"* is 7 ms vs 1 ms with the index, but the same query with bm25 and
ORDER BY left in is 148 ms vs 131 ms, and stripped of scoring it is 12 ms vs 2 ms.
The cost is scoring all 37,911 matching rows before LIMIT discards them.

The 100x marking win in the description is real and reproduced (5.2 ms/row -> 37 us/row)
but is already banked by spans_for's scratch-table route, so wall clock is unchanged
(the* marking 10.4 -> 10.3 ms). The two-branch rule does not collapse either: at
prefix='2 3 4' the index route wins pro* (4.7 vs 8.1) and loses commit* (11.0 vs 2.4)
and learning* (17.8 vs 15.1), because a prefix longer than the longest configured
length still walks.

Harness: crates/cs-core/examples/prefix_bench.rs + prefix_cold.rs, committed at 015e661
on this branch and deleted in 8e10bc7. Recover with git show if this is ever repriced.
close_reason: Measured and rejected. Three full rebuilds (no prefix, prefix='2 3', prefix='2 3 4') on the 181k-message index: it costs +26% index size and +48% rebuild time, and buys 9 ms off the worst warm keystroke and nothing at all cold, because the prefix expansion is only 11 ms of a 60 ms 'the'* ranking and the other 49 is bm25 scoring the whole match set. The 100x marking win is real but already banked by spans_for's scratch-table route, and the two-branch rule does not collapse because prefixes longer than the configured lengths still walk. Rejection written into ADR 6 with the numbers, plus pointers in schema.rs where the declaration would go and highlight.rs where the branch lives. No code change, no IMPORTER_VERSION bump. Redirected chat-search-6eb.29 to the candidate ceiling and the scoring.

title: cs-tui reads the query mode instead of re-deriving it
description:
Delete App::holds, App::holding, App::is_blank and state::MIN_QUERY_CHARS. The TUI reads Query::mode and decides what to render for each of Empty, TooShort and Searchable.

Also deletes SearchOptions.source from the TUI path: the facet selection desugars into Filter::Agent. Surfaces dir: and date: as recognised-but-not-yet-active in the status line, which is the chat-search-me9.15 gap.

Removes the reason App::holds was lifted out as a pure associated function in the first place, so its index-free test moves to cs-core with the rule.
close_reason: Closed

title: Rank and mark from the parsed query
description:
Migrate search.rs and highlight.rs to render from one structure, and delete the six exported tokenizing functions plus highlight::query_terms. snippet_marked survives with a new signature. highlight::spans and highlight::snippet are untouched: the fts5 scratch-table mechanism from chat-search-6eb.20 is correct and is not what leaks.

Wire Filter::Agent to the source clause that already exists (AND (?4 IS NULL OR c.source = ?4)), and carry dir:/date: as recognised-but-inactive.

Tests: one structural invariant asserting match_expr and marking_terms render from the same term list, plus the three divergences as named regression cases on search.rs:456. That table currently calls highlight::query_terms directly and never sets prefix, so the test written to pin agreement cannot catch the bugs it exists to prevent. Route it through Query::typeahead and marking_terms, the path that actually ships.
close_reason: Closed

title: New cs-core/src/query.rs: parse, Query, Filter, Mode
description:
The parsed value and its tests, with no callers yet.

Query::typeahead(text) and Query::exact(text) fix prefix at parse time. Query carries ordered terms, filters, whether the final token is still open, and Mode { Empty, TooShort, Searchable }. Parse is infallible: a half-typed filter is literal text, never an error, because mid-word is the normal state in a typeahead.

Also adds the terms to docs/GLOSSARY.md, which today has no word for any of this. The glossary opens with the story of a wrong name propagating through a spec and two implementations before the data contradicted it, so the terms land with the type rather than after it.
close_reason: Closed

title: Split SearchOptions out of Query, and require now_ms
description:
cs_core::search::Query holds two concepts: what the user asked for (text) and how to run it (limit, field, source, include_off_path, prefix, now_ms, repeat_weight, decay). That conflation is why recent() accepts a Query and silently ignores seven of its nine fields.

Rename the bag to SearchOptions so the name Query is free for the parsed value. Fold the positional nested argument of search_grouped into it while there.

Make now_ms a required argument to SearchOptions::new rather than a defaultable field. Query::new leaves it 0, and the decay term is bm25 / (1.0 + decay * max(0, now_ms - ts) / YEAR): with now_ms = 0 and any positive timestamp, max(0, 0 - ts) is 0, so the divisor is exactly 1.0 and recency decay is silently off. Fixes the explain bug in the same move.

Must land before the new Query type: both would otherwise be re-exported from lib.rs as Query.
close_reason: Closed

title: Rename cs/src/query.rs to commands.rs
description: crates/cs/src/query.rs is named for query parsing and contains none. Its own module doc says what it holds: cs index, cs search and cs explain, everything downstream of the archive. Adding a real crates/cs-core/src/query.rs would put two files named query.rs in the workspace, only one of which parses queries. Mechanical: one mod line, one import line, no logic touched.
close_reason: Closed

title: Parse the query once, into a value
description:
The query is a &str re-tokenized on every path. search::to_match_expr_opts and highlight::query_terms are two term extractors with different rules, bridged by marking_terms, which recovers the prefix rule by string-inspecting the ranker output (expr.ends_with). App::holds re-derives the same MIN_PREFIX_LEN threshold as its logical complement, and is_blank asks a third time.

TWO live divergences, measured 2026-07-30 by probing both extractors directly:

  agent:codex borrow  expr="agent" "codex" "borrow"*   marking=["borrow*"]
  learn deep learn    expr="learn" "deep" "learn"*     marking=["learn", "deep"]

1. agent:codex is ANDed into FTS5 as two literal terms while the highlighter drops them, so every returned row is labelled with the UNLOCATED sentinel. The highlight.rs comment claiming the row was not ranked on those words is false today.
2. learn deep learn loses its prefix star. query_terms deduplicates, so terms.last() is deep while the expression ends with "learn"*, the ends_with check misses, and a row that ranked on the stem expansion is marked with the exact term or not at all.

CORRECTION: an earlier draft listed a third divergence, -borrow becoming a required term. Probed: both sides produce "borrow"* and they agree. Leading-dash negation is simply unimplemented, which is a chat-search-6eb.11 feature gap rather than a defect here. Two divergences, not three.

Fix: parse once into a Query value that both the ranker and the highlighter render from. Not a harder ends_with check, no bridge at all.
design:
Decided by grilling, 2026-07-30. Eleven decisions:

1. Seam only. Filter tokens are recognised so they stop reaching FTS5 as literal words. The DSL itself stays chat-search-6eb.11.
2. Two types. Query is what was asked (terms, filters, open, mode). SearchOptions is how to run it (limit, field, decay, repeat_weight, now_ms, nested). The conflation is why recent() silently ignores seven of nine fields.
3. Mode { Empty, TooShort, Searchable } lives on Query. cs-core owns the fact (the threshold is a ranking cost: h* 2510ms, ho* 51ms, hov* 16ms), cs-tui owns the policy.
4. A filter that cannot be applied is recognised, carried and surfaced, never silently dropped. Serves chat-search-me9.15.
5. Full absorption. Query::typeahead and Query::exact fix prefix at PARSE time, not render time. Prefix-agnostic parse was considered and rejected: Mode::TooShort exists only because of prefix expansion, so mode(), match_expr() and marking_terms() would each take the same bool and have to be passed it consistently, which is the bug class being removed.
6. One internal home for filters. --source and facet clicks desugar into Query.filters at the edge. TUI-DESIGN section 5: fast-resume kept a second source of truth and paid six reconciliation methods.
7. agent: goes live, dir: and date: are surfaced-inactive. The source clause already exists as AND (?4 IS NULL OR c.source = ?4), so Filter::Agent feeds ?4 rather than adding a clause. Without this, deleting SearchOptions.source would silently break --source and the facet bar.
8. New crates/cs-core/src/query.rs. crates/cs/src/query.rs is renamed to commands.rs, since it holds command handlers and no parser.
9. now_ms becomes a required argument to SearchOptions::new. The 0 default silently disables decay.
10. Structural invariant test plus regression table, routed through Query::typeahead and marking_terms rather than query_terms.
11. Five commits, each green.

Parse is infallible, per chat-search-6eb.11 acceptance criteria: a half-typed filter is literal text, never an error.

Deleted: to_match_expr, to_match_expr_opts, snippet, snippet_opts, marking_terms, is_blank, highlight::query_terms, App::holds, App::holding, App::is_blank, state::MIN_QUERY_CHARS, SearchOptions.source. snippet_marked survives with a new signature. highlight::spans and highlight::snippet are untouched, the 6eb.20 scratch-table mechanism is correct.
acceptance_criteria: agent:codex borrow ranks on borrow alone and filters to source=codex. -borrow is not a required term. learn deep learn keeps its prefix star. dir: and date: are carried and surfaced as not-yet-active rather than silently ignored. One structural test asserts match_expr and marking_terms render from the same term list. cargo test --workspace green at every one of the five commits, and cargo build --workspace --all-targets warning-free.
close_reason: Closed

title: Cache the preview layout between frames so scrolling stops rebuilding it
description:
Preview::layout does not depend on scroll, yet every frame rebuilt every row of the conversation to move the viewport a few lines. Measured on the corpus longest conversation: 38.9 ms to lay out 9,261 rows at width 96, of which ~85% is wrapping (6.1 ms at a width nothing can exceed) and 0% is mark-splitting (38.9 with marks vs 38.7 with none). None of that changes as the pane scrolls.

Rows are now cached behind an Rc, keyed on (width, focus, generation). scroll is deliberately absent from the key - that is the entire saving. focus is present because it styles the focused chevron; generation is bumped by every fold and density change. Keyed rather than eagerly cleared so a resize or a fold can never be served rows measured for a different pane.

MEASURED AFTER (same conversation, width 96, 9,261 rows):
  layout, scroll-only frame : 0.0000 ms  (was 38.9 ms)
  layout, cold after a fold : 51 ms      (unchanged - see me9.1.1.11)
  lines() clone for Paragraph: 0.65 ms   (cheap; no borrow rework needed)
Stress harness of 168,000 scroll notches across 7 pane sizes: 67 s -> 17.6 s.

Also checked what ratatui could take over, and it cannot. Paragraph already stops painting at area.height, which is why drawing is only 1.6 ms. Paragraph::wrap(Wrap) would do the wrapping, but with wrap enabled its scroll is O(scroll offset) per frame - paragraph.rs runs next_line() scroll.y times to skip - and it will not report where it broke, so the row-to-message map that clicks and follow_focus need would be lost.
acceptance_criteria: A scroll-only frame reuses the same rows by identity; width, focus, folds and density each rebuild them.
close_reason: Landed 2026-07-30. Scroll-only frames went 38.9 ms -> 0.0000 ms; the stress harness of 168,000 notches across 7 pane sizes went 67 s -> 17.6 s. 364 tests passing, zero warnings.

title: Preview lays out the whole conversation every frame; 43ms on the largest
description:
Separate from me9.1.1.6, which is the one-time open cost. This is per-frame.

render::preview calls p.lines() -> Preview::layout() on every draw, and layout walks the entire conversation building styled, wrapped rows for all of it - then Paragraph::scroll throws away everything outside the viewport. Measured on the largest conversation (1,468 blocks, 942 KB, width 96): 43.4 ms to produce 9,261 rows, of which about 35 are on screen. Painting the frame is 1.6 ms, so essentially all of it is layout.

That is paid on every keystroke and every scroll burst, and on its own it exceeds the 30 ms budget for a conversation of that size. The scroll-burst coalescing in me9.1.1.10 reduced how OFTEN it is paid but not what it costs.

Note the height memoisation added in me9.1.1.10 does not help here: it caches the row COUNT for the scroll clamp, while rendering still needs the rows themselves.
design: Lay out only the visible window. layout() would take (scroll, viewport_rows) and skip blocks whose height puts them off screen - but block heights are exactly what layout computes, so it needs a cheap height pass or a per-block height cache to skip ahead without building rows. Note that block_at_row and follow_focus also read layout(), so whatever shape this takes must keep them reading the same geometry - that single-source property is what me9.1.1.9 established and it must not be traded away for speed.
acceptance_criteria: A frame of the largest conversation lays out in well under the 30ms budget; clicks and scrolling still resolve to the same rows the renderer drew.
notes:
NARROWED by me9.1.1.12 (layout caching), which landed 2026-07-30. Scroll-only frames are now free, so this is no longer a per-frame cost on the hot path.

What remains is the COLD path: the first layout after a fold, a density change, a resize, or selecting a new conversation still builds every row. Measured 51 ms on the corpus longest conversation (9,261 rows at width 96), and ~85% of that is wrapping rows that are never on screen.

Windowing is still the fix and the constraint is unchanged - block_at_row and follow_focus read the same layout, and that single-source property must survive. The cache makes it easier: per-block heights can live beside the cached rows rather than being recomputed to skip ahead.
close_reason:
Closed 2026-07-30 without windowing the layout, which measurement said was the wrong fix.

The 51 ms was not the breadth of the work but a quadratic loop inside it: prefix_end re-measured the whole prefix for every character, ~w²/2 width lookups per row, ~42M over the 9,261 rows of the longest conversation. A printable-ASCII fast path takes layout to 22.6 ms. Selecting that conversation - load, marking and first frame - is now 82 ms against 240 ms before this and the batching in me9.1.1.6; a scroll frame is 2.9 ms p50; the stress harness of 168,000 notches is 4.2 s against 67 s at the start.

Windowing was prototyped far enough to price it. A height-only pass measured 65% of a full layout before the fix and ~43% after, so it would now save ~13 ms on the cold path only, and it would cost the single-source-of-geometry property: block_at_row and follow_focus reading a height derived separately from the rows drawn is exactly the arrangement that put clicks on the wrong message. Not worth it. The scaffolding (text::wrapped_rows) was removed rather than left as unused API.

Reopen if the cold path matters again - the note above records where the remaining time is (SQL read and hydration, ~44 ms).

title: claude-desktop importer for local-agent-mode sessions
description:
Claude Desktop's Cowork and Chat tabs write full transcripts to disk in the clear, and nothing reads them. Surveyed 2026-07-30: ~/Library/Application Support/Claude/local-agent-mode-sessions/<account>/<org>/ holds 14 sessions, 30 MB, 736 assistant + 598 user messages. This is the only dark surface that needs no export, no API, no browser and no credentials — it is the cheapest coverage in the Capture epic.

Earlier notes concluded 'Claude desktop needs export or API' after inspecting IndexedDB alone. That part is right (it is a React Query cache, zero message bodies) but the conclusion was drawn from the wrong directory.

Format detail in docs/FORMAT-NOTES.md, section 'Claude desktop - local agent mode'.
design:
New source id 'claude-desktop' (permanent, ADR 16). Distinct from 'claude-ai', which theme.rs already reserves for the cloud-synced conversations this does NOT cover.

Wiring is the standard five touches: SOURCE const + import fn in crates/cs-import/src/claude_desktop.rs, pub mod in lib.rs, a match arm in crates/cs/src/query.rs::import_source, a detect_sources() candidate in crates/cs-archive/src/config.rs, and a KNOWN_SOURCES entry in crates/cs-tui/src/theme.rs.

Three traps, all measured:
1. The transcript is local_<uuid>/audit.jsonl but title/model/cwd/timestamps live in the SIBLING local_<uuid>.json. Neither is sufficient alone. The importer is a pure fn over (logical_path, bytes), so it cannot read the sibling - either the glob covers both and a second pass folds them on the uuid in the logical path, or titles come from initialMessage in-band. Prefer the fold; it matches how Codex folds threads on session_id.
2. Shape is Agent SDK stream-json, NOT Claude Code JSONL. snake_case session_id/parent_tool_use_id vs camelCase sessionId/parentUuid. Close enough to invite widening the claude-code glob, different enough that doing so imports zero.
3. parent_tool_use_id is not a message parent - it marks subagent messages under a tool call. Feeding it to parent_native_id breaks index::on_head_path, which requires a parent the importer actually emitted. The file is linear; leave parent_native_id as the previous emitted message.

Only 14 of 165 JSON files here are conversation-bearing. Decline by shape the way gemini.rs declines logs.json, not by trusting the glob.
acceptance_criteria: cs index reports a claude-desktop row with a non-zero conversation count against the real archive. Sessions carry a title (not a uuid) and a model. A session directory with no audit.jsonl is skipped without an error. Widening the claude-code glob to these files is shown by test to import zero, so the two importers cannot be collapsed by a later reader.
close_reason:
Implemented and verified end to end against the real archive on 2026-07-30: 106 archived files -> 14 conversations, 1,200 messages, 203 prose, 0 off-head-path. Titles and models land from the state file, timestamps from the audit clock, and cs search returns them under a claude.app badge.

Three findings worth carrying forward, all recorded in docs/FORMAT-NOTES.md:
- A transcript carries TWO session ids and the one matching the directory is the minority holder (19 records vs 405 for the CLI session underneath). Keying on either splits the conversation, so the importer keys on the local_<uuid> path segment.
- Repeated uuids are almost entirely isReplay turns re-emitted on resume, not corruption.
- The acceptance criterion 'widening the claude-code glob imports zero' was WRONG and the test now pins the truth: claude_code::import already accepts both sessionId and session_id, so it parses these files happily and files them under the wrong source with a claude --resume command that cannot reopen a desktop session, and without titles. The failure looks like success, which is the reason to keep two importers.

title: Preview scroll ran to u16::MAX past the end and rebuilt the layout per notch
description:
Reported: scrolling the preview too far makes it "freak out" and the program crashes, leaving a flood of raw SGR mouse reports in the terminal.

Could NOT reproduce a panic. A stress harness drove 168,000 scroll notches to u16 saturation and back across 7 pane sizes (140x40, 116x40, 115x40, 60x12, 20x6, 8x4, 400x100) over 25 conversations of the real index, redrawing through TestBackend and click-mapping every row at each step: no crash. The leaked escape sequences are unread mouse reports still in the tty buffer being echoed by the shell once the app exited, so they say the app went away mid-gesture, not where.

Three real defects found and fixed on the way, two of which fully explain the "freaks out":

1. SCROLL WAS UNBOUNDED. scroll_preview did a saturating_add with no ceiling, so scrolling past the last line kept counting to 65535. The pane went blank with nothing to say how far past the end it was, and getting back meant winding the same distance in reverse. Now clamped to the last screenful via Preview::scroll_by.

2. SCROLLING WAS O(CONVERSATION) PER NOTCH. The clamp needs the rendered height, and laying the whole pane out per notch made a trackpad flick quadratic in conversation length. Memoised on Preview, keyed by width, dropped by every edit that changes what is drawn. The stress run went from >600s to 67s for the same events.

3. ONE UNREADABLE EVENT KILLED THE SESSION. event::read()? sent any error straight out of event_loop, so a single transient parse or I/O failure during a fast scroll threw away the query and tore the session down - which matches the report exactly. Now tolerates up to MAX_MISREADS consecutive failures; a persistently unreadable stream still stops.

Also: the loop redrew once per event, so a flick of hundreds of reports meant hundreds of full renders and the pane crawled behind the finger. It now absorbs a burst of up to BURST queued events into one frame.
acceptance_criteria: Scrolling stops at the end of the conversation and one notch back up is one notch; folding invalidates the cached height; a transient input error does not end the session.
close_reason: Landed 2026-07-30. Fenced blocks render dim behind a two-column rule (section 8 treatment, no dependency; syntect measured at +2.1MB and ~110us/line to colour the 3.9% of prose messages that tag a language). Match highlight takes Color::Blue from the indexed palette - index 4 is the slot Solarized fills with #268BD2, so a Solarized terminal gets that exact hue and every other terminal inherits its own; DIM is subtracted so a match never recedes inside dim snippet or code text. Preview body text now wraps at word boundaries instead of truncating, which forced the real fix: Preview::layout is the single source of geometry, returning each drawn row paired with the message that put it there, so what is drawn, what a click resolves to and what scrolling counts cannot drift. Scroll is clamped to the last screenful, its height memoised per width and invalidated on every fold, and the event loop absorbs an input burst into one frame and survives a transient unreadable event instead of ending the session. Verified against the real 2,980-conversation index and a 168,000-notch stress harness across 7 pane sizes. 363 tests passing (317 at the start of this work), zero warnings.

title: Wrap preview body text instead of truncating each line to the pane
description:
Requested: wrap text in the preview window instead of showing one line and truncating. Long prose is currently unreadable - every source line is cut at the pane width.

Not a rendering-only change. Preview::rendered_rows computed a message height as 2 + line count, which only held while one source line was exactly one terminal row; the click map and follow_focus both counted with it. Wrapping ends that, and a second derivation of the same geometry would drift the moment a line wrapped - invisibly, until a click folded the wrong message. The old block_at_row comment called this out as the hazard.

Fixed structurally: Preview::layout is now the single source of geometry, returning each drawn row paired with the message that put it there. lines(), block_at_row() and follow_focus() all read it, so what is drawn, what a click resolves to and what scrolling counts cannot disagree. Callers pass the pane inner width via render::preview_body_width, because resolving a click at any other width wraps differently and counts a row that is not on screen.
acceptance_criteria: A long paragraph occupies several rows and every one resolves to its own message; a narrow pane needs more rows than a wide one; the gutter rule repeats down every wrapped row of a fenced block.
close_reason: Landed 2026-07-30. Scroll is clamped to the last screenful, its height memoised per width and invalidated on every fold, and the event loop absorbs an input burst into one frame and survives a transient unreadable event instead of ending the session. Verified against the real 2,980-conversation index and a 168,000-notch stress harness across 7 pane sizes. 363 tests passing (317 at the start of this work), zero warnings.

title: Collapsed prose shows the matching line, and the preview anchors on the best hit
description:
Two halves of the same idea: put the reason the row is here in front of the user without making them scroll.

MATCHING LINE. Section 8 specs collapsed prose as 'role sigil + the MATCHING line, else the first non-empty line'. preview.rs:304 first_line() always takes the first non-empty. This is the whole reason section 8 argues outline mode beats a density knob — 'you see every place the query hit, across the whole conversation, in conversation order'. Today outline mode is a table of contents, not a match map.

ANCHORING. Preview::load hardcodes focus: 0, scroll: 0, so selecting a result always opens at message 1 rather than the message that matched.

TRAP: do NOT anchor on g.hits[0]. state.rs:123 runs search_grouped(.., 0) — no snippets per keystroke — so hits are empty until the row is expanded with Tab, and anchoring would silently work only on expanded rows. Anchor on Group::match_seqs (search.rs:526), which IS populated at nested=0; it already drives the density strip.
acceptance_criteria: Outline mode over a matching conversation shows the matching line of each matching message; selecting a result opens the preview at a matching message, including for a collapsed (un-Tabbed) row; a conversation with no matches still opens at the top.
close_reason: Landed 2026-07-30. Highlighting now runs end to end: Hit carries snippet_spans (additive, ADR 12 intact), text::marked_runs/truncate_runs render styled runs truncated by display column, and the preview marks message bodies and collapsed lines from marks located once per (conversation, query) at load. Collapsed prose shows the line the query hit, so outline mode is a match map rather than a table of contents. The preview anchors on a matching message — from the marks, NOT Group::match_seqs, whose flat message positions cannot be resolved against the thread-contiguous order the pane draws in. sync_preview now keys on (conv_id, terms), which fixes marks going stale on a still-selected row as the query is edited. Clicking a message header line folds it, clicking body text only moves focus; the line->block map derives from the same rendered_rows the keyboard scrolls by, and PREVIEW_HEADER_LINES replaces the duplicated header offset. Fold chevron now carries fold state with focus as its style, resolving the collision where the results pane spent arrows on fold state and the preview spent one on focus. Verified end to end against a real 2,980-conversation / 175,988-message index: stemmed and prefix matches mark correctly. 347 tests passing (317 baseline), zero warnings. Remaining eager-marking cost is chat-search-me9.1.1.6.

title: Preview highlights message bodies; marks computed once per message, never per line
description:
preview.rs:222-225 defers highlighting to 6eb.20, which is now CLOSED — the blocker is gone. Preview::lines() does not take the query terms yet.

Two traps:

1. COST. highlight::spans costs ~25us FIXED per call (delete+insert+match on the scratch fts5 table) plus ~60ns/byte. Calling it per body line means a 500-line message pays 12.5ms of fixed cost before scanning a byte. Call it ONCE per message on the whole text and walk the byte offsets against line boundaries — the same one-pass trick highlight::snippet already uses at highlight.rs:187-199.

2. STALENESS. state::sync_preview early-returns when wanted == have (state.rs:202), so the preview is NOT reloaded when the query changes, only when the selected conversation changes. Marks computed at load would go stale on the next keystroke while the row stays selected.

render::preview calls p.lines() every frame — every keystroke, every wheel notch — so marks must not be recomputed there (docs/TUI-DESIGN.md section 8, 'build once, not per frame').
acceptance_criteria: Typing another character updates the marks on an already-selected conversation; spans() is called at most once per message per (conversation, query); a stemmed hit (commits/commit, learning/learned, cafe/cafe) is marked in the preview body.

Fold chevron now carries fold state with focus as its style, resolving the collision where the results pane spent arrows on fold state and the preview spent one on focus. Remaining eager-marking cost is chat-search-me9.1.1.6.

title: Span-aware line building and truncation in cs-tui::text
description:
render::cell() writes one Paragraph with one Style, truncated by text::truncate_end. Highlighted text is a list of styled runs that must be truncated to N DISPLAY COLUMNS while the match offsets are BYTES. Needed by both the results hit rows and the preview body, so it belongs in text.rs where every fits-a-cell rule already lives.

Two pure functions: split text at byte spans into styled ratatui spans, and truncate a styled span list to a display width with the same ellipsis convention truncate_end uses. Note the name collision between cs_core::highlight::Span (byte offsets) and ratatui::text::Span (styled run).
acceptance_criteria: Multibyte and CJK text truncates by display column, never by byte or char count; a span cut by the truncation keeps its style on the surviving part; spans out of order or out of bounds do not panic.

title: Hit carries its snippet spans; results rows draw the match
description:
search::snippet_opts calls highlight::snippet, which returns (String, Vec<Span>), uses the spans only for an is_empty() check and drops them (search.rs:151-158). Hit.snippet is a bare String, so the results list cannot highlight — the information is not in the struct. Carrying the spans is free: they are already computed on every snippet built.

Hit derives Serialize and its field names are a JSON contract (ADR 12), so this must be ADDITIVE: keep snippet: String, add a spans field. Do not restructure snippet into a struct. UNLOCATED (search.rs:115) stays — it is the CLI/JSON channel and the eval harness reads it; the spans are the TUI channel, not a replacement.
acceptance_criteria: Hit exposes the byte spans of its snippet; snippet string unchanged; UNLOCATED behaviour unchanged; cs search --json still emits every existing field with the same name.
close_reason: Landed 2026-07-30 together with me9.1.1.2, which it was marked as depending on and which is now closed. Hit gained snippet_spans (additive; the JSON contract in ADR 12 is intact and asserted by a test naming all 14 pre-existing keys), snippet_marked keeps the offsets snippet_opts was discarding, and render::hit_row draws them through cell_runs so the match is marked in the results list. Verified against a real index: cs search --json emits the spans and they slice out the stemmed, diacritic-folded and prefix-matched words.

title: Highlighting re-indexes every message it marks; external-content fts5 would make it free
description:
highlight::spans agrees with the ranker by handing the message text to a throwaway in-memory
fts5 table declared with the same tokenizer and reading SQLite's own highlight(). Correct, and
it pays an insert per snippet.

Measured, release, against the 172k-message index: ~25 us fixed plus ~60 ns per byte of
message. search_grouped at TUI settings (limit 50 x MAX_HITS 3 = 150 snippets), nested=0 ->
nested=3: `borrow` 0.3 -> 11 ms, `learning` 6.4 -> 36 ms, `deep learning` 1.9 -> 29 ms, `pro`
30 -> 46 ms, `the` 61 -> 84 ms. The substring scan it replaced did the same 150 in 0.3-1.9 ms.
So this is a 10-25 ms addition per keystroke, and `learning` crosses the 30 ms budget of
chat-search-me9.1 on it.

The cost is the insert, not the matching. On a row already resident in the table, highlight()
is 8 us for a small message and 373 us for the largest prose message in the corpus (104 KB) —
against 1.5 ms to insert that same message.
design:
fts_prose and fts_tools are declared content='' (contentless), which is why the SQL
highlight()/snippet() auxiliary functions cannot be used against the index itself and a
scratch table is needed at all.

External content — content='message', content_rowid='rowid' — stores no more than contentless
does (it reads the column back from `message` on demand), and `message` is already joined by
rowid on every ranking query. highlight() would then run against the real index with no
insert: ~10-15 us per snippet, so ~2 ms for a full TUI keystroke instead of 11-36 ms.

Costs: schema change plus an IMPORTER_VERSION bump and a reindex, which ADR 1 / ADR 3 make the
sanctioned response. The fts column name must match the message column name — both are `text`,
so it already does. Postings are written explicitly by the importer today, which external
content also expects, so no triggers are needed.

Verify by re-running the numbers above. The invariant test
`every_row_the_ranker_returns_has_something_to_highlight` must keep passing.
acceptance_criteria: Locating a match is no longer the reason any keystroke misses the 30 ms budget of chat-search-me9.1, and every returned row still locates its own match. Measured at limit 50 / nested 3 over the candidate sets search_grouped really builds: marking costs 2.4-17.7 ms, down from 10.7-29.1 ms, with 100% of returned rows marked.
notes:
branch: worktree-bead-6eb30-external-content
Acceptance criterion rewritten 2026-08-01, by the owner's decision on gate chat-search-6m9. It read: 'search_grouped at limit 50 / nested 3 costs no more than ~2 ms of snippet time on the queries measured above, with every returned row still locating its match.'

The ~2 ms half was not achievable and is not a tuning problem. Every way of saying which words of a message matched has to tokenize that message; the floor is ~28 ns/byte, and the candidate set at limit 50 / nested 3 is 60-680 KB, so 2-18 ms. The ~2 ms estimate came from this bead's own design, which extrapolated the 8 us figure for a small already-resident message; real result sets average 2-18 KB per message. 2 ms is reachable only for small sets - 'commit' does hit 2.4 ms.

The second half of the criterion was kept verbatim, and holds: 100% of returned rows locate their match, across all twelve query/mode combinations measured.

Do not re-file the 2 ms target against a cleverer marking strategy. The remaining lever is not marking at all - it is the prefix expansion that dominates 'pro' (29.4 ms) and 'the' (59.3 ms) at nested=0, before a snippet exists. That is chat-search-6eb.38 and chat-search-6eb.29.
close_reason: Merged to work/2026-07-30 as 613dac6 after review. Acceptance criterion rewritten (gate chat-search-6m9, reading (a)): marking is off the critical path — 10.7-29.1 ms to 2.4-17.7 ms at limit 50 / nested 3 — rather than the unreachable ~2 ms. Verified beyond the branch's own gate: full-corpus rebuild of 3,019 conversations / 180,564 messages in 7.3 s on the new schema, exact and prefix searches both locate their matches, and explain's indexed_prose reports 396 against 2,553 messages where the old count would have inflated it. 462 tests green, warning-free --all-targets.

title: Log what was searched for and what was opened
description: Ground truth the eval set cannot invent. 'cs search' appends query + returned ids + latency; 'cs pick <conv_id> --query <text>' appends the selection with its rank; 'cs needs' folds the log into one row per distinct query. cs-fzf carries conv_id as a hidden field and calls 'cs pick' on selection.
design:
Log at <archive_root>/queries.jsonl, append-only. Deliberately NOT in index.db: index.db is a pure function of the archive and can be deleted at will, while this cannot be reconstructed from anything and wants backing up. First authored data the project keeps, and the first thing that will move into library.db (chat-search-6eb.14).

Typeahead is excluded — '--prefix' fires once per keystroke, so logging it would bury the handful of real queries under every prefix of each. Clients doing typeahead record the finished query via 'cs pick' instead, which is why cs-fzf uses fzf's --print-query.

'cs pick' recomputes the result list rather than being handed it, because the caller is a shell script holding one chosen line. Costs a few ms and keeps the recorded rank honest about what the ranking would actually return.

A pick with rank=None is kept, not dropped: it means the conversation was reached some other way, and discarding those would bias the log toward things that already ranked well.

Writes never fail the operation they describe — a search that cannot write its log line still returns results.
acceptance_criteria: Searches and picks are recorded; 'cs needs' shows queries with their picks and ranks; log_queries=false in config suppresses everything; a corrupt line costs that line and not the history.
close_reason: Landed 2026-07-30. cs-core/src/querylog.rs (Event, append, load, needs — 6 synthetic tests), Config::query_log() + log_queries, 'cs pick', 'cs needs', search logging in query.rs, cs-fzf wired via --print-query and a hidden conv_id field. Verified end to end against the real index: rank-3 pick recorded as rank=3, opt-out honoured.

title: Preview pane: fold model, collapsed tool traffic, outline mode
description:
The preview is what answers 'is this the one I meant', and it is a separable chunk of chat-search-me9.1 rather than a detail of it. Spec: docs/TUI-DESIGN.md §8.

Renders from message rows, never from a flattened blob — we have role, kind, seq, parent_id, on_head_path, so none of fast-resume's prose-sniffing heuristics are needed.

**Revised 2026-07-30 from first real use of the TUI.** The placeholder preview shipped in me9.1 is 'not all that useful' — the gap list, in the user's words:

1. **No way to expand/collapse messages.** Needs expand-all / collapse-all AND per-message toggling. Currently every message is fixed at whatever the renderer chose.
2. **Both user and agent messages are interesting.** Do not privilege user turns; an assistant answer is often the thing being looked for.
3. **Highlight the hits inside the message text.** Currently only the row-level snippet exists, so within a long message there is nothing showing why it matched. Depends on chat-search-6eb.20 — a substring highlighter disagrees with the stemmed ranker.
4. **Show where in a long conversation the visible part sits.** The row-level ten-cell density strip answers this for the list; the preview needs its own version — a position indicator, or the outline mode already specced, so scrolling has context.
5. **Tool responses omitted entirely, tool calls collapsed.** This REVISES the spec, which had both collapsed to one line. The result is a blob whose existence the call already implies. Keep the exception for a FAILED tool result: 'the tool broke here' is recognition information and should stay legible in the error colour.

Original three pieces stand: the fold model, tool traffic collapsed by default, and outline mode. Item 1 above is the fold model's per-message override; item 4 is what outline mode is for.
design:
Block { msg_id, role, kind, on_path, collapsed: Vec<Line>, expanded: Vec<Line> }, with Fold { Auto, Collapsed, Expanded } per message and Density { Full, Outline } pane-wide. Blocks carry provenance (which message, on-path or not) because the off-path branch display needs it — see docs/TUI-DESIGN.md §7.

No hand-rolled syntax highlighting. fast-resume spends ~150 lines on it and it is barely language-aware — the keyword list is a flat union across languages, so 'def' highlights inside JavaScript. Render fenced blocks dim, keep the match highlight applied inside them, stop.

Keymap constraint: the search box consumes every unmodified keystroke, so each command costs a modifier. Ctrl+O cycles density; the per-message fold override needs a second key and that choice is still open.

Depends on chat-search-6eb.20: highlighting must come from the same tokenizer that ranked, or a stemmed hit highlights nothing.
acceptance_criteria: Preview renders from a message-row query, not a parsed blob; a multi-paragraph user message keeps its role throughout. Tool calls and results render as one collapsed line by default, expand on override, and auto-expand when the hit came from fts_tools. A failed tool result is legible while collapsed. Outline mode collapses every turn to one line and prefers the matching line, so every hit in the conversation is visible on one screen. Blocks are built once per (conv, query, density, folds), not per frame. Match highlighting agrees with the ranker on a stemmed query.
notes: 2026-07-30: user feedback after driving the shipped placeholder preview. Their item 5 is a genuine correction to docs/TUI-DESIGN.md §8, which specced tool_result as a collapsed one-liner — omit it instead, keeping only failures. Update the doc when this lands.
close_reason: All five revised items verified in the merged code and exercised end to end under a pty on 2026-08-04. (1) toggle_all/toggle_focused with ctrl-e and alt-enter, plus click-on-header; (2) speaker() draws user and assistant alike, subagent turns labelled; (3) in-text marks from cs_core::highlight, ranked and unranked told apart by a text modifier so NO_COLOR still distinguishes them; (4) Density::Outline plus position(); (5) drawn() omits successful tool_result and keeps failures, now cs_core::blocks::drawn shared by every client. The fold model and outline mode moved to cs-core under me9.17.

title: snippet() substring-matches a Porter-stemmed index, so stemmed hits show the wrong text
description:
fts_prose and fts_tools tokenize with `porter unicode61 remove_diacritics 2` (crates/cs-core/src/schema.rs:54-57), but snippet() locates the match with a raw substring scan — `lower.find(t)` at crates/cs-core/src/search.rs:93. The two disagree for every term whose stem differs from the literal text in the message.

When find() misses, `at` is None, start falls back to 0, and the leading ellipsis is omitted (search.rs:97-107) — so the snippet renders the first 160 chars of the message as though that were the match site. It looks like a deliberate summary, not a fallback. Wrong output presented as correct output.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Index a conversation whose prose reads `Commit current changes`.
2. `cs search commits` — Porter stems both `commits` and `commit` to `commit`, so the row ranks and appears.
3. The snippet shows the head of the message with no ellipsis, and the matching word is not in it. Same for `learning` against text containing `learned`, and any plural/gerund/past-tense pair.
4. `remove_diacritics 2` adds a smaller case: query `cafe` matches text `café`, find() does not.

The existing test only covers a literal exact term (`snippet_centres_on_the_first_matching_term`, search.rs:303), which is why this is uncovered.

## Also wrong: the term set

snippet() splits the raw query string, so once the query DSL lands (chat-search-6eb.11) `agent:codex learning` contributes `agent` and `codex` as snippet anchors. fast-resume already solved this — see is_search_filter_token in its tui/preview.rs:462-467. Strip filter tokens before deriving snippet terms.

Blocks any correct match highlighting in the TUI preview (chat-search-me9.1), and chat-search-6eb.10 fuzzy-on-failure would make it total: a fuzzy hit never substring-matches.
design:
Contentless fts5 rules out the SQL snippet() and highlight() auxiliary functions — they need reconstructable content — so hand-rolling is forced, not a shortcut. The fix is to match at token level with the same rules the index uses: tokenize the message text (unicode61 + diacritic folding), Porter-stem each token, and mark tokens whose stem is in the query's stem set. That yields both the anchor position and the highlight spans from one pass, and it stays correct when fuzzy matching lands (compare edit distance on stems rather than raw text).

Anchor on the best match rather than the earliest. Both this code and fast-resume take min(position), so one incidental early mention beats the dense cluster later in a long conversation. search_grouped already ranks per message before grouping, so the best-hit message is known at hydrate time — use it.
acceptance_criteria: A query whose term stems to a different surface form than the text renders a snippet centred on the actual matching token, with the token marked. Filter keywords from the query DSL never act as snippet anchors. A snippet that genuinely cannot locate a match says so rather than silently rendering the head of the message. Tests cover a plural, a gerund, and a diacritic case, not only a literal exact term.
notes:
Weight increased 2026-07-30 without the bug changing. The eval sheet (chat-search-6eb.9) shows exactly one snippet per candidate as the primary evidence for a grade — the design deliberately chose one accurate snippet plus a match-position strip over three noisy ones. So a snippet that shows the wrong span for a stemmed hit no longer just looks scruffy in a result list; it means a relevance judgement gets made against text that is not what matched, and that judgement then becomes ground truth for tuning.

Same applies to the harvested log (chat-search-6eb.21): a pick is a vote cast on what the row showed.

Fix this before any serious judging pass.
close_reason:
Landed 2026-07-30. Highlighting now asks SQLite rather than re-implementing Porter — a scratch fts5 table declared with the identical tokenizer, so agreement with the ranker is structural rather than hoped for. The agent measured the alternative before rejecting it: over the 30,000 most frequent words of the real corpus, SQLite's porter and rust-stemmers' Porter2 disagree on 1,140 words (3.8%), and of ~21.7k word pairs one stemmer groups, 1,425 are grouped by only one of them — the same bug class being fixed.

Decisive test: every_row_the_ranker_returns_has_something_to_highlight builds an in-memory index and asserts, for commits/'Commit current changes', learning/'I learned about', running/'runs', cafe/'café' and general/'generated', that the ranker returns the row AND the highlighter marks something. Held for all 789 rows across six queries against the real corpus.

Also: spans honour a trailing prefix star, read back off to_match_expr_opts rather than re-derived, so a typeahead query does not label every in-progress word unmatched. An unlocatable match is now labelled rather than silently rendering the head of the message, which was the original defect.

Cost: snippet building is 5-20x the ranking, because each one inserts its message into the scratch table. Mitigated in the TUI by deferring snippets to expansion (nested=0 per keystroke); the structural fix is chat-search-6eb.30.

title: Codex IDE context block leaks into 224 titles
description:
The Codex VS Code extension prepends a markdown context block to user turns — `# Context from my IDE setup:`
with `## Active file:`, `## Open tabs:`, and sometimes `## My request for Codex:` carrying the
real prose INSIDE it. It reaches the title verbatim on 198 conversations (6.7% of the
corpus). A related `# Files mentioned by the user:` block accounts for 26 more. 224 total.

Found while fixing chat-search-n58.3, which covered a different and smaller set (5 patterns,
37 conversations, 1.3%). This is 5x the blast radius of that bug.

Not pseudo-XML and not slash-command markup, so neither the claude_code strip_injected_markup
literal tag scan nor the new codex is_command_line/unwrap_skill_links handles it. Needs its
own rule: a markdown-heading-structured prelude, where the useful prose may be nested under a
`## My request for Codex:` subheading rather than following the block.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. `cs index`
2. `cs search` with a blank query to list recent conversations, or search for
   `Context from my IDE setup`.
3. 198 conversation headers begin with `# Context from my IDE setup:` followed by
   `## Active file:` / `## Open tabs:`; 26 more begin with `# Files mentioned by the user:`.
   In the subset carrying `## My request for Codex:`, the prose that should have been the
   title is visible further down the same block.
design: Distinct from n58.3's patterns — deliberately left out of that fix rather than bolted on. The prelude is structured markdown, so the rule is heading-aware rather than tag-literal. Note the recovery case: when '## My request for Codex:' is present the real prose is inside the block, so this cannot simply drop the block wholesale the way DROPPED_TAGS does.
acceptance_criteria: No conversation title begins with '# Context from my IDE setup:' or '# Files mentioned by the user:'. Where '## My request for Codex:' is present, the title is the prose from inside it. Synthetic tests only.

title: Move client-shared helpers out of the cs binary into cs-core
description: default_db(), now_ms() and local date formatting all live in crates/cs/src/query.rs, but every client needs them. Any second client either duplicates them or reaches into the binary. The date rule already exists in three places: ymd() in the binary, a strflocaltime call in the cs-fzf jq, and implicitly in anything a future client writes. Prerequisite for the native TUI (chat-search-me9.1) and for any non-Rust client.
design: Move into cs-core (or cs-archive for the config-dependent path resolution). render_groups() deliberately stays in the binary: that is terminal presentation and the TUI wants its own. Fixing the UTC date bug (chat-search-6eb.8) should happen as part of this move rather than separately, so the corrected rule lands in one place instead of three.
acceptance_criteria: default_db(), now_ms() and local date formatting live in cs-core (or cs-archive for the config-dependent path resolution) and crates/cs/src/query.rs calls them rather than defining them. render_groups() deliberately stays in the binary — that is terminal presentation and the TUI wants its own. The date rule exists in exactly one place: ymd() in the binary and the strflocaltime call in the cs-fzf jq are both gone. The bundled chat-search-6eb.8 fix is included, so an evening-local conversation renders its local civil date. A second Rust client can link cs-core and get all three without touching the binary.
notes: Dependency call for the bundled 6eb.8 fix is DECIDED: chrono, converting to local at the parse boundary. Full rationale on chat-search-6eb.8's design field. Practical consequence for this move: the helper that lands in cs-core is a *formatting* function over an already-local DateTime, not a function that does timezone math — which is what lets the date rule genuinely live in one place instead of three.
close_reason: Verified: Config::default_db() in cs-archive, now_ms()/local_ymd()/ymd_in() in cs-core::time re-exported from cs-core, query.rs calls all three rather than defining them, render_groups() deliberately still in the binary, cs-fzf reads ended_date. Bundled 6eb.8 fix included.

title: fzf stopgap client for ranking evaluation
description: scripts/cs-fzf plus scripts/cs-fzf.sh. fzf used purely as a renderer: --disabled turns off its own filtering and change:reload re-runs cs search per keystroke, so ranking stays ours. Exists to make the eval set (chat-search-6eb.9) practical to build long before a native TUI lands. Measured 8-26 ms per keystroke on a 168k-message index, of which 1.4-6.4 ms is the query and the rest is spawning cs and jq.
design: Launching the agent from inside the script proved fragile: fzf stdin is a pipe, and both become() and a plain exec left Claude Code unable to read keystrokes and Codex panicking in crossterm with "reader source not set". Final shape prints the command on stdout and lets the caller run it — csf() as a sourced shell function, or --run for a direct exec with no shell in between. ChatGPT rows resume via a URL rather than a command, so fmt rewrites those to open "<url>"; that rewrite is a workaround living in jq and should be deleted once chat-search-me9.3 lands.
close_reason: Shipped scripts/cs-fzf and scripts/cs-fzf.sh. Opens on recent conversations, live search per keystroke, csf() and --run both verified under a pty to give the launched agent a tty on all three fds.

title: Synthetic golden-file fixtures
description: A Codex subagent thread, a declared fork, a renamed session, a ChatGPT edit-branch. Must be synthetic: real transcripts contain secrets, and without them the repo can never be shared.
design: Hand-authored, not captured-and-scrubbed. Scrubbing a real transcript leaves you asserting that you found every secret, which is unfalsifiable and only has to be wrong once; authoring from scratch makes the claim structural. Keep each fixture minimal — the smallest file that still exhibits the structure under test — so a golden diff points at one behaviour instead of a wall of noise. These are the fixtures every other parser bug (chat-search-n58.6, n58.7, n58.13, n58.14) will need, so shape them for reuse rather than per-issue.
acceptance_criteria: Fixtures exist for a Codex subagent thread, a declared fork, a renamed session, and a ChatGPT edit-branch, each with a golden expected-output file. Every byte is synthetic — a grep of the fixture tree for real paths, hostnames, API-key shapes and the machine UUID returns nothing. Each importer's test suite runs against them, and a deliberate regression in the importer fails the golden diff rather than passing silently.
close_reason:
Landed 2026-07-30. Four synthetic cases under crates/cs-import/tests/fixtures — a Codex subagent thread (two rollouts sharing a session_id, exercising per-file ordinals that would collide unscoped), a declared fork, a renamed Claude Code session (custom-title over ai-title over first user turn), and a ChatGPT edit-branch whose node carries a deliberately disagreeing metadata.parent_id so the edge must come from the node's own parent. Goldens regenerate with CS_UPDATE_GOLDEN=1 and serialise through the model's own Serialize, so a new field lands in every golden rather than going uncovered.

The synthetic-content guard (7 tests) scans inputs and goldens for non-invented home dirs, any UUID-shaped string, 14 credential prefixes, emails, .local hostnames, and the live values of HOME/USER/HOSTNAME. Verified independently by poisoning the tree with a real path and an sk- key: 3 of 7 tests failed naming file, line and the offending substring, and passed again once removed. No file under crates/*/src was touched. 98 tests in cs-import.

title: resume_cmd is the wrong shape for open it somewhere
description: It is a string format!ed inside each importer and frozen into a column, so it can express exactly one way to reopen a conversation. The stated core use case is web / native app / VS Code / terminal, and one string cannot hold four. It is also not a property of the conversation — it is a property of (source, native_id) evaluated now, so a CLI syntax change staleness-bombs every row until reindex.
design: Resolve at display time from the source and native_id columns (both already present, both stable per ADR 2) via one table of open targets per source. Compare fast-resume resume_command(&self, session, yolo) -> Vec<String>: a method, computed late, and already carrying one variant axis.
acceptance_criteria: The resume_cmd column is gone from the conversations table. A reopen target is computed at display time from (source, native_id) — both already present and stable per ADR 2 — via one table of open targets per source. It returns more than one variant: at minimum a terminal command, plus web / native app / editor where the source supports them. Changing a CLI's resume syntax takes effect with no reindex. cs search --json emits the variants as structured data, not one pre-rendered string, so a GUI picks rather than parses (ADR 12).
notes:
New consumer as of 2026-07-30: 'cs pick <conv_id> --query <text>' records the selection for the query log (chat-search-6eb.22) and prints resume_cmd, so a client can pipe through it and get the string it already had with the pick recorded on the way past. cs-fzf now does exactly that.

Relevant to the redesign in two ways. It is one more caller to migrate whenever resume_cmd stops being a single frozen string. And it is probably where 'open it somewhere' belongs: the selection point is already the place that knows which conversation was chosen and is already being asked to produce a way to open it. A 'cs pick --in vscode|web|terminal' shape would satisfy this issue and the logging at once.
close_reason: Landed. conversation.resume_cmd is gone (IMPORTER_VERSION 2->3); cs_core::destinations(source, native_id) -> Vec<Destination> resolves at action time from the two columns ADR 2 makes permanent. Destination is a typed enum (Terminal{argv} | Web{url}), so the http:// sniff and the whitespace command-line split both died with the string. cs search --json emits the variants as structure (ADR 12); cs pick gains --in terminal|web and fails naming what a source does offer. Verified against the real 3,002-conversation corpus: changing the table and rebuilding changed the rendered line with the index untouched, which is the staleness claim the bead was filed on. Not demonstrated: more than one variant for any single source — the type admits it, but no current source has both a terminal and a web surface, and inventing unverified URL schemes was declined. Adding one is a line in the table.

title: Query DSL parsed out of the search string
description: agent:claude,codex / -agent:codex / dir:!web-app / date:<3h / date:today. A TUI has one input box, so filters have to live in the query text; flags like --source do not survive the move off the CLI.
design: fast-resume query.rs is 273 lines including tests and is worth reading before writing ours. Handle the date arithmetic in civil time — adding 24h across a DST boundary lands on the wrong day.
acceptance_criteria: agent:claude,codex / -agent:codex / dir:!web-app / date:<3h / date:today all parse out of a single input string and filter results. A malformed or half-typed filter token is searched as literal text rather than erroring — mid-word is the normal state in a typeahead, so a parse error is a broken UI. Date arithmetic is civil-time, with a test proving a next-day boundary is 82,800 s across spring-forward and 90,000 s across fall-back. One parser serves both the CLI and the TUI, so filters survive the move off the CLI where --source cannot. Keystroke cost stays inside the budget on me9.1's revisit trigger.
notes:
DONE 2026-07-31, commit 72e0a11 on branch worktree-bead-6eb11-query-dsl (local only — this repo has no git remote).

WHAT LANDED. Filter carries a parsed value instead of a string. agent:/dir: split on commas into a Selection of includes and excludes, with prefix -agent:x and inline agent:!x folded together at parse time so the SQL never learns which spelling arrived. date: parses to a DateSpec resolved against the caller's clock. Repeated tokens of one facet union; repeated date: tokens intersect, so date:>1d date:<1w is a range. One renderer, search::filter_sql, feeds all three call sites (flat, grouped, and the recency fallback), so they cannot drift the way the two term extractors did.

recent() is filtered too, which it was not before: date:today with no search terms is a real question and the old code dropped every filter but the source.

CIVIL TIME. cs_core::time gained day_start_in, shift_days_in, shift_months_in. d/w/mo/y are calendar steps; m/h are durations. Tests pin a civil day across a DST boundary at 82,800 s (spring forward, 2026-03-08) and 90,000 s (fall back, 2026-11-01) in America/Los_Angeles. A wall clock that never happened — Havana springs forward at 00:00, so 2026-03-08 has no midnight — resolves forward into its own day rather than failing.

MEASURED, real 2,976-conversation index, 2026-07-31:
  dir:personal-site       122 hits, all in that cwd; case-insensitive (dir:PERSONAL-SITE identical)
  dir:personal-site (no terms, recency path)  128 — exactly the corpus count for that cwd
  date:yesterday          15 — exactly the corpus count for 2026-07-30
  date:today              0 — correct, the index was built 2026-07-30
  -agent:claude-code      drops 16 of 18 hits, leaving the 2 chatgpt-export
  date:nope               does not filter, reported in unapplied_filters

COST. Measured in-process (the CLI's numbers are meaningless here — it opens a 306 MB db per invocation, which made a filter look 4x more expensive than it is). Best of seven at TUI settings, limit 50 nested 3: worst filter overhead 0.8 ms, and most filters make a keystroke cheaper by narrowing it. The unfiltered baselines in that run are 36 ms for 'borrow checker' and 87 ms for 'the' — both already over me9.1's 30 ms budget, both untouched by this, and both are chat-search-6eb.29 and chat-search-6eb.30. search::filter_cost keeps the measurement runnable: CS_INDEX=<path> cargo test --release -p cs-core --lib filter_cost -- --ignored --nocapture

TWO THINGS FOUND ON THE WAY.
1. clap ate any query starting with '-', so -agent:codex — a form named in the acceptance criteria — failed outright with 'unexpected argument -a'. Fixed with allow_hyphen_values on cs search and cs explain. Worth knowing this was invisible until the DSL made a leading dash meaningful.
2. My first SQL-level date tests passed on this machine and were zone-dependent: they anchored fixtures at a literal offset from local midnight while NOW is a fixed instant, so the distance between them varied with the machine's offset. Rewritten to derive fixtures through the same day_start/shift_days rules the filter resolves through, then verified green under UTC, America/New_York, America/Los_Angeles, Asia/Kathmandu (+5:45), Pacific/Kiritimati (+14), Etc/GMT+12 and Australia/Lord_Howe.

API CHANGE. unapplied() -> rejected(), and it narrows: every filter the parser accepts now applies, so the only thing left to report is a value nothing can select on. The published unapplied_filters JSON key keeps its name (ADR 12). recent()'s signature takes &Query and now_ms. source_filter() is gone, replaced by selection(Facet).

VERIFICATION. 420 tests pass, zero warnings under cargo build --workspace --all-targets. 8 of the 10 new SQL-level tests fail when filter_sql is stubbed to return an empty string, so they are discriminating rather than green by construction.

NOT DONE, deliberately, each now its own issue: quoted values (dir:"my project") is chat-search-6eb.34; the TUI's parallel App.source field is chat-search-me9.16; the live syntax highlighting and ghost-text completion from docs/TUI-DESIGN.md §5 belong to chat-search-me9.15, whose stale 'there is no DSL yet' premise has been corrected.

docs/TUI-DESIGN.md §5's sequencing note was stale and is rewritten: it said the DSL was blocked and unavailable at TUI v1, which stopped being true when the 6eb.26 dependency was removed on 2026-07-30.
REBASED AND REVIEWED 2026-07-31. Landed on work/2026-07-30 as commit faf895b, not 72e0a11 — the branch worktree-bead-6eb11-query-dsl forked from 36ca274, before the destinations refactor (chat-search-me9.3), and the two had rewritten the same five SELECT sites. Conflict resolved by taking the filter_sql structure with c.resume_cmd -> c.native_id throughout; search() also lost its standalone source_filter() bind, which filter_sql now subsumes. 435 tests green, zero warnings.

Independently verified against the real 3,003-conversation index rather than taken from the notes above: agent:codex rust = 5 codex; agent:codex,chatgpt-export rust = 21 = 5 + 16, matching the unfiltered split exactly; dir:chat-search and dir:CHAT-SEARCH both 43; dir:chat_search = 0, so the underscore is escaped; date:today = 7 and date:yesterday = 35, both exactly the corpus counts for those civil days; -date:today = 2996 = 3003 - 7, so the 2 rows with a NULL ended_at survived the negation. The claim that the tests discriminate also holds: stubbing filter_sql to return an empty string fails 9 tests. filter_cost re-run on this machine reports worst filter overhead 0.0 ms.

One caveat on the acceptance criterion about keystroke budget: the filters themselves cost nothing and usually save time by narrowing, but the unfiltered baselines are 50-83 ms on this machine, still over me9.1's 30 ms. That is chat-search-6eb.29 and chat-search-6eb.30, untouched by this work.

Review found one defect, fixed in 4bc8883 as chat-search-6eb.36: cs explain did not know a filter could be why a conversation was missing, so it blamed the tokenizer. chat-search-6eb.37 files the dir: case-folding mismatch, latent.
close_reason: Implemented and verified against the real corpus; commit 72e0a11.

title: Native TUI
description: scripts/cs-fzf is the stopgap: fzf as a pure renderer, change:reload re-running cs search per keystroke. 8-26 ms per keystroke on a 168k-message index. A native TUI is worth ~300-400 lines and buys the 1.4-6.4 ms query cost without the cs + jq spawn.
design:
Full spec: docs/TUI-DESIGN.md (written 2026-07-29/30 after reading fast-resume v2.5.0 source). Crate boundary, layout bands and breakpoints, the row model, titles, filter surface, destinations, colour discipline and the preview pane all live there.
