title: No CI: the gate runs only where the branch was written
description:
There is no .github/ in this repository, so the gate — `cargo test --workspace` and a warning-free `cargo build --workspace --all-targets` — runs only on the machine that wrote the branch, against that branch alone. Nothing ever compiles two branches together until a human merges them.

Measured on 2026-08-04, when four branches were open at once:

  me9.27 x me9.28      index_state undocumented        caught by the contract test, after merging
  o1i.5 x me9.27       Group.sitting undocumented      caught by the contract test, after merging
  n58.25 x a7k.29      Message.model fixture shape     caught only by a hand test-merge
  n58.25 x me9.36.1    two ADRs numbered 23            caught only by diffing the branches by hand
  o1i.5 x me9.36.1     the fold landed on the ranked   caught only by rebasing and compiling
                       row, not the wire envelope

Every branch was green alone. Four of the five defects existed only in the combination, and the last two would have merged clean and shipped a field no client could see.
design:
GitHub Actions on `pull_request` builds the *merge* commit by default, which is exactly the check missing: it compiles the branch against the target as it would land, not as it was written. One workflow file, and the gate is already a single command.

Worth pinning in the same run, because both were load-bearing today: CARGO_TERM_COLOR=never (cargo prefixes 'warning'/'error' with ANSI colour, so a grep anchored at ^ silently matches nothing), and the MSRV in Cargo.toml, currently 1.89, so the floor is checked rather than declared.

The open question is whether this makes PRs the merge path. It does not have to — a branch can be pushed and checked without a PR — but a PR is where the merge-commit build is free.

Note the corollary if this does not land: the mitigation is procedural — merge each closed bead before dispatching the next wave, so two branches are rarely open against the same crate.
acceptance_criteria: A push or PR runs the full gate against the merge result on a clean checkout, and a branch that is green alone but breaks against main fails before a human merges it.
notes:
Implemented on branch worktree-ci-u7c, PR #22 (draft). .github/workflows/ci.yml:

  gate  (ubuntu-latest + macos-latest)  build --workspace --all-targets --locked, then test --workspace --locked
  msrv  (ubuntu-latest)                 check --workspace --all-targets --locked against the floor

Both pins from the design landed: CARGO_TERM_COLOR=never, and the MSRV read out of
Cargo.toml with grep rather than retyped into the workflow. Warnings are denied via
RUSTFLAGS=-D warnings rather than by grepping the log -- registry deps are built with
--cap-lints allow, so it holds only this workspace. --locked was added on top: the
lockfile is committed, so a branch needing a different resolution has to say so in
the diff.

Measured before pushing, so neither leg was a guess: the full workspace builds
warning-free and passes 678 tests on Linux (Docker) as well as macOS, and passes
under rustc 1.89; `check --all-targets` is also warning-free at 1.89, so -D warnings
and the floor do not collide. Both GitHub runs since have been green on all three
jobs.

THE OPEN QUESTION IN THE DESIGN IS STILL OPEN, and deliberately so. main has no
branch protection, so CI currently reports rather than enforces -- a red PR can
still be merged by hand. Making the check required is what turns "fails before a
human merges it" into something the forge enforces, and it is also what makes PRs
the merge path. That is the user's call, not this bead's:

  gh api -X PUT repos/tylercrosse/chat-search/branches/main/protection \
    -F required_status_checks[strict]=true \
    -f 'required_status_checks[contexts][]=gate (ubuntu-latest)' \
    -f 'required_status_checks[contexts][]=gate (macos-latest)' \
    -f 'required_status_checks[contexts][]=msrv' \
    -F enforce_admins=false -F required_pull_request_reviews=null -F restrictions=null

Deliberately NOT included: cargo fmt --check. rustfmt is not installed on the dev
machine, so it would be a gate the author cannot reproduce locally. Worth its own
decision rather than a silent addition here.

title: cs init --force silently deletes every hand-written source
description:
`init()` builds `Config::default()` and saves it over the existing file, so `--force` regenerates `sources` from `detect_sources()` and drops everything hand-added — on this machine that is chatgpt-export and google-takeout, the two entries no detection can ever put back (ADR 21). machine_alias and log_queries go the same way unless re-passed on the command line.

Found while doing chat-search-a7k.22, which makes it sharper rather than merely adjacent: that bead's whole output is an instruction to hand-write [[sources]] blocks, and this is the one command that deletes them without saying so. It is also the command someone reaches for after editing the config wrongly.

Nothing in the archive is lost — an id is permanent and re-adding the block resumes capture (ADR 16) — but the config is the only record of where an export was unpacked, and that path is not recoverable from anything.
acceptance_criteria: cs init --force either preserves [[sources]] entries that detection cannot reproduce, or refuses and says what it would drop. A config carrying chatgpt-export survives it. Whichever is chosen, a test drives the real binary over a config with a hand-added export source.

title: JSON-CONTRACT.md names a refusal code the binary never emits
description:
docs/JSON-CONTRACT.md's refusal table (The refusal) says code is one of 'no_index', 'building', 'stale'. The binary emits 'index_stale' — cs-core/src/build.rs:288, 'Unreadable::Stale(_) => "index_stale"', pinned by build.rs:479 and exercised by crates/cs/tests/index_states.rs. A client written from the document switches on 'stale', never matches, and falls through to whatever its unknown-code arm does.

Found by chat-search-me9.8.7 while porting the Swift spike's IndexHealth off stderr prose onto the refusal code: probing --db at a zero-byte file and at 4 KB of the letter A both return exit 1 with {"error":{"code":"index_stale",...}}. The spike now switches on 'index_stale', which is what the wire says and not what the document says.

The refusal codes are the one part of this contract no test parses out of the prose — the json_contract.rs parser reads the five field tables and this table is not one of them, which is why the two could drift.
design:
Either the document is wrong or the code is. Renaming the emitted code is a wire change to a published interface and would break the Swift spike and anything else already switching on it; correcting the document is a one-word edit. Prefer the document unless there is a reason 'stale' is the name that was meant.

Whichever way it goes, consider extending crates/cs/tests/json_contract.rs to read this table too, since a code table nothing parses is the same rot in a smaller hat.
acceptance_criteria: docs/JSON-CONTRACT.md and the code emitted by cs-core agree on the spelling of every refusal code, and a test fails if they stop agreeing.

title: Decide what the query log's ms means now that it excludes opening the index
description:
chat-search-me9.36.2 moved the search clock inside cs_core::answer(), which starts after the index is open. Before it, commands.rs started t0 above open_index. Every Search event appended since carries a slightly smaller number for the same work, and nothing in the file marks where the change is.

MEASURED, so the size of the question is known: warm on the real index, same query, main reported 41.05 / 48.00 ms where the new binary reports 40.77 / 38.96 ms. Single-digit milliseconds. Cold the difference is lost in noise.

NOTHING READS IT TODAY. querylog::fold works on query text, picks and driven spans; ms is recorded and never summed, compared or thresholded. So this costs nothing right now, which is exactly why it is easy to leave until it costs something.

WHY IT WANTS DECIDING EARLY RATHER THAN LATER. queries.jsonl is append-only and authored — DECISIONS.md and config.rs both call it precious and say it cannot be reconstructed from anything. The boundary is a timestamp, and today that timestamp is recent and known. Every week it recedes, and more entries accumulate on both sides of a discontinuity nobody wrote down. A latency question asked in six months would straddle it silently, which is the same shape as the driven-span problem Event::Driven exists to prevent: an exclusion nobody explained is a silent one a week from now.
design:
Three options, cheapest first.

1. DECIDE IT DOES NOT MATTER and say so in DECISIONS.md's query-log ADR. Defensible: the difference is single-digit ms, ms is the least load-bearing field in the event, and the log's value is which queries were asked and what answered them. Costs one paragraph.

2. MARK THE BOUNDARY the way the log already marks things it cannot infer. There is precedent and machinery: Event::Driven is an authored line saying 'this span is not what it looks like'. A sibling one-off — or a Driven line with a why that names the change — puts the discontinuity in the file rather than in somebody's memory.

3. RESTORE THE OLD MEANING by timing from before open_index. Rejected on sight unless someone argues for it: it would put a second clock back in commands.rs, which is precisely the duplication me9.36 deleted, and it would make ms measure something the Answer cannot know about itself.

Option 2 is the one that keeps the log honest without re-litigating the design; option 1 is the one that admits ms was never worth much. Either is fine. What is not fine is neither.
acceptance_criteria: A decision is recorded where this project keeps them, and if it is option 2 the line is in the log. Whoever asks a latency question of this file next can tell from the file, or from DECISIONS.md, that the boundary exists.
notes: Filed out of the me9.36 review, not out of a failure — the gate was green and stayed green. Raised as a question rather than a task because all three options are defensible and the cost of picking wrong is near zero; the cost of picking nothing is that the boundary recedes out of living memory while the file keeps growing.

title: The Swift spike decodes the retired envelope and will fail on the first response
description:
chat-search-me9.36 renamed Group.hits to Group.matches and dropped the grouped discriminator, but poc/swift/Sources/cs-spike/Model.swift still declares 'let hits: [Hit]' (Model.swift:36) and 'let grouped: Bool?' (:17). 'grouped' is optional so it decodes as nil, but 'hits' is non-optional and its key no longer exists, so Codable throws keyNotFound on the first conversation of the first response.

Nothing catches this. poc/ is excluded from the cargo workspace (Cargo.toml:6, deliberately - it is a throwaway measurement instrument), so 'cargo test --workspace' is green while the repo's only non-Rust decoder is broken. That decoder is not incidental: it is what found the title-nullability defect (me9.27) and the UTF-8-versus-character span defect (me9.33), both by decoding real output rather than by reading the structs. It is the only evidence the contract is decodable by a Codable client at all.
design: Model.swift's Conversation gains 'let matches: [Match]' in place of 'let hits: [Hit]', and Hit splits the way the wire did: a Match carries message fields only, a Hit keeps its parent identity and is used only on the --flat path if the spike exercises it. 'grouped' comes out. Consider also decoding the new envelope keys the spike could now assert on - v, total, settled, mark_offsets - since mark_offsets is the field me9.33 added precisely so a Swift client stops guessing the span encoding, and this spike is the client that guessed wrong.
acceptance_criteria: poc/swift builds and decodes a real 'cs search --json' response without throwing, on both the grouped and --flat paths. If the spike is instead judged spent and deleted, that is an acceptable close - but it is a decision recorded here, not a silent rot.
notes: branch: worktree-me9-8-7-swift-envelope
close_reason:
Migrated the spike rather than deleting it: it is the repo's only non-Rust decoder and the only evidence the contract is decodable by a Codable client at all, and it earns that by decoding real output — this bead's own two follow-ups (chat-search-4n4, chat-search-5sd) came out of the migration. Conversation.matches replaces hits, Match is message fields only, Hit survives in a separate FlatResponse because --flat is a separate shape, and the rest of the documented row fields are decoded too (destinations as a tagged enum, kind_runs as the wire's two-element array, score, match_seqs, native_id, ended_at, on_head_path, thread_key). Spans are read in the units mark_offsets names instead of assumed, and IndexHealth reads the refusal code off stdout instead of grepping stderr prose, which splits stale out from noIndex.

New: 'swift run -c release cs-spike contract' decodes both envelopes out of a real index and exits nonzero if either breaks, which is the gate poc/ has never had.

Gate run: cargo test --workspace green (14 binaries, 618 passed, 0 failed) and cargo build --workspace --all-targets with 0 warnings, both on the branch; 'swift build -c release' clean from a deleted .build with 0 warnings — SwiftPM's own tooling, which the README already documents as how this is built. End-to-end against the real index at ~/.chat-archive/index.db through a scratch config (archive_root in a temp dir, log_queries = false): 'cs-spike contract' green — 4,530 conversations and 432 messages decoded, 980 spans resolved, mark_offsets utf8-bytes — and red with the offending bytes printed when the same response is transformed back into the retired shape. 'cs-spike states' and 'cs-spike snapshot' also run; the snapshot PNG shows marks landing correctly on a query containing an em-dash.

Not done: RESULTS.md §4's tables were not re-measured, only annotated as superseded, and §7's line count is stale by the size of Contract.swift.

title: Add Codex-native bd-dispatch skill
description: Port the existing Claude Code bd-dispatch workflow into a discoverable personal Codex skill. Preserve Beads selection and confirmation guards, bundle the detached Codex worker launcher and shared worker contract without hidden ~/.claude dependencies, and validate the resulting skill.
acceptance_criteria: ~/.codex/skills/bd-dispatch validates as a Codex skill; invoking it selects ready non-epic beads, requires explicit batch confirmation, claims safely, launches isolated Codex workers, and reports durable review handles; a dry run succeeds without mutating Beads.
close_reason: Created the personal Codex bd-dispatch skill at ~/.codex/skills/bd-dispatch with Codex-native queue selection and confirmation guidance, a self-contained detached-worker contract, and an isolated-worktree launcher. quick_validate and bash syntax checks pass; a live dry run against chat-search-a7k.30 made no tracker or git mutation; a fresh-agent read-only forward test stopped correctly for missing count and queue slice.

title: The CLI stops assembling envelopes by hand
description: Four inline json! sites in commands.rs collapse into one serialization. search becomes parse, answer, serialize. The rebuilding note and the rejected-filter note read fields off the Answer instead of recomputing them, so commands.rs stops calling parsed.rejected() entirely.
design: serde_json::to_value(&answer) IS the JSON path - the same trick cs show --json already uses for Transcript. --flat serializes a FlatAnswer. The error site becomes Refusal::from(&why), so the machine-readable error body is core's shape rather than a fifth thing assembled at the printer. All three copies of (ms*100).round()/100 are deleted, including the one feeding log_search, so a logged Need and a printed answer can no longer round differently. One-shot CLI callers settle before printing; --prefix (typeahead over argv) does not.
acceptance_criteria: No json! macro builds a search envelope. The three ms roundings are gone. Text and JSON output read the same Answer. Exit codes and the error body are unchanged in meaning.
notes: branch: worktree-me9-36-2-cli-answer
close_reason: cs search is now parse, answer, serialize: the grouped reply is a serialized Answer, --flat a FlatAnswer, the error body a Refusal, and the text listing reads the same Answer the JSON does. All three (ms*100).round()/100 copies are gone, the query log's among them. The rebuilding and rejected-filter notes read index_state and unapplied_filters off the answer, so commands.rs no longer calls parsed.rejected(). New on the wire: total and settled — a one-shot search settles before printing (measured warm on 2026-08-04, 'the' at --limit 50 reports 4,224 in 0.22s wall where --prefix reports a floor of 1,025 in 0.21s); only --prefix leaves a floor standing. Beyond what was filed: docs/JSON-CONTRACT.md's field tables and json_contract.rs moved with the code, because that test parses the doc against real binary output and the gate cannot be green otherwise — me9.36.4 is noted with what remains to it (the opaque-score and possibly-empty-spans promises, and the extension policy). cargo test --workspace green, 599 tests, zero warnings. branch: worktree-me9-36-2-cli-answer

title: The TUI reads the same Answer, and the parallel entry point goes away
description: The deepening is not real until the five old entry points can actually be made private, and they cannot while the TUI still calls them. This is the second adapter, and migrating it is the proof the interface works.
design: state.rs holds an Answer instead of a Counted plus a Total. The keystroke path never pays for the total - answer() reports whatever the ranking pass saw for free - and settle_count() becomes answer.settle(&reader), which replays the receipt. That deletes the reason App::options() had to exist as a correctness crutch, and with it the second SearchOptions the pick path builds at state.rs:383. Counted, Total, search_grouped_counted, count_matching and recent leave the public interface in this bead, not a follow-up. Verify with the pty harness as well as cargo test: the fold glyphs and pane titles are what proved the preview actually loaded last time, and a vacuous screen comparison is the failure mode to design against.
acceptance_criteria: cs-tui calls answer() and settle() and nothing else from the search family. The five old entry points and Counted/Total are private. Keystroke latency is unchanged or better. The pty harness shows a loaded preview, not just nine identical screens.
notes: branch: worktree-me9-36-3-tui-answer (built on worktree-me9-36-2-cli-answer, which is unmerged — the two land together)
close_reason: cs-tui holds a cs_core::Answer and a Reader instead of groups+Total+last_ms+Connection, and calls only answer() and settle(). cs pick and cs eval, the two other callers of the ranked row, moved too. search/search_grouped_counted/count_matching/recent, Counted, Total and search::Group are pub(crate); search_grouped is deleted (nothing wants a ranking whose size it cannot report) and 14 tests moved to a test-only shim. cs_core::Group is now answer::Group. Gate green: 599 tests, zero build warnings. Verified under a pyte pty harness on the real 4,377-conversation index — preview loads 36 body lines with 18 fold chevrons, Alt-Enter changes the pane, 'the' draws … then 4,243 — and every screen matches the pre-migration capture but relative ages. Keystroke p50 across 3 interleaved runs: 13.41->13.52, 1.10->1.08, 28.29->27.57 ms.

title: Rewrite the contract doc, and promise two things it does not promise yet
description: JSON-CONTRACT.md is the interface a Swift reader learns, and json_contract.rs parses its tables against real binary output - so the doc is the change, not documentation of the change.
design: New tables for Answer, Group, Match and FlatAnswer; the grouped flag and the polymorphic results row come out. Two promises are added because they are free today and breaking later: score is OPAQUE ORDERING (clients never re-sort, never parse it), which is what lets hybrid BM25+vector ranking arrive without a v bump - the glossary's Indexer entry already says 'and later vectors'; and snippet_spans MAY BE EMPTY, because a semantic match need contain no lexical term to highlight. State the extension policy in the doc as well: additions are silent, v bumps only when a field changes meaning. Keep the published key unapplied_filters exactly as spelled (ADR 12).
acceptance_criteria: The doc describes the new envelope and json_contract.rs passes against real output. The envelope names its span offset encoding, spelled the same as cs show --json (subsumes chat-search-me9.33). score is documented as opaque ordering and snippet_spans as possibly empty. The extension policy is written down. unapplied_filters keeps its name.
notes:
chat-search-me9.36.2 had to move the doc's field tables with the code: json_contract.rs parses them against real binary output, so the workspace cannot be green with the wire on one side and the tables on the other. Already landed on worktree-me9-36-2-cli-answer: tables for both envelopes, Group, Match and Hit; the grouped discriminator and the polymorphic results row deleted along with the wart documenting them; a 'The refusal' section; Span no longer claiming nothing on the wire names its encoding, now that mark_offsets does. WHAT IS LEFT for this bead: the two forward promises it was filed for — score documented as OPAQUE ORDERING (clients never re-sort, never parse it) and snippet_spans documented as MAY BE EMPTY because a semantic match need contain no lexical term — plus the extension policy written down (additions are silent, v bumps only when a field changes meaning). The score cell still describes bm25-over-decay and tells a reader they could re-derive the order from it, which is exactly the sentence the opaque-ordering promise has to replace.
branch: worktree-me9-36-4-contract-promises (based on worktree-me9-36-3-tui-answer, not main); worktree .claude/worktrees/me9-36-4-contract-promises; commit d85110f
close_reason: JSON-CONTRACT.md now promises what me9.36 designed it to. score is opaque ordering (row order is the ranking, never re-sorted on, never parsed; today's formula kept but marked unpromised); snippet_spans is may-be-empty as an ordinary outcome, not the machine half of the no-match prefix; and the extension policy is one section instead of two half-statements in the intro and the v row, both of which now point at it. unapplied_filters unchanged. Also corrected three comments that still asserted the prefix/empty-spans equivalence to clients (Match.snippet's rustdoc and the answer.rs test's framing - the test keeps its name and assertion, because the equality is true and enforced by snippet_marked_at, just not a promise), and json_contract.rs's stale claim that nothing on the wire names the offset encoding, which now asserts mark_offsets beside the offsets it describes (me9.33's criterion). Pin verified by planting a bogus Group row and watching the key test fail. Gate green: 599 tests, zero warnings, plus a real-index check (the at --limit 60 returns ascending scores -1.88e-05..-6.18e-06, so sorting by the number reverses the ranking). EPIC me9.36: every criterion now holds on this branch - the search family and Counted/Total are pub(crate) (me9.36.3), commands.rs builds no search envelope by hand (the four remaining json! calls are cs index/scan/needs operator output, which the contract explicitly excludes), the TUI holds an Answer, the doc describes both envelopes plus Group, Match and Hit, and json_contract.rs passes against the real binary. Not closing the epic here; nothing from it is on main, and the four branches are stacked main -> me9-36-2 -> me9-36-3 -> me9-36-4.

title: answer.rs: the Answer type, the receipt, and the routing
description: The module itself. Answer, Group, Match, FlatAnswer, Refusal, and the private receipt that makes settle() replay the ask it was born from. The empty and too-short query routes to recent results INSIDE answer(), so no caller ever learns that recent() existed - the TUI's old habit of blanking its own query text to force that branch stays dead.
design: Sibling to blocks.rs and built the same way: content and rules, never rendering. answer(reader, &Query, &SearchOptions) -> Answer; Answer::settle(&mut self, reader) -> Result<bool>, idempotent, and on failure the answer is unchanged and still true because the floor stands. The receipt holds the parsed Query, the resolved options and now_ms. Take &Reader rather than a bare Connection - that is what lets index_state land in the envelope by construction instead of being stapled on by a caller. ms is measured here and rounded to 2dp exactly once. Tests go through the interface: a fixture index, a fixed now_ms, and assertions on answer() and settle() alone; rank, hydrate and best_of stay private and are tested through it.
acceptance_criteria: answer() and settle() are the only public doors. Empty query returns recent results through the same call with an exact total. settle() is idempotent and cannot count a different set than was ranked. Every field of the wire types is exercised by a test.
notes:
2026-08-04. THE ENVELOPE MUST ALSO NAME ITS SPAN OFFSET ENCODING, folded in from chat-search-me9.33 (closed as subsumed).

The design above specified v but not this, and it is the half that actually drew blood: the Swift spike read snippet_spans as character offsets and mis-highlighted every snippet containing an em-dash, which in this corpus is most of them. cs show --json already prevents exactly that by emitting mark_offsets = 'utf8-bytes' - named on the wire rather than only in documentation, because it is the one place the reader's language leaks into the contract and a silently wrong offset highlights the wrong word rather than failing.

Use the SAME SPELLING as cs show --json, which is mark_offsets. If that reads wrong beside snippet_spans, change both contracts together and never just one - me9.33's acceptance was explicit that the two must match.
branch: worktree-me9-36-1-answer-module (worktree at ../chat-search-me9361, off answer-envelope-adr).

TWO DEPARTURES FROM THE EPIC'S PROSE, both deliberate, both for me9.36.4 to write down.

(1) thread_key stays on Match. The epic lists it among the parent identity a group states once, but a conversation is a DAG (ADR 4) and the strand is a property of the message — a group carrying one thread_key would assert a fact about several threads about one. Every other field it lists (conv_id, source, native_id, title, destinations, deleted_upstream) did move up.

(2) The wire Group is a NEW type built `From<search::Group>` rather than a rename of it, because commands.rs still prints the old envelope and json_contract.rs reads docs/JSON-CONTRACT.md against real binary output — changing the ranked row's shape here would have broken a document me9.36.4 owns. Consequence for me9.36.2/.3: the wire type is `cs_core::answer::Group` (NOT re-exported at the crate root, where search::Group still holds the name). When the clients stop reading the ranked row, delete search::Group and hoist the export — lib.rs carries a comment saying so. Both conversions destructure exhaustively, so a new column on a ranked row fails to compile rather than silently never reaching the wire.

FlatAnswer::of is a second constructor beside answer(). 'answer() and settle() are the only public doors' is honoured for the grouped reply; --flat needs some way in, and `FlatAnswer::of` mirrors `Transcript::of`. It has no recent route and no total/settled — the number worth settling counts conversations, and that envelope is messages.

mark_offsets now reads highlight::OFFSETS, which blocks.rs::Transcript also reads, so the two contracts cannot be changed one at a time (me9.33's acceptance).

MEASURED against the real index 2026-08-04 (4,377 conversations, no query-log writes — this went through a throwaway example against cs-core, not through cs search): '' and 'bo' both route to recent, total 4,377 exact; 'borrow checker' 51 exact in 65.8 ms; typeahead 'the' floor 1,025 vs true 4,243, settling in 49.6 ms; 'the agent:codex' floor 433 -> 649 in 68.6 ms (the receipt counting the FILTERED set, not the 4,243); 'borrow date:nope' returns results and reports the token in unapplied_filters. No span landed mid-character on any of them. The AtLeast floor is ~24% of the truth on today's corpus, not the ~50% the old doc comment estimated.
close_reason: cs-core/src/answer.rs ships the envelope ADR 23 specifies: Answer, Group, Match, FlatAnswer, Refusal, a private receipt, and answer()/settle() as the way in. Empty and too-short queries route to recent inside answer() with an exact total; settle() replays the receipt, is idempotent, and cannot be handed a different question. mark_offsets is folded in from me9.33 and shares one constant with cs show --json. 18 new tests exercise every wire field; cargo test --workspace green (603 tests), zero warnings. Verified against the real 4,377-conversation index: 'the' floors at 1,025 and settles to 4,243 in 49.6 ms, 'the agent:codex' settles to 649. Nothing calls it yet by design — me9.36.2/.3 migrate the CLI and TUI, and two notes on this bead record where the implementation departs from the epic's prose (thread_key stays on Match; the wire Group is built From the ranked row rather than replacing it, so the contract test and its document stay green until me9.36.4).

title: The reply to a search is a core-owned type, not four inline envelopes
description:
The answer to a search has no home. `cs/src/commands.rs` assembles the JSON envelope inline at four sites (flat ~:221, grouped ~:598, explain ~:518 with no envelope at all, error ~:576), and the two key lists agree only because `json_contract.rs` asserts it. Meanwhile `cs-tui/src/state.rs:140` reaches a richer parallel entry point — `search_grouped_counted` returning `Counted` with a `Total` — that no JSON client can reach, so `cs search --json` cannot report a total at all.

Five public entry points (`search`, `search_grouped`, `search_grouped_counted`, `count_matching`, `recent`) expose routing that was never the caller's decision to make, and the envelope's rules are spread across the clients that print it: `(ms*100).round()/100` appears three times in commands.rs, one of those feeding the query log, so a logged Need and a printed answer can round differently.

The deletion test fails loudly: delete the inline envelopes and the complexity reappears at every call site. That is what makes this a module rather than a formatting habit.

Timing is the argument for doing it now. me9.8.1 writes the first non-Rust decoder against this envelope. Every field added after that ships twice — once in Rust, once in Swift — and every field added before is free.
design:
Designed three ways in parallel (minimal interface / maximum flexibility / optimise the common caller) and settled on a hybrid of the first and third. `crates/cs-core/src/answer.rs`, sibling and structural twin to `blocks.rs`: this module holds the rules of the reply, never the rendering.

THE INTERFACE

    pub fn answer(reader: &Reader, query: &Query, opts: &SearchOptions) -> Result<Answer>
    impl Answer { pub fn settle(&mut self, reader: &Reader) -> Result<bool> }
    pub struct Refusal { .. }   // From<&Unreadable>; the error body, core-owned

Takes a parsed `&Query`, not raw text: the TUI holds a Query for its facet chips (`Query::toggling`/`without`), and rendering it back to text so core could re-parse would reopen exactly the representation-disagreement bug class the one-rule-one-place convention exists to close. No new `Ask` wrapper — `SearchOptions` already exists and typeahead-vs-exact already lives on `Query`.

`settle` replays a PRIVATE RECEIPT of the original ask — the parsed Query, the resolved options, and the `now_ms` the answer ran under. Counting a set other than the one on screen becomes unwritable rather than merely discouraged. Today that invariant lives in a doc comment on the TUI's `options()`, and the pick path at state.rs:383 already builds a second options struct anyway.

THE WIRE (breaking, in bounded ways all three designs converged on)

    { v: 1, query, ms, count, total, settled, unapplied_filters, index_state, results }

- `results` is ALWAYS groups. The polymorphic `results` (Vec<Group> or Vec<Hit>) and its sometimes-present `grouped: true` discriminator both die; a decoder never branches to learn what type a key holds.
- A group carries `matches`: message fields only. Parent identity (conv_id, source, native_id, title, thread_key, deleted_upstream, the whole destinations array) is stated once on the group instead of repeated per nested hit — which was bytes and a second place for two copies to disagree.
- The dual-role `Hit` survives only in `FlatAnswer`, a separate small envelope for `--flat` keyed `hits`. That is now its one role.
- `total` + `settled` are two flat scalars. The `Total::Exact/AtLeast` enum stays honest in Rust; Swift Codable never meets a polymorphic key.
- `ms` measured and rounded once, in core. The query log and the wire can no longer disagree.
- `v: 1`, matching what `Transcript` already carries.

TWO PROMISES ADDED FOR FUTURES THAT ARE OTHERWISE FREE

- `score` is documented as OPAQUE ORDERING — clients never re-sort and never parse it. Without this, hybrid BM25+vector ranking (the glossary's Indexer entry already says "and later vectors") is a breaking change; with it, invisible.
- `snippet_spans` MAY BE EMPTY. A semantic match need contain no lexical term to highlight. The model already has the cousin concept in `MarkKind::Unranked`.

Both are one contract row each, free today, a `v` bump later.

EXTENSION POLICY, stated in JSON-CONTRACT.md: additions are silent, `v` bumps only when a field changes meaning.

WHAT WAS DECLINED, AND WHY, so it is not re-proposed

- A sectioned reply (Parts/TotalPolicy, sections keyed by conv_id, serde-symmetric Ask). Genuinely better for three futures: retiring kind_runs by economics rather than schema, additive facets (me9.18), and a cheap wire-side settle for `cs serve --stdio` (me9.21). Declined because the Option-unwrapping tax lands on the hottest paths every day while the benefit arrives only if those futures ship, Swift would join excerpts to cards by key instead of reading nesting, and "asked implies present" is a runtime law the type system cannot prove. It also designs for a transport ADR 14 deliberately deferred and me9.22 measured as unnecessary — one adapter is a hypothetical seam.
- One envelope with a `unit: conversation|message` field covering `--flat` too. Fewer documented shapes, but it readmits a discriminator every decoder must model for a case the app never asks for, and its per-unit `count`-vs-`total` semantics are the kind of rule misread in year two.
- Core parsing raw text (`Answer::ask(&ix, text, ..)`). Deepest possible call for CLI and Swift, but the TUI would round-trip its Query through text.

HOW THE EXTENSION FUTURES LAND, checked before choosing: semantic embeddings sit behind the ranking seam entirely (only `score` and empty spans graze the wire, both now covered); topics are Query-side as a filter — and `unapplied_filters` already reports `topic:` gracefully before topics exist — plus an additive optional group field; LLM summaries are blocked upstream by the derived-data invariant (non-deterministic, so not an index column) long before they are a wire question, and then land like `title_origin: generated` already does.
acceptance_criteria: cs-core owns the reply: search, search_grouped, search_grouped_counted, count_matching and recent are no longer public. commands.rs builds no envelope by hand. The TUI reads the same Answer the JSON client does, and Counted/Total leave the public interface. JSON-CONTRACT.md describes Answer, Group, Match and FlatAnswer, and json_contract.rs passes against real binary output. cargo test --workspace green, zero warnings.
close_reason: Merged to main as PR #11 (40c3296). cs_core::answer owns the reply; commands.rs, cs-tui and cs eval all read the same Answer; search/search_grouped_counted/count_matching/recent and Counted/Total are pub(crate) and search_grouped is deleted; JSON-CONTRACT.md describes both envelopes plus Group, Match and Hit, and json_contract.rs passes against real binary output. Gate on merged main: 618 tests, zero warnings — which also confirms no semantic conflict with PR #10, developed in parallel over the same contract. Two follow-ups filed from the review rather than left implicit: me9.8.7 (the Swift spike still decodes the retired envelope) and 0cg (the query log's ms changed meaning).

title: cs show renders one record of a sitting, not the sitting
description:
chat-search-o1i.5 made the search layer read Google's activity log back as sittings: a row for google-takeout:2026-07-28T16:27:48.790Z reports 22 messages and 11 user turns, because it stands for 11 records. Opening it does not agree. 'cs show google-takeout:2026-07-28T16:27:48.790Z' prints '2 messages, 2 drawn, 1 thread(s)' and renders the opening prompt and its answer, because show takes a conversation id and that id is one record.

So the two halves of the product now disagree about what a row is. The search layer says 22, the reader says 2, and nothing says why. The same gap is in cs-tui's preview pane, which loads by conv_id the same way.
design:
DECIDED 2026-08-04 by the maintainer, which settles the open question this bead was filed with: a sitting is rendered as one conversation, because that is the shape every other source already has. Google's export is the odd one out — it shredded a chat into per-turn records — and cs_core::sittings exists to undo that. A reader should not have to know which upstream tool happened to serialize a conversation in one piece.

So: one Transcript, the records' messages concatenated in the sitting's order. Not a Transcript per record, and not a hard break in the middle of a reading experience that every other source renders continuously.

WHAT RESOLVES. cs_core::sittings::members(conn, id) already returns every conversation in a sitting in time order, and is what Group::sitting is built from. cs show resolves its argument through that call and concatenates. A sitting still acquires no id (ADR 16) — the argument stays a conversation id, and any MEMBER id must resolve to the whole sitting, not only the opening record, because a client copying an id out of sitting.members has no reason to prefer the first.

ORDERING. ORDER BY is_sidechain, thread_key, seq holds within a record; across records the order is the sitting's, which is msg_offset. Both, in that nesting.

THE SEAM. Those were separate HTTP requests with no shared context on Google's side, so the boundary is real information and is not thrown away — it stays available as data (the members list and their offsets are already there) for chat-search-o1i.9 to draw as lightly as it wants. What this bead rules out is the seam being structural: it must not split the transcript, and a reader who does not care must not have to see it. Erasing it from the data would be the opposite error, since the fold is a heuristic over timestamps and the contract says so.

SAME FIX, SAME PLACE. cs explain takes a conversation id too, so explaining a row copied out of a result set explains the record that opened the sitting rather than the sitting. Whatever resolves show resolves explain. cs-tui's preview pane loads by conv_id the same way and is the third caller.

CONTRACT DOC. docs/JSON-CONTRACT.md's Sitting section currently ends by telling clients that 'cs show <conv_id> opens the opening record, not the sitting' and that they should expect the two halves to differ. That paragraph is this bead's definition of done — it must be rewritten, not left describing a defect that no longer exists.
acceptance_criteria: cs show <id> for any member of a sitting renders the whole sitting as one transcript, in the sitting's order, and its counts agree with what the search row claimed for the same query — the 57 messages / 31 user turns / 31 records case is the standing example. cs explain answers for the same unit. docs/JSON-CONTRACT.md no longer documents the disagreement. A conversation that is not part of a sitting renders exactly as it does today.
notes:
Same family, same cause: cs explain takes a conversation id too, so explaining a row copied out of a result set explains the record that opened the sitting and not the sitting. Whatever resolves show should resolve explain, or explain should say which of the two it answered for.
Maintainer's framing, recorded verbatim because it is the reasoning and not just the verdict: 'the google export split up a conversation into multiple records and we went back and tried to concatenate it into a single conversation. That sounds like the right call to try to massage the shape to match the other conversations from Claude/ChatGPT/etc.'

Live on main as of e2d2898 — the row for google-takeout:2026-04-14T03:43:14.330Z reports 57 messages and 31 user turns over 31 records, and cs show on that id prints '2 messages, 2 drawn, 1 thread(s)'. That is the reproduction; no fixture needed.
branch: worktree-agent-a45713446889032a6
close_reason: cs show and cs explain resolve their argument through the new sittings::resolve, so any member id renders or explains the whole sitting as one unit — google-takeout:2026-04-14T03:43:14.330Z now reads 57 messages and 31 user turns over 31 records from any of its members, matching the search row exactly. Transcript.seq is sittings::POSITION so it shares match_seqs' coordinate space; Transcript and Explain both carry the Sitting the row already did, keeping the seam as data without splitting the transcript. cs-tui's preview was fixed by the same blocks::load change. JSON-CONTRACT.md, ARCHITECTURE.md and GLOSSARY.md no longer document the disagreement. Not done: nothing still draws the fold in the TUI row or preview, which is chat-search-o1i.9.

title: Facets, and opening a conversation where it lives
description: Two things the shell defers: narrowing a search, and the action the whole tool exists for - getting back to the conversation.
design:
LAYOUT: poc/ui's left rail is the visual reference for where facets live and how they read - open index.html and narrow something. me9.8 records what the mockup does and does not decide; its structure and density are the reference, its pixel values are not, and it has nothing to say about the states it never had.

FACETS: every facet narrows the conversation list and nothing else. The filter must be visible as query text rather than hidden UI state, which is how the TUI does it and why there is exactly one source of truth for what is being filtered (TUI-DESIGN section 5). unapplied_filters in the envelope is not an error and exits 0 - a client that ignores it silently shows unfiltered results for a filtered query (6eb.11), so it has to be surfaced. Note that the mockup does NOT model this: poc/ui has no empty, error or loading states anywhere, so the rail it shows is always the populated one.

OPENING: Group::destinations is already in the JSON, best first, and may be empty - which means the source offers no known way to reopen, and must be reported rather than treated as a failure. cs pick records that a search ended in an open, which is the signal 6eb.21 learns ranking from, so the app should record it too rather than opening silently.
acceptance_criteria: Facets narrow the list and are visible as query text. unapplied_filters is surfaced. A conversation opens at its best destination; an empty destinations list says so. The open is recorded.

title: The result row, at real data
description: poc/ui settled the row MODEL against measurements, and this is where it meets a real client. Open index.html for the layout and build what it shows; me9.8 records what the mockup does and does not decide, and the short version is that its structure is the reference and its pixel values are not. Three lines with a query, two without: metadata and shape on line 1, title full width on line 2, best match on line 3 spent only when there is something to show. The row is two clusters split by a gutter - agent, model, size, change and shape left; directory, forks and age right - because cwd answers which of my worlds was this rather than what is it.
design:
The agent badge is icon-only in poc/ui because the list column was 706px and the word cost 66px, which is exactly what cwd needed to stop collapsing. A native window is resizable, so re-measure rather than inheriting that trade: it was forced by a fixed mockup width, not chosen.

Total edit lines are blank on 194 of 354 rows, so that cell must vanish when empty rather than sit there.

THE RIBBON IS DELIBERATELY NOT HERE. It needs kind_runs, which is parked on me9.31 pending the fold change, and me9.25 says match_seqs and kind_runs are different coordinate spaces so the two cannot yet be drawn on one strip. Build the row without it and leave the space; a row with no ribbon is useful and a ribbon drawn in the wrong coordinate space is worse than none.

title: The reader pane: one conversation, folded
description: The drawer. cs show --json already carries everything needed - per-message role, kind, seq, is_error, is_sidechain, marks, and both answers core owes a client: drawn and mark_kind (me9.17). Payload is ~924 KB for a 923-message conversation, median ~10 KB, so the whole transcript in one call is affordable.
design:
LAYOUT: poc/ui's drawer is the visual reference - open index.html and select a conversation. me9.8 records what the mockup does and does not decide; the short version is that its structure and density are the reference and its pixel values are not.

Do NOT re-derive which messages are drawn or which matches are entitled to look ranked. Both travel with the message: drawn is cs_core::blocks::drawn and mark_kind is Ranked or Unranked, where Unranked means the word matched but carries no postings, so cs search will not return the conversation for it. Marking those identically states something false in the one place a reader has gone to check.

marks are UTF-8 byte offsets - the payload says so in mark_offsets. Convert through String.utf8.

me9.20 IS CLOSED BUT WAS NOT MERGED - check before trusting it. Its close reason says cs_core::blocks owns tool_summary, recognition_line, offset_lines and Block::collapsed, and that is true only on worktree-bead-me9-20-collapsed-forms, which was still 7 commits ahead of main on 2026-08-05; on main those two functions are private in cs-tui/src/preview.rs. Verify cs-core actually exports them before starting. If the branch still has not merged, build the expanded reader first and leave outline mode alone; do not port those two functions into Swift, because reimplementing them is exactly the duplication me9.17 exists to stop.
acceptance_criteria: A conversation renders from cs show --json with tool traffic collapsed and failed results kept. Highlights land on the right characters in text containing multi-byte characters. Outline mode either works from core or is absent, never reimplemented client-side.

title: Shell: promote the spike's transport, and give the app its four index states
description:
Wave 0, and the only thing in it. Everything else in me9.8 is blocked on this because a skeleton invented twice is two apps.

RE-SCOPED 2026-08-05, against the code rather than against a close message. The decoder this bead was written to produce already exists on main and is already exercised against a real index — chat-search-me9.8.7 migrated the spike instead of deleting it. Model.swift decodes both envelopes with every documented field, Destination is tagged on kind, spans are read in the units mark_offsets names, and IndexHealth.classify reads error.code off stdout: the stderr substring table this bead was told to delete is already gone, not pending. CsClient carries the readability-handler transport. SearchView already renders the refusal states as distinct non-error placeholders and marks snippets through the UTF-8 conversion.

So the acceptance criteria as written are mostly already met, by code that is sitting in poc/. What is left is the promotion itself, one real gap, and a re-measurement.
design:
ALREADY DONE ON MAIN, AND NOT TO BE REWRITTEN. Read these before writing anything; the fastest way to fail this bead is to reimplement one of them.

  - THE DECODER — poc/swift/Sources/cs-spike/Model.swift. Both envelopes (SearchResponse and
    FlatResponse, separate shapes on purpose), every field in docs/JSON-CONTRACT.md, nullable
    fields optional, Destination a tagged enum with an `unsupported` arm so an added kind is not
    a coordinated release, Run as the wire's two-element array.
  - THE SPAN CONVERSION — String.range(of:in:) reads mark_offsets off the envelope and refuses
    rather than clamps when an offset does not land on a character boundary. This is the fix for
    chat-search-me9.33 and it is already correct.
  - THE REFUSAL PATH — IndexHealth.classify branches on error.code: no_index, building,
    index_stale, and an unrecognised code becomes .failed carrying the code rather than a guess.
  - THE TRANSPORT — CsClient: readability handlers plus a termination handler, never
    waitUntilExit plus two blocking pipe reads. The 85 ms to 30 ms fix is in the code already.
  - THE CONTRACT GATE — `swift run -c release cs-spike contract` decodes both envelopes out of a
    real index and exits nonzero if either breaks.

THE ONE REAL GAP: index_state on a SUCCESSFUL response is decoded and then thrown away.
SearchModel.apply() sets `health = .ready` unconditionally, and nothing outside Contract.swift's
diagnostic line ever reads SearchResponse.indexState. The four values are split across two paths —
`ready` and `rebuilding` arrive on a successful envelope, `building` and `no_index` arrive as
refusals — and only the refusal half is wired to the screen.

Both `ready` and `rebuilding` mean the results are COMPLETE, since a rebuild assembles a sibling
and swaps it in whole (chat-search-me9.28). `rebuilding` only means a newer one is coming, which
is exactly what lets the app offer to ask again instead of presenting the answer as final. That
affordance does not exist today, and it is the substance of this bead's second criterion.

THE PROMOTION. poc/ is an instrument and not the product — poc/swift/README.md says so in its own
words — so the app cannot live there, and it cannot depend on something that does.

The decoder is written once. That rule is why chat-search-me9.36 was sequenced ahead of this bead
at all: every field added after the first non-Rust decoder ships twice. Copying Model.swift into a
new target would spend that sequencing for nothing. So the decoder moves OUT of poc/ into a
library target that both the app and the spike consume, and the dependency points instrument at
product rather than the reverse.

`cs-spike contract` must still run and still gate after the move. It is the only thing in the repo
that catches a contract break, `cargo test --workspace` structurally cannot see it, and it was
green-fielded three days ago precisely because its absence let a break sit on main for a release.

THE APP TARGET LANDS AT apps/macos/. Nothing in the repo named a location and there is no existing
apps/ directory, so this bead names one rather than leaving each worker to pick a different one.
If that is wrong it is one `git mv` and a bead note, which is cheaper than two skeletons.

DROP THE INSTRUMENT SCAFFOLDING from the app. The List / LazyVStack / VStack picker and the bench
footer exist to answer me9.22's virtualisation question, and it is answered: List recycles, at
5.2 MB against LazyVStack's 65.6 MB and VStack's 566 MB. The app uses List and does not offer the
other two. Keep a timing readout only if it costs nothing to keep.

NOT IN SCOPE: the row's final look, the reader, grouping, facets. Those are the beads this
unblocks, and taking any of them here is what re-blocks them. A plain one-line row is correct.
acceptance_criteria: An app target at apps/macos/ that builds and runs outside poc/, searches the live index, and lists results in a List. THE DECODER IS SHARED, NOT COPIED: one source of truth decodes the contract for both the app and the spike, and 'swift run -c release cs-spike contract' still passes after the move. index_state from a SUCCESSFUL envelope reaches the screen - rebuilding is visibly distinct from ready and offers to ask again, and neither is styled as an error. The refusal states (no_index, building, index_stale) keep working through error.code. Keystroke-to-frame re-measured on the promoted target and recorded, superseding RESULTS.md section 4. No feature work beyond the shell.
notes:
2026-08-04, from an architecture review. Two changes, neither a scope change.

(1) BLOCKED ON chat-search-me9.36. The reply envelope moves into cs-core and its shape changes - results is always groups, a match carries message fields only, and v/total/settled arrive. This bead writes the first non-Rust decoder, so it must be written once, against that envelope. Decode against docs/JSON-CONTRACT.md as the design already says; the tables there will describe Answer, Group and Match.

(2) THE ERROR PATH IS PART OF THE SEAM, and the spike gets it wrong today. Model.swift:105-118 classifies index health by substring-matching seven phrases of the CLI's stderr prose. commands.rs now emits a machine-readable body on stdout - and its comment names this very spike as the reason. Promoting CsClient.swift unchanged would import the leak the finding was filed to kill. Branch on error.code (ADR 12), the same rule the four index_state values already follow.

2026-08-05, RE-SCOPE AND RE-DISPATCH. The previous claim (bd-worker/chat-search-me9.8.1, codex thread 019fd042-756b-75f2-a060-5ac12a82dde8) died on turn one: its log holds thread.started and turn.started and nothing else, and branch worktree-bead-me9.8.1-shell-promote-the-spike is 0 commits ahead of main. No work was lost because none was done. Claim cleared.

The re-scope is against the code on main, not against me9.8.7's close message. Audited: Model.swift 336 lines decoding both envelopes; String.range(of:in:) at Model.swift:264 doing the UTF-8 conversion; IndexHealth.classify at Model.swift:321 branching on error.code; CsClient.swift:162-174 carrying readabilityHandler plus terminationHandler. SearchView.swift:149-179 already renders noIndex, rebuilding and stale as distinct non-error placeholders.

The gap that survives the audit is narrow and specific: 'grep -rn indexState poc/swift' returns three hits, two of them the struct fields and one a diagnostic print in Contract.swift. SearchModel.apply() (SearchView.swift:92-105) sets health = .ready unconditionally. So a successful envelope that says rebuilding is indistinguishable on screen from one that says ready, and the 'ask again' affordance the epic's design argues for has nowhere to hang.

The blocker this bead carried is discharged: me9.36 closed and merged as PR #11 (40c3296), so the envelope is settled and the decoder was written once against it, which was the whole point of the sequencing.

IndexHealth now models all four index states rather than only the refusal half: the successful envelope's index_state is read by IndexHealth.answering, rebuilding draws a dim non-error line above complete results with an Ask again button, an unrecognised state names itself, and no_index/building/index_stale keep their own screens off error.code. Keystroke-to-frame re-measured on the promoted target (62-115 ms p50, main-thread lag p50 0.6 ms) and recorded in apps/macos/README.md, superseding RESULTS.md §1 — §4 the bead named was already retired by me9.8.7. The slowdown against §1 is not the promotion: the spike gives the same figures on the same index, and sqlite p50 went 21.6 to 44.8 ms, filed as chat-search-tpf. Gate green: 671 cargo tests, zero-warning cargo and swift builds, contract exit 0. title: cs search --json carries neither a contract version nor its offset encoding; cs show --json carries both
description:
The two published client contracts (ADR 12, made load-bearing by ADR 14) disagree about how much they say for themselves.

cs show --json emits Transcript.v = 1 — 'bumped when a field changes meaning, which is the change a client cannot detect any other way' — and mark_offsets = "utf8-bytes", 'named on the wire rather than only in documentation because it is the one place the reader's language leaks into the contract, and a silently wrong offset highlights the wrong word rather than failing'.

cs search --json emits neither, and its snippet_spans are the same UTF-8 byte offsets. The Swift spike read them as character offsets and mis-highlighted every snippet containing an em-dash, which in this corpus is most of them — the exact failure the sibling contract's mark_offsets field exists to prevent. Both facts are now written in docs/JSON-CONTRACT.md (chat-search-me9.27), which is better than nothing and is still documentation where the sibling chose the wire.

Found while writing that doc: the asymmetry is not a decision anyone made, it is one contract having been thought about later than the other.
design:
Additive by ADR 12: two new envelope keys, v and span_offsets (or mark_offsets, to match the sibling's spelling — pick one and make both contracts use it). Nothing existing changes meaning.

The version is the load-bearing half. Documentation cannot help a client that decoded an older shape and is now silently reading a field that means something else; a version integer is the only signal that survives that. The offset name is the cheap half and retires a defect a real client already hit.

Open question the bead should settle: whether v is per-command or one number for the whole seam. Per-command is what cs show already did. One number means every client rechecks on any change, which is noisier but harder to get wrong.
acceptance_criteria: cs search --json emits a version and names its span offset encoding; docs/JSON-CONTRACT.md and crates/cs/tests/json_contract.rs are updated together; the spelling matches cs show --json or both are changed to match each other.
close_reason: Subsumed by chat-search-me9.36, which gives the search reply an author and does this and more. me9.33 asked for two things: a contract version and a named span offset encoding, with JSON-CONTRACT.md and json_contract.rs updated together and the spelling matching cs show --json. me9.36 carries v: 1 on the Answer envelope (me9.36.1), rewrites the doc and its parsing test in one bead (me9.36.4), and as of today also carries the offset encoding - that requirement was folded into me9.36.1's notes and me9.36.4's acceptance rather than left implicit, so closing this does not drop it. Closed here to stop two workers colliding on the same envelope.

title: Wire google-takeout source: config candidate, dispatch, docs
description: Add the source to candidate_sources() in cs-archive/src/config.rs, dispatch it in cs/src/commands.rs::import_source, and register the module in cs-import/src/lib.rs.
design:
chatgpt-export is the precedent and it is NOT in candidate_sources(): an export-style source has no canonical home directory, so auto-detection cannot work and drift cannot meaningfully report it missing. google-takeout follows that - hand-added to config.toml, dispatched by id in commands.rs, and left out of candidate_sources() rather than given a fake default path.

include globs must not swallow the 311MB of NotebookLM source PDFs and .wav audio overviews - only the conversation files. globset's '*' does not cross '/', so the patterns can be specific.
notes: Unlike every other candidate source this one has no fixed home directory: it points at wherever exports are unpacked. chatgpt-export has the same property and is hand-added to config rather than auto-detected, so this follows that shape.
close_reason: Implemented and verified end to end against the real export: 11 files -> 1,280 conversations / 2,439 messages, split gemini-apps 1,133 / ai-mode 138 / gemini-workspace 7 / notebooklm 2. 535 workspace tests green, zero build warnings.

title: google_takeout importer: Gemini in Workspace + NotebookLM
description:
Two smaller formats in the same export.

Gemini in Workspace: 'Gemini in Workspace/Conversation History/conversation_<id>.txt' - JSON despite the .txt extension. {title, creation_time, last_modification_time, conversation_turns[]} with exactly two turn kinds, user_turn.prompt and system_turn.text[].data. 7 files, 32 turns.

NotebookLM: '<Notebook>/Chat History/Chat Session - <uuid>.html' - blank-line-separated blocks prefixed 'USER: ' or 'MODEL: ', each body an HTML fragment. 2 sessions, 24 turns. The notebook title comes from the sibling '<Notebook> metadata.json'.
design: NotebookLM's notebook title comes from the containing DIRECTORY NAME, not from the sibling metadata.json: an importer is a pure function over (logical_path, bytes) with no filesystem access (ADR 1), so it cannot open a neighbouring file. Takeout names the folder after the notebook, so the string is the same in practice. A title may be derived from a path; an id may not.
acceptance_criteria: 7 + 2 conversations; NotebookLM title falls back to the directory name when metadata.json is absent
close_reason: Implemented and verified end to end against the real export: 11 files -> 1,280 conversations / 2,439 messages, split gemini-apps 1,133 / ai-mode 138 / gemini-workspace 7 / notebooklm 2. 535 workspace tests green, zero build warnings.

title: HTML-to-text helper for response bodies
description: Three of the four formats carry HTML fragments rather than plain text: safeHtmlItem[].html in both activity logs, and every USER/MODEL block in NotebookLM. Needs block-level tags to become newlines, <li> to become a bullet, and entities decoded (& < > " ' "    ).
design: Hand-rolled rather than pulling in scraper/html5ever. The tag vocabulary is small and closed - p, ul, ol, li, h1-h6, blockquote, hr, br, strong, em, code, pre, a - and cs-import currently depends on nothing but serde_json and thiserror. A dependency that parses arbitrary HTML buys nothing against a fragment this regular.
close_reason: Implemented and verified end to end against the real export: 11 files -> 1,280 conversations / 2,439 messages, split gemini-apps 1,133 / ai-mode 138 / gemini-workspace 7 / notebooklm 2. 535 workspace tests green, zero build warnings.

title: google_takeout importer: MyActivity.json activity log
description: Gemini Apps + AI Mode both export a flat JSON array at 'My Activity/<product>/MyActivity.json'. Fields: header, title ('Prompted <full prompt>' | 'Created ...' | 'Used ...' | 'Searched for ...'), time (ISO-8601 UTC millis), products, activityControls, safeHtmlItem[].html (the response, on 1,070/1,173 Gemini Apps and 129/145 AI Mode records), subtitles[].name/.url (cited sources), attachedFiles[], imageFile.
design:
NO CONVERSATION ID EXISTS at any nesting level - MyActivity is a flat activity log, so one record becomes one two-message conversation rather than being regrouped by a time heuristic. A clustering-derived id would break ADR 16 permanence the first time the heuristic changed.

native_id = '<surface>/<time>'. Timestamps are unique within each file (1173/1173 and 145/145 distinct, verified) and are a property of the record rather than of the export, so the same logical record keeps its id across re-exports and a second export collapses onto the first instead of doubling the corpus - the same overlap-collapse property ADR 9 relies on for ChatGPT.
acceptance_criteria: 1,173 + 145 conversations from the real files; ids stable across two different export directories
close_reason: Implemented and verified end to end against the real export: 11 files -> 1,280 conversations / 2,439 messages, split gemini-apps 1,133 / ai-mode 138 / gemini-workspace 7 / notebooklm 2. 535 workspace tests green, zero build warnings.

title: Ingest Google Takeout: Gemini Apps, AI Mode, Workspace, NotebookLM
description:
A Google Takeout export holds four distinct conversation formats that this project cannot currently read. Measured against the real export at ~/dev/sandbox/chat-history/data/Takeout-gemini and Takeout-html: 1,173 Gemini Apps records, 145 AI Mode records, 7 Gemini in Workspace conversations, 2 NotebookLM chat sessions - ~1,327 conversations against a current corpus of 3,059.

The existing crates/cs-import/src/gemini.rs is for Gemini CLI session files and shares no format with any of these.
design:
ONE permanent source id 'google-takeout' (ADR 16), not four. The four formats are one export mechanism, and burning four permanent ids to describe one is worse than distinguishing them with Conversation::surface, which exists for exactly this and is explicitly never part of an id.

Importer dispatches on path shape, following the gemini.rs precedent of declining by shape rather than teaching the module the archive layout.
acceptance_criteria: cs index reads all four formats from the real export; cargo test --workspace green; cargo build --workspace --all-targets warning-free
close_reason: google-takeout ships. One permanent source id covering four formats, dispatched on path shape. Verified against the real export and against a simulated re-export: the same records arriving from a second export directory folded together into 1,271 conversations rather than doubling to 2,542, which is the ADR 9 overlap-collapse property the timestamp-keyed native_id was chosen for. Read-time regrouping of the flat activity log is left open as chat-search-o1i.5.

title: kind_runs is 35% of a search response and compresses only 1.9x
description:
Measured on the merged binary 2026-08-04, cs search --json --limit 60 against the live index: the response is 100 KB, of which kind_runs is 34 KB (35%). Runs per row: median 5, max 688. Drawn messages divided by runs is 1.90x - essentially no compression.

me9.19's design predicted runs would compress hard because tool traffic is 66-85% of volume and arrives in long stretches. It does arrive in stretches, but agent prose alternates with nearly every tool call, so the encoding is agent,1 / tool,N repeated hundreds of times. The premise was right about the volume and wrong about the runs.

The work itself is correct and tested - this is about what it costs on the wire for a mark drawn at 200x9px.
design:
NOT READY TO DECIDE, and deliberately parked rather than guessed at. The fold model may change (owner, 2026-08-04), and kind_runs counts DRAWN messages via cs_core::blocks::drawn - so any change to what a reader draws changes the runs directly. Deciding the payload shape before the fold shape settles would mean deciding it twice.

Options when it is time, cheapest first:
1. Downsample server-side to the ~200px the ribbon is actually drawn at. The strip cannot show 688 runs; it has ~200 columns. Sending full resolution for a mark that quantises it anyway is the clearest waste, and it is the only option that needs no client change.
2. Cap runs per conversation and say so in the payload, so a client knows it got a summary rather than the truth.
3. Leave it. 34 KB on a 10 ms path may simply not matter - me9.22 measured the whole seam at 5-13 ms with stdout at 111 KB, and the bottleneck was sqlite, not bytes.

Option 3 is not obviously wrong, which is part of why this is worth a decision rather than a reflex.

DO NOT decide this before the fold model settles.
acceptance_criteria: A decision recorded on which option applies, taken after the fold model is settled. If the answer is option 3, that is recorded too rather than left implicit.
notes:
Found at integration on 2026-08-04, not by the worker that wrote it - the cost is only visible once a real query runs against the merged binary.
From chat-search-me9.26 (2026-08-05), a number this decision now has that it did not: with idx_message_reading covering the shape query, FILLING kind_runs costs +1.8 to +9.8 ms in-process at limit 100 (49-100 rows, 10k-58k messages read). So the 34 KB on the wire is bought with single-digit milliseconds of server time, not with the +205 ms me9.19 was filed against. That weakens option 1 (downsample server-side) as a LATENCY argument — the sqlite read is the cost and downsampling does not avoid it, it only shrinks what is serialised afterwards. It leaves option 1's BYTES argument untouched. Option 3 (leave it) is correspondingly stronger than it was. Still parked behind the fold model, per this bead's own design.

title: Client language for the native surface: Swift, or keep the web front end
description:
chat-search-me9.22 produced a recommendation and the measurements behind it (poc/swift/RESULTS.md §7). This bead exists so the choice is ratified and written into docs/DECISIONS.md as an ADR rather than living in a poc/ findings file, which is not where this project keeps decisions.

RECOMMENDED: Swift for the client, with poc/ui kept as the design instrument it already is. The two are not competing.

The argument is equipment, not speed. Both clear a type-ahead budget through the subprocess seam, and the Swift client's own JSON decode was 1.2 ms against 21.7 ms of sqlite — the client's language is not on the critical path either way.

  - Virtualisation is free and correct. SwiftUI List: 13 ms to first frame for 3,059 rows and +5.2 MB after scrolling the whole corpus, because NSTableView recycles. poc/ui/NOTES.md §5 carries the same problem as an open item at a fifth of the row count.
  - The transport already exists. Process is in the standard library; the seam measured 8 ms p50 with nothing added. A browser-hosted front end needs a transport built for it — a local HTTP server or a Tauri-style IPC bridge — which is the infrastructure ADR 14 declined to build, arriving through a side door.
  - 31 MB idle, 35 MB with the whole corpus listed, from a 0.6 MB binary.
  - Focus, scroll physics, text selection, system appearance and accessibility all arrived unasked.

The framing in me9.22 — whether the prototype's ~3,700 lines of front end survive — did not survive inspection. poc/ui is a mockup over a 13 MB baked export with no transport, no client state, and by its own NOTES no empty, error or loading states. It was never a client. What it actually produced is NOTES.md and DESIGN-BRIEF.md, which are written in constraints and transfer to either language unchanged.
design:
What would overturn it, so the ADR can state a revisit condition rather than closing the question:

  - A settled design needing a graphic SwiftUI cannot draw well. The fused ribbon is the candidate and Canvas was NOT tested by the spike — that is the largest untested risk in the recommendation.
  - A reason to run anywhere but macOS.

Also worth writing into the ADR: the spike's most expensive bug was a Swift concurrency bug (RESULTS.md §2), not a Rust one. ADR 13 flags concurrency and FFI as the parts of Rust this project has never exercised; choosing Swift relocates that risk rather than retiring it, and the ADR should say so rather than let the choice read as risk-free.
acceptance_criteria: An ADR in docs/DECISIONS.md records the choice, the measurements it rests on, what was not tested (Canvas, packaging, accessibility), and the revisit condition. If the answer is 'not Swift', the same ADR records why the numbers were not decisive.
close_reason: Decided by the owner 2026-08-04: Swift over cs-core, keeping poc/ui as the design instrument. Matches me9.22's recommendation, which argued the 'do the prototype's 3,700 lines survive' framing was the wrong question - poc/ui is a mockup over a baked export with no transport, no client state and no empty/error/loading states, and what actually transfers is NOTES.md and DESIGN-BRIEF.md. Work tracked under me9.8, undeferred.

title: cs search --json: title and ended_date are nullable and nothing says so
description:
Found by chat-search-me9.22, the Swift spike — the first second client to decode the contract without reading the Rust structs that produce it.

conversation.title is null for 11 of 3,059 conversations and ended_date/ended_at for 2. Neither is documented as optional and neither appears in the first 10 rows of anything, so a client that types them as non-optional passes every hand test and then throws on a real result set. The Swift decoder failed at results[54] of a --limit 60 query, which is exactly the size a GUI asks for and exactly the size nobody tests by hand.

ADR 14 makes this contract load-bearing for every non-Rust surface. A field's nullability is part of the contract whether or not it is written down, and right now the only way to learn it is to hit it in production.
design:
Two candidate fixes, and they are not equivalent.

A. Document it. Add nullability to whatever states the contract (ADR 12 / the --json help) and leave the data alone. Cheap, honest, and every client still has to handle it.

B. Make it non-null at the source. A conversation with no title could emit "" and one with no timestamps could omit ended_date entirely rather than emitting null — an absent key and a null mean different things to most decoders, and absent is the one that says 'not applicable'. Note that 11 untitled conversations may itself be an import defect worth understanding before it is papered over.

Whichever is chosen, the general rule matters more than these two fields: a published JSON contract needs a written statement of which keys are optional, or the next client rediscovers this the same way.
acceptance_criteria: The nullability of every field in cs search --json is written down somewhere a client author will find it, and a test pins it. If the answer is 'these should never be null', the fix is at the source and the 11 untitled conversations are explained.
notes: branch: worktree-me9-27-json-contract (worktree at .claude/worktrees/me9-27-json-contract; the session was not auto-isolated, so it was made by hand)
close_reason:
Documented rather than changed at the source, on the evidence: all 11 untitled conversations are sessions whose every title candidate was harness machinery the importers decline on purpose (3 codex slash commands, 1 codex IDE block with an empty request section, 6 claude-code command expansions, 1 gemini-cli with no user turn at all), and both null ended_at rows are ChatGPT entries opened and abandoned with zero messages. Null is the right answer in every case, so option B would have erased a real distinction and broken a published contract to do it.

Shipped docs/JSON-CONTRACT.md — every field of the envelope, Group, Hit, Destination, Span and Run, each marked never-null / nullable / absent, with a section on what each of the six nulls means and one on the four arrays that are empty rather than null. Pinned by crates/cs/tests/json_contract.rs, which parses the doc's own tables and asserts both that a never-null key is null nowhere and that a nullable key is null somewhere; both mutations verified to fail. Also verified against the real 3,059-conversation index: key sets identical, nulls only where documented, all 1,809 spans of a broad query inside their snippet's bytes. Pointers added from cs search --help, ADR 12 and ARCHITECTURE.md.

Three findings filed rather than fixed: me9.32 (grouped absent under --flat), me9.33 (this contract has neither a version nor a name for its offset encoding while cs show --json has both), me9.34 (cs show --json still undocumented). Gate green: 509 tests, zero warnings from cargo build --workspace --all-targets.

branch: worktree-me9-27-json-contract

title: Prototype: choose one of the four visual directions
description:
poc/ui/directions.html now carries four named directions - terminal (the incumbent, and the control), paper, blueprint, ink - shown on the row and the ribbon at real size in both themes. All four hold every fenced measurement: the kind ramp stays on an even ~1.8x luminance step, the quiet text tier clears 4.5:1 on both grounds it lands on, and rows-per-screen is equal or better (terminal 66.3px/12, paper 64.9/12, blueprint 60.6/13, ink 65.3/12).

That is exactly why the measurements cannot choose. What is left is judgement, and it is not a worker's to make.
design:
Look at index.html?dir=<name> against the real 354-conversation sample, not only at the specimen page - the two costs found so far were both invisible on specimens. paper's serif is wide enough to wrap the left rail's WHEN heading onto two lines. blueprint sets the entire drawer transcript in mono, which is the one pane where the product stops being a list, and buys one row per screen for it.

A fifth direction that ignores all four is a better outcome than a refinement of one; the brief asked for directions, and these are worked answers rather than the answer.
acceptance_criteria: One direction named as the working answer, or a fifth asked for. If one is chosen, its tokens fold into styles.css and directions.css keeps the rest as the record of what was considered.
notes: NOT A GATE ON THE NATIVE APP'S FIRST PHASE (recorded 2026-08-05). me9.8 now names poc/ui/index.html at default as the visual and layout reference for that phase, and index.html with no ?dir= renders terminal, which directions.css defines as styles.css exactly as it stands. So the reference is fully determined without answering this bead. 4ar.12 blocks only me9.8.6 (P3, last) and 4ar.13; me9.8.1/.2/.3/.4/.5 do not reference it. Still worth answering on its own merits - the two observed costs are on the live pages rather than the specimens - but nothing in the build is waiting.
close_reason:
DECIDED 2026-08-05 by Tyler Crosse: terminal, the incumbent — and decided by naming poc/ui/index.html itself as the target for the initial native app rather than by picking a name off the list.

Those are the same answer. index.html opened with no ?dir= renders terminal, which directions.css defines as styles.css exactly as it stands, so 'build what index.html shows' and 'apply the terminal direction' specify the same pixels. The difference is which one is the artifact: the mockup is, and the direction list is not.

That makes the four-direction framing the thing that went out of date rather than the work behind it. 4ar.11's findings are not discarded and are not conditional on which direction won: palette.py's ramp solver, the surface token layer that makes a direction ~40 declarations rather than a fork, and the --verify pass that caught the quiet tier sitting at 4.23:1 on --panel all apply to the incumbent, because the incumbent was fixed alongside the other three.

The two costs 4ar.12 was filed to weigh are now moot rather than unresolved — paper's serif wrapping the left rail's WHEN heading, and blueprint setting the whole drawer transcript in mono. Neither is a property of the incumbent.

Scoped to the INITIAL app. A visual direction is ~40 declarations over a surface layer precisely so that revisiting it later is cheap; if a redesign is wanted after the app exists and can be looked at, re-file it then against a real surface instead of against specimens. That is a better question than this one was.
