title: The query log records keystrokes and benchmarks, so the eval harvest would inherit both
description:
chat-search-6eb.21 harvests an eval set from the query log, and its trigger is "roughly 50-100 picks across 20+ distinct queries". Measured against ~/.chat-archive/queries.jsonl on 2026-08-04: 919 search events, 37 picks, 124 distinct query strings. That is about halfway to the trigger, so there is still time to fix what the log is recording before the harvest depends on it.

Three problems, all of which would survive into the generated eval set:

1. PREFIX LADDERS. The TUI logs a Search per keystroke (the sink in crates/cs/src/tui.rs, gated on cfg.log_queries), and cs needs folds by literal query text. So one typed query becomes seven rows: l, la, lau, laun, launc, launch, launchd, each with 12 searches. sqlite fts5 contributes ten rows, ratatui preview seven. This is not confined to the search side — it is already in the pick data: deep learn and deep learning both have picks, as do bead/beads and organize/organize convers. 6eb.21 converts "each Need into a [[query]] with q = the literal text", so the harvested set would carry fragments as separate queries, and the 20+ distinct queries bar clears spuriously while real distinct needs is nearer 13.

2. BENCHMARK CONTAMINATION. The three highest-volume queries in the log are borrow checker (99 searches), the (76) and commits (51), with zero picks between them. Those are the queries typed to measure performance in chat-search-6eb.30, chat-search-6eb.38 and chat-search-e2n, not information needs. 6eb.21 carries unpicked queries across deliberately, as evidence of a search the ranking failed, which is right for a real abandoned search and wrong for a benchmark.

3. EMPTY-QUERY PICKS. 12 of the 37 picks have q = "", which is the TUI recent list being browsed rather than a search being answered. A pick with no query is not a relevance judgement and must not become a grade-3.
design:
Not obviously a logging fix or a folding fix, and the bead should not pre-decide it.

Logging less is the cheaper answer and loses information: a settled-query-only log cannot tell you which prefix a user gave up on, and abandonment is exactly what 6eb.21 wants to keep.

Folding better keeps everything and puts the rule in cs needs and the harvest: collapse a ladder to its longest member when the shorter ones are strict prefixes within the same session, and let the Search events stay as they are. Note the Event enum (crates/cs-core/src/querylog.rs) has no session or generation field today, so "within the same session" may need one — which is a schema question worth answering before more log accumulates under the old shape.

Benchmark contamination is separate and probably wants a different lever: either benchmarking runs with log_queries off, or the log records enough to tell a driven run from a human one. The first is free and retroactively useless; the existing 919 events would need excluding by hand either way.

Whatever is chosen, the existing log is the test case: the rule is right when it turns these 943 events into something close to the 13 real needs a human would count.
acceptance_criteria: cs needs reports needs rather than keystrokes: a query typed one character at a time appears once, not once per prefix. Benchmark traffic is either kept out of the log or distinguishable within it, and the 919 events already accumulated are dealt with explicitly rather than silently carried into the eval set. A pick with an empty query does not become a judgement. The fold is demonstrated against the real ~/.chat-archive/queries.jsonl, not only fixtures, and the resulting distinct-need count is recorded so chat-search-6eb.21's 20+ distinct queries trigger can be read honestly.
notes: branch: bead-6eb44-query-log-fold
close_reason:
cs needs folds needs rather than keystrokes, and the log's 2,720 accumulated
events were dealt with by hand rather than carried.

The fold (cs_core::querylog::fold, was needs()) collapses a search into whatever
followed it when the follower repeated or extended its text under the same
filter within UNREAD_MS. Two seconds is measured, not chosen: the slowest gap
inside a ladder in the real log is 1,328 ms and the next one up is 10.9 s. A
pick never collapses, so no judgement is folded away. A pick with no query is
counted as browsing and never becomes a need.

Benchmarks got both levers the bead's design named. CS_LOG_QUERIES=0 keeps a
driven run out of the log going forward and wraps subprocesses, which --config
does not; verified end to end against the real config. Event::Driven declares a
half-open span as machine-driven after the fact, appended by
`cs needs --driven FROM..UNTIL --why`, because a benchmark query is ordinary
text that goes unpicked and so is indistinguishable by shape from the abandoned
search 6eb.21 wants to keep. That asymmetry is ADR 22.

Demonstrated against the real ~/.chat-archive/queries.jsonl, and applied to it:
2,720 events -> 93 needs on the fold alone; six declared spans covering 2,641
events -> 35 needs, 19 judgements across 17 answered queries. No span excluded a
pick, and the original 2,720 lines are byte-identical (append-only; a copy is at
~/.chat-archive/queries.jsonl.bak-6eb44, safe to delete). Raw, the log had read
as 37 picks across 124 distinct strings — nearly 6eb.21's trigger. It is about a
third of the way there, and cs needs now prints both numbers so it cannot be
misread again. Recorded in ADR 22, evals/README.md and a note on 6eb.21.

Two corrections to the bead's premises, both in ADR 22. The TUI does not log per
keystroke — it writes one event per session — so the ladders came from
benchmark drivers calling cs search per prefix, and no session field was needed.
And a fix found by using it: a driven span ending in the future is refused,
since `..tomorrow` is the natural way to write one and would silently discard a
day of real searches.

Left undone deliberately: 2026-07-31 08:36-08:51 is a mixed session (a cs pick
smoke test beside one real pick) and was not spanned. chat-search-6eb.45 filed
for the AGENTS.md line about CS_LOG_QUERIES, which cannot be committed from here
because AGENTS.md is untracked.

Gate green: cargo test --workspace 522 passing across 12 binaries, cargo build
--workspace --all-targets clean.

title: A covering index would make the conversation shape close to free, and retire SearchOptions::shape
description:
Group::kind_runs is opt-in (SearchOptions::shape, default off) purely because of what it costs to read. The query selects role, kind, is_error for every head-path message of every returned conversation. message stores text inline and no index covers those columns, so SQLite walks the fat rows: 324 MB of table to read three narrow columns.

MEASURED on the real index (2026-08-04, medians of 5 warm runs, release build), cost of turning the shape on:
  limit  20, 'commits'         13.1 ->  20.9 ms   (+7.8)
  limit  20, 'the'             75.8 ->  91.9 ms   (+16.1)
  limit  50, 'borrow checker'  27.5 ->  57.0 ms   (+29.5)
  limit 354, 'commits'         82.2 -> 143.0 ms   (+60.8)
  limit 354, 'the'            213.8 -> 418.9 ms   (+205.1)
The 354 conversations that broad query returns hold 108,192 messages between them, so this is ~4 microseconds per message and it scales with conversations returned rather than with matches in them. That is why the TUI, which re-searches on every keystroke, must not pay it: chat-search-4ar already bought back typeahead milliseconds elsewhere.

An index on (conv_id, on_head_path, is_sidechain, thread_key, seq, role, kind, is_error) would answer the query from the index alone. ~184k rows of narrow columns, so single-digit MB. Adding an index is compatible with the disposable-index rule -- it is not a column and rm index.db && cs index still rebuilds everything -- but it needs measuring, not assuming: index build time is part of the ~7s rebuild, and a wide index may not beat the table walk by as much as it looks.
design: If the numbers hold, SearchOptions::shape can default on and then be deleted, and cs/src/commands.rs stops choosing per surface. Do not delete the flag before the measurement: an always-on shape at today's cost is a typeahead regression paid on every keystroke for a strip the TUI does not draw.
acceptance_criteria: The shape costs little enough at TUI limits to be unconditional, measured the same way as the numbers above, or the bead closes saying the index did not pay and the flag stays.
notes:
2026-08-04, from a tracker audit. Raised P3 -> P2 to match what it gates: chat-search-me9.31 is P2 and depends on this, which in turn blocks chat-search-me9.25. Scope unchanged.
branch: worktree-me9-26-shape-index (worktree .claude/worktrees/me9-26-shape-index). Commit 0fa5141 adds idx_message_reading and drops idx_message_thread; gate green. Still open: the rebuild-cost A/B, and the decision on SearchOptions::shape — measured at the TUI's own limit of 100 with prefix queries the shape still costs +2 to +12 ms per keystroke with the index (down from +7 to +80), against the 1.4-6.4 ms synchronous search TUI-DESIGN rests on, for a strip the TUI does not draw. Leaning: keep the flag.
branch: worktree-me9-26-shape-index (worktree .claude/worktrees/me9-26-shape-index). Both open items done in 7d6d60f. REBUILD A/B: interleaved, 10 alternating full rebuilds of 4,490 convs / 207,857 msgs — medians 9.40 s with the covering index vs 9.71 s without, paired deltas -1.0 to +1.1 s, +4.4 MB on 388 MB. No measurable cost. The commit's earlier 12-15 s vs 9.7 s was warm-up drift: rounds 1-5 ran 9.7-12.2 s and rounds 6-10 ran 7.6-9.1 s whichever schema was running. SHAPE DECISION: flag stays. In-process at limit 100 on one connection (what cs-tui holds), shape adds +1.8 to +9.8 ms, down from +5.4 to +30.4 without the index — the per-message constant fell ~520 ns to ~180 ns, so the index paid, but the work is still proportional to messages in returned conversations (10k-58k per keystroke at limit 100). An ordinary query searches in 0.4-0.8 ms there, so unconditional shape = a keystroke 5-7x longer for a strip the TUI does not draw.
pr: https://github.com/tylercrosse/chat-search/pull/39
2026-08-06: merged main (d8e22c1) and re-took both measurements against it (1be54dc), since main landed sittings + importer v5 after the numbers were taken. Conclusions unchanged. Shape at limit 100 now +2.00 to +11.11 ms (was +1.8 to +9.8) against searches of 0.5-1.1 ms, so ~5x the keystroke rather than 5-7x; per-message constant 195 ns with the index vs 570 without, linear within 4% over 10k-56k messages. Rebuild A/B re-run: medians 7.54 s vs 7.59 s, median paired delta 0 ms. NEW FACT from sittings: fill_shape runs once per sitting member, so the broad prefix returning 100 rows issues 196 shape reads — cost follows conversations, not rows. PR 39 mergeable, CI green on macos+ubuntu+msrv.
close_reason: Both open items measured; the index stays and the flag stays with it. Rebuild A/B interleaved over 10 alternating full rebuilds: no measurable cost (medians 9.40 s with, 9.71 s without, +4.4 MB on 388 MB) — the earlier 12-15 s vs 9.7 s reading was machine warm-up, not the schema. SearchOptions::shape is NOT retired: the covering index cut the per-message constant ~520 ns to ~180 ns, but the cost is still proportional to messages in returned conversations, so at the TUI's limit of 100 the shape adds +1.8 to +9.8 ms in-process against searches that take 0.4-0.8 ms — a keystroke 5-7x longer for a strip the TUI does not draw. That is the second branch of the acceptance criteria. Shipped in 7d6d60f on worktree-me9-26-shape-index: the numbers and the reasoning recorded on the flag itself, the rebuild A/B recorded beside the DDL, and two EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN tests pinning that the shape is answered from the index alone and that reading a conversation in order costs no sort — the claim idx_message_thread made in a comment for its whole life with nothing behind it. Gate green: cargo test --workspace and cargo build --workspace --all-targets, zero warnings. No follow-up beads filed; nothing was left undone.

title: match_seqs and kind_runs are two different coordinate spaces, so a client cannot draw both on one strip
description:
cs search --json now carries kind_runs (chat-search-me9.19), a run-length shape in blocks::READING_ORDER over DRAWN messages only. match_seqs is a list of raw message.seq values, documented as positions relative to msg_count. The two do not index the same thing, in two independent ways:

1. ORDER. seq is per-thread (ADR 4), so on a multi-thread conversation the two orders are simply different. preview.rs::anchor already records this for its own case and refuses to use match_seqs for it. 28 of the 354 conversations a broad query returns are multi-thread, up to 10 threads.

2. DENOMINATOR. kind_runs omits successful tool_results (blocks::drawn) because a strip position a reader cannot click is a lie. Those are 34% of the corpus. So sum(kind_runs) is well below msg_count: 563 against 937 on a real conversation, 1479 against 2553 on the longest.

The consequence is concrete: the prototype draws a match tick at (seq / n) along the ribbon. Fed real data, every tick after the first tool result lands early, and on a conversation with a subagent it can land in the wrong thread entirely.

Deciding what to do is the work here, not just doing it. Options: emit match positions in the same drawn-reading-order space beside match_seqs; or emit a per-match msg_id and let the client resolve; or state on the wire that match_seqs is a different space and give clients a rule. The first costs a lookup per match, the second is what cs show already does, the third is free and honest but leaves the strip unable to show matches.
design: Whatever lands must not silently redefine match_seqs: it is a published field (ADR 12) and cs-tui::match_density reads it against msg_count today. Additive is the only safe direction.
acceptance_criteria: A client can place a match on the same axis kind_runs describes, without re-deriving either order. A test pins it on a multi-thread conversation containing a successful tool_result.

title: Dispatch beads to Codex workers from bd-dispatch
description: bd-dispatch only speaks 'claude --bg --agent bd-worker'. Add an --engine=codex path so ready beads can be fanned out to detached 'codex exec' workers in their own worktrees. Deliverable lives in ~/.claude (skills/bd-dispatch, agents/bd-worker), not this repo; filed here for traceability since this is the tracker the workers drive.
acceptance_criteria: /bd-dispatch --engine=codex claims a bead, creates a worktree, launches a detached codex exec worker that reads the same bd-worker contract, and the worker can run bd writes (claim/close/gate) and the project gate from inside its sandbox.
notes: codex sandbox write probe
close_reason: Added --engine=codex to bd-dispatch: dispatch-codex.sh claims a bead, creates its worktree, symlinks the gitignored AGENTS.md in, and launches a detached codex exec worker fed the same bd-worker contract. bd-review gained a Codex worker panel so live workers are not mistaken for dead claims. Verified end to end on chat-search-n8b.

title: No client can ask which sources are configured, only which ones produced rows
description:
cs-core knows only what the index contains. A grep for "configured" across crates/cs-core/src returns nothing: the source inventory it can answer questions about is the set of sources that produced rows, not the set a machine is configured to capture.

The config and the detection both live in cs-archive — cs_archive::drift::detect (chat-search-a7k.12) already computes exactly the three states a client needs: configured-and-present, configured-but-missing, and detected-but-unconfigured. It reports them as a printed line in cs archive, not as a value any other crate can read.

So a client asking "which sources exist, and which of them have zero rows" cannot be answered, and chat-search-me9.14 — the facet bar showing coverage state — cannot be built. chat-search-me9.16 hit this exact wall on the way past: its close reason records "me9.14 zero-row chip still needs config the TUI cannot see."

This is the same shape the project already names in CLAUDE.md: a rule lives in exactly one place. Three clients each deriving the source inventory from a different place is how the local-date bug happened.
design:
The deliverable is a value, not a printed line: cs-core returns the source inventory with per-source coverage state, and every client renders from it.

Open question worth settling in the bead rather than in code — cs-core does not read config today, and giving it a config dependency may be the wrong direction. The alternative is cs-archive exporting drift::detect's result as a public type and clients joining it against index counts themselves, which keeps the config reader in one crate but puts the join in every client. Whichever way it goes, the join rule must exist once.

Note that the zero-rows-vs-never-ran distinction matters and is not derivable from the index: a source with zero rows because its importer threw looks identical to one that was configured this morning.
acceptance_criteria: A client can ask for the full source inventory and get, per source, whether it is configured, whether its directory is present, and how many conversations it indexed — without reading config itself or reimplementing the join. cs-tui and the CLI per-source table both render from that one answer. A source configured with zero indexed rows is distinguishable from a source that was never configured.
notes:
branch: worktree-agent-a2c8bedc20c662309
Settled the design open question in favour of a third option the bead did not name. Not 'cs-core reads config' and not 'each client joins drift::detect against index counts' (the acceptance criteria rules the second out - the join is a rule and must exist once). Instead cs-core takes the facts: cs_core::inventory::of(conn, &[Watched{id, configured, present}]) unions the watched set with the index census and returns the four cells of configured x present as names (live/missing/unconfigured/retired), with the conversation count as a separate field. cs-core still reads no config, and cs-tui - which depends on cs-core and nothing else - can name the result type, which it could not have done had this lived in cs-archive. Recorded in docs/TUI-DESIGN.md section 1 and docs/GLOSSARY.md rather than as a new ADR: it applies ADR 14 and the existing crate boundary rather than changing either.
close_reason: cs_core::inventory joins what the config watches against what the index holds and returns it as a value: per source, the four cells of configured x present (live/missing/unconfigured/retired) plus the conversation count, so a configured source with zero rows is distinguishable from one nobody configured. cs-core still reads no config - the caller supplies Watched{id, configured, present}. Both clients render from that one answer: cs status lists every source the machine knows about with coverage and conversations (replacing exists), and the TUI's read_facets is gone in favour of the same join. 591 tests green, zero-warning build. Not done here, and left with me9.14 which this unblocks: the dim/marked chip styling and the explained empty state a zero chip selects. Also noted for me9.29: when the index cannot be read at all, cs status reports counts as 0 - index.state names two of the four reasons and the other two warn on stderr.

title: Spike: a Swift surface over cs search --json, to answer Swift-or-web before committing
description: The interface prototype in poc/ui answers information-design questions and structurally cannot answer interaction ones: does typing into it feel fast against 3,059 conversations, does a list that size need virtualisation, what is on screen while the index rebuilds. Those need a running client. This is the smallest one that answers them AND answers the question that decides everything downstream - whether the surface is Swift or web tech - because that is what decides whether the prototype's ~3,700 lines of front end survive.
design:
SCOPE, deliberately small: a search field, a result list fed by cs search --json, and nothing else. No reader pane, no ribbon, no grouping.

TRANSPORT: spawn cs search --json over argv. Measured 2026-08-04 at ~10ms end to end warm, and ADR 14 explicitly sanctions exactly this for non-Rust clients. Do NOT build cs serve --stdio first - the transport should follow the direction, not lead it, and a spike that needs no new infrastructure is one that can be thrown away honestly.

WHAT IT HAS TO ANSWER, in order:
1. Does typing feel fast when every keystroke spawns a process? This is the one number that decides whether --stdio is urgent or can wait.
2. Does a 3,000-row list need virtualisation, and what does SwiftUI do at that size?
3. What is on screen while the index is being rebuilt, and while no index exists at all? ADR 14 requires clients to treat both as first-class states rather than transport errors, and the prototype has no empty, error or loading states anywhere.
4. What does the FFI story actually feel like? ADR 13 flags concurrency, async and FFI as the parts of Rust this project has never exercised, and this is the cheapest place to find out.

WHY NOW AND NOT LATER: the seam is already at C and already implemented - me9.17 confirmed Block serialises with no presentation attached - so the expensive axis is settled and what is left is packaging. Fig 02 of the design-space artifact: the seam is months and one-way, the mechanism is about a week and reversible. This spike is on the reversible side.

EXPLICIT NON-GOAL: a reader pane. cs show --json exists, but tool_summary and recognition_line are still in cs-tui (me9.20), so a Swift reader would either render raw message text or reimplement them - and reimplementing them is the duplication me9.17 exists to stop. Add the reader after me9.20, not before.
acceptance_criteria: A Swift binary that searches the real index and lists results. Written down: the measured keystroke latency, whether the list needed virtualisation, and what it did with no index present. A recommendation on Swift versus keeping the web front end, with the reason.
notes:
Filed 2026-08-04. Reordered ahead of cs serve --stdio deliberately: the earlier sequencing had the transport first, which is building infrastructure for a direction not yet confirmed.
branch: worktree-me9-22-swift-spike (worktree .claude/worktrees/me9-22-swift-spike). Deliverable poc/swift/RESULTS.md. Filed me9.27, me9.28 (P1), me9.29 from contract defects the spike surfaced.
close_reason:
Shipped poc/swift: a SwiftUI client over 'cs search --json' (919 non-comment lines incl. the bench harness) plus poc/swift/RESULTS.md, which is the deliverable. All four questions answered with measurements against the live 3,059-conversation index, re-derivable from five scripted benches.

Typing: 29-40 ms keystroke-to-frame at --limit 10, 44 of 47 keystrokes rendering, no debounce. The seam is 5-13 ms and barely moves; fork/exec is 0.3 ms. List: SwiftUI List virtualises for free (13 ms, +5.2 MB over the whole corpus) where LazyVStack leaks 65 MB per pass and VStack costs 1,585 ms and 566 MB. No index: three distinct conditions produce one English sentence on stderr, and a rebuild has a ~5 s window of silently partial successful answers. Recommendation: Swift for the client, poc/ui kept as the design instrument — on equipment rather than speed.

The most useful finding was a bug in the spike itself: the naive transport parks three threads per keystroke against an eight-wide pool and measured as 85 ms of transport cost that did not exist. Recorded in RESULTS.md §2 because a --stdio transport built on that evidence would have been built for nothing.

Filed from contract defects only a second client could surface: me9.27 (title/ended_date nullable, undocumented), me9.28 P1 (rebuild invisible, partial answers look complete), me9.29 (no error contract; --json pretty-printed at 1.56x). me9.30 files the language choice as a decision for docs/DECISIONS.md, since a recommendation in a poc/ file is not where this project keeps decisions.

Not done, deliberately: no reader pane (blocked on me9.20), no Canvas/ribbon drawing, no packaging, no --stdio, no FFI. Gate green: 485 tests pass, cargo build --workspace --all-targets and swift build -c release both zero-warning.

title: Emit kind runs in cs search --json, so a client can draw a conversation's shape
description: cs search --json carries match_seqs (where the query landed) but no per-message kinds, so no client can draw the density strip the interface prototype puts on every row: user / agent prose / reasoning / tool traffic, run-length encoded over the message index. cs show --json emits per-message kinds but is the wrong tool here - one process and one full transcript per conversation, against 354 rows on screen. THIS BEAD IS THE EMIT HALF ONLY: cs-core, no poc/ui. Drawing it is the consume half, split out so the prototype has one owner while a visual pass is in flight.
design:
Smallest correct shape is a run-length encoding on Group, not a kind per message: the strip is drawn at ~200x9px and tool traffic is 66-85% of volume arriving in long stretches, so runs compress hard. Something like kind_runs: [[kind, count], ...].

ORDERING IS LOAD-BEARING: it must match cs_core::blocks::load - ORDER BY is_sidechain, thread_key, seq - or the strip will not line up with what cs show returns for the same conversation. seq alone interleaves threads; that bug is already recorded in blocks.rs.

Reuse cs_core::blocks::Block::drawn so undrawn messages do not occupy strip positions a reader cannot click. Do NOT re-derive that rule - it is in cs-core precisely so it is not written twice.

FILES: crates/cs-core/src/search.rs (Group, line 828) and its query. render_groups in cs/src/commands.rs serialises Group wholesale, so the CLI needs no change.
acceptance_criteria: cs search --json emits per-conversation kind runs summing to the drawn message count. The ordering matches cs_core::blocks::load, with a test pinning that against a multi-thread conversation. No poc/ui files are touched.
notes:
branch: worktree-bead-me9-19-kind-runs  (worktree: .claude/worktrees/bead-me9-19-kind-runs)

NOTE FOR WHOEVER LANDS THIS: the branch opens with a commit (40c68a2) carrying me9.17's work verbatim. That work was closed but existed only as uncommitted changes in the shared checkout — no commit in this repository contained crates/cs-core/src/blocks.rs — and me9.19 builds directly on it. Not one byte was edited. If me9.17 lands from its own tree first, the content is identical and 40c68a2 drops out of a rebase.
close_reason:
cs search --json carries kind_runs: [[band,count],...] over user|agent|reasoning|tool, in blocks::READING_ORDER, counting only drawn messages. Band, band(), drawn(), Run, runs() and READING_ORDER live in cs_core::blocks beside the rules they belong to; Block::drawn now delegates so there is still one copy. Verified against cs show on all 354 conversations a broad query returns (108,192 messages, 28 multi-thread, up to 10 threads): identical runs, identical order, sums matching drawn exactly. 501 tests green, zero warnings.

One departure from the filed design, on measurement: the field is opt-in (SearchOptions::shape, default off, set by cs search --json) rather than always filled, because filling it costs +4-30 ms at TUI-sized limits and +205 ms at 354 rows, and the TUI re-searches on every keystroke while drawing match_density rather than a band strip. So the CLI did need the one-line change the design said it would not. me9.26 is the covering index that could retire the flag, filed with the numbers.

Filed: me9.25 (match_seqs is a different coordinate space, so match ticks cannot go on this axis yet), me9.26 (covering index). me9.23 has notes on what to consume.

title: Move the collapsed forms to cs-core, so outline mode is reproducible by any client
description: me9.17 moved the block model but left tool_summary and recognition_line in cs-tui/src/preview.rs. Both are content extraction rather than presentation - which argument identifies a tool call, and which one line stands in for a whole message - and both are already duplicated: poc/ui/export.py has call_detail() doing the first, and app.js renders it. A client reading cs show --json today can list messages but cannot reproduce outline mode, which is the mode that makes a long conversation legible.
design: Move tool_summary and recognition_line to cs_core::blocks, returning content only. The sigils that front them - the gear, the ellipsis, the cross - stay in the client, same line me9.17 drew for mark_kind: core states what the line says, the client decides how it looks. recognition_line returns (byte offset, text) so a caller can still rebase marks onto it; that offset is load-bearing and is what the rebase tests pin.
acceptance_criteria: cs_core::blocks owns both functions with their tests. cs-tui renders from them. A JSON client can build an outline row without reimplementing either. export.py's call_detail is deleted or reduced to calling cs show.
notes:
2026-08-04, from a tracker audit. Raised P3 -> P2 to match what it gates: chat-search-me9.8.3 and chat-search-me9.24 both depend on this, and me9.8.3 is P2, so the queue was showing a P2 waiting on a P3. Scope is unchanged — this is still the move of tool_summary and recognition_line described above.
branch: worktree-bead-me9-20-collapsed-forms (worktree .claude/worktrees/me9-20-collapsed-forms, branched off main)
close_reason:
cs_core::blocks owns tool_summary, recognition_line and offset_lines with their tests, plus Block::collapsed which picks between them; cs show --json carries the collapsed line and the offset it was lifted from, so a JSON client builds an outline row and rebases its marks without re-deriving anything. cs-tui keeps only the sigil and the style; cs show's text form reads its outline from core too, deleting a third copy. export.py's call_detail is gone - it asks cs show instead.

Two things beyond a pure move, both measured against the real index. Deleting call_detail proved it was not a duplicate: it answered for 88% of tool calls where tool_summary managed 34%, agreeing exactly where both answered, so the union is folded in (cmd alongside command, 25,790 calls; apply_patch targets, 4,366; the prose argument keys). The raw-body fallback for the 13.3% of non-JSON bodies is deliberately not folded in - an_unparseable_body_still_yields_the_tool_name is an existing decision - and chat-search-2rr asks whether it was made against that shape.

Also fixed a latent bug the move made load-bearing: the argv branch of tool_summary never flattened newlines, so 469 calls collapsed to something that was not a line. Harmless while only ratatui read it, wrong once cs show printed it and the wire published it as a row.

Gate green: 590 tests, zero warnings from cargo build --workspace --all-targets. Verified end to end against ~/.chat-archive/index.db throughout - offsets checked over a 2,431-message conversation and a multi-byte sample with zero mismatches. collapsed.at is null for a synthesised tool_call line, the first null in cs show --json; JSON-CONTRACT.md updated to say so.

title: A conversation reports one model, and the two importers disagree about which one
description:
conversation.model is a single TEXT column and there is no per-message model anywhere in the index, so 'did the model change mid-conversation' is unanswerable — even though the archive carries the answer. claude-code JSONL records message.model on every assistant turn.

Worse, the two importers collapse it in opposite directions and neither says so:

  crates/cs-import/src/claude_desktop.rs:167
      if let Some(m) = text(message, "model") { model = Some(m); }
      inside the per-record loop, so the LAST model seen wins.

  crates/cs-import/src/chatgpt_export.rs:165
      if model.is_none() { model = ...model_slug... }
      so the FIRST model seen wins.

A conversation where the model was switched therefore reports a different answer depending on which importer read it, and nothing anywhere records that a switch happened. Both behaviours are silent and untested — the claude_desktop tests only cover the single-model and init-record cases.
design:
Two questions, and the second depends on the first.

1. Make the collapse consistent and deliberate. Whichever rule wins - first, last, or 'the model of the head message' - it should be one rule, stated, and covered by a test that feeds a conversation with two models. This is the part that is unambiguously a bug.

2. Decide whether a model switch is worth representing at all. If yes the natural home is a per-message column, since that is the shape of the source data, and it is a pure function of the archive so it costs nothing but width. It would also let the preview show where a switch happened, which for a long agentic conversation is a real epistemic boundary. If no, then conversation.model should be documented as 'the model this conversation mostly ran on' rather than implying it is the model.

Do not guess at (2) before measuring it, and it cannot be measured from the index today - that is the point. The measurement has to run against the archive.
acceptance_criteria: One collapse rule, shared by both importers, stated where the next reader looks, with a test that feeds a conversation carrying two models and pins the answer. claude_desktop.rs and chatgpt_export.rs no longer disagree by accident. The second question is answered rather than left open: either a model switch is representable per-message, in which case it is a pure function of the archive and rides an IMPORTER_VERSION bump, or it is deliberately not represented and the reason is recorded so the vacuous zero-of-3059 measurement is not repeated.
notes:
Found while checking whether model changes were worth visualising in the interface prototype. I had claimed '0 of 3,059 conversations use more than one model'; that measurement was vacuous - it joined conversation.model to each message and counted distinct, which is 1 by construction. Corrected in poc/ui/NOTES.md section 3.

Related and separate: compaction boundaries are visible in message text (11 conversations, always claude-code, always mid-stream) but are not represented structurally either. See chat-search-n58.26 if filed.
branch: worktree-agent-aab8024d0b2ccf16c
close_reason: One collapse rule, in the indexer's rollup: a conversation is labelled with the model of the last message that named one, ordered by ts. All five importers stopped collapsing privately; message.model now carries what produced each message (IMPORTER_VERSION 5). Measured first against the archive since the index could not say — 166 of 3,134 conversations name more than one model, so the switch is represented rather than documented away (ADR 23). Also fixed 134 ChatGPT conversations labelled 'auto' (the router setting) and claude_desktop's missing <synthetic> filter. Full corpus: 195 labels change, zero disagree with the rule. branch: worktree-agent-aab8024d0b2ccf16c

title: Query grammar has no facet for topic or time range
description:
cs_core::query::Facet is {Agent, Dir, Date} and nothing else. The interface prototype now narrows the list by two things the grammar cannot express: a topic chip and a timeline range from the scrubber.

TUI-DESIGN section 5 and chat-search-me9.16 both settle that query text is the only filter state, and me9.16 shipped that for the TUI by making a facet click rewrite the query via Query::toggling. A filter with no grammar cannot be rewritten into the text, so it becomes exactly the second source of truth those two decisions exist to prevent - and it is invisible when copied out, unreplayable from a log, and unavailable to cs search.

The prototype currently draws these as tokens with a dashed border meaning 'narrowing the list, but not typeable'. That is honest, not a fix.
design:
Two candidates, different weights.

date: already parses DateSpec::{Day, Younger(Age)} - today, yesterday, week, month, <7d, <2w. A scrubber produces an absolute window, so it needs a range form, e.g. date:2026-07-28..2026-08-02, plus Older/Between variants in DateSpec and the SQL to match. Contained, and it also gives the CLI something it cannot say today.

topic: is larger and should probably not be a Facet at all. A seeded topic is already expressible as a collection - matches(query) union pinned minus excluded - so 'topic:rust-and-cargo' is really a named saved query, which lands in library.db (ADR 3) rather than in the grammar. That makes this depend on the authored store rather than on query.rs.

Recommend doing the date range first and alone. It is the one that is genuinely a grammar gap; the topic one is a question about where authored names live.
acceptance_criteria: Either the grammar expresses what a client narrows by, or the client stops offering it. Concretely: a timeline scrubber produces an arbitrary bounded window, and DateSpec today is {Day, Younger, Older} with no way to type one, so either date: grows a bounded-range form that Query::toggling can rewrite into the text, or the scrubber is cut. Same test for the topic chip, which additionally has no data source until chat-search-6eb.24 or chat-search-6eb.18 land. No filter survives as a dashed-border not-typeable token in a shipped client. Whatever ships is reachable from cs search, copyable out of the box, and replayable from a query log.
notes:
Surfaced by the interface-prototype IA pass (chat-search-4ar.9 / 4ar.11). Neither blocks the prototype - both are drawn and both work - but the prototype is currently modelling a filter model the core cannot express, and that gap should be a decision rather than an accident.
branch: worktree-me9-18-date-range (worktree at ~/dev/projects/.chat-search-worktrees/me9-18-date-range, 2 commits off 998e732)
pr: https://github.com/tylercrosse/chat-search/pull/33
close_reason: date: grew the absolute half-open span the scrubber needs — date:2026-07-28..2026-08-02, either end optional, and a lone YYYY-MM-DD for the day it names — with the separator, reading and bound spellings taken from cs pick --driven so there is one grammar for a span rather than two. Query::toggling rewrites it into the query text like any other filter, no SQL changed (search already binds both edges of a Window), and Window::value_in renders a dragged pair of instants back into typeable text so no client re-implements the rule. Verified end to end against the 358 MB index: 47 + 11 = 58 across two abutting spans, so the half-open edges tile. The topic half is answered rather than built — a seeded topic is a named saved query in library.db (ADR 3), not a facet, and it has no taxonomy until 6eb.24 or 6eb.18 lands; written up in TUI-DESIGN §5 and filed as chat-search-me9.40, with the macOS GROUP control's dashed topic chip repointed at it. It stays dashed because it is a grouping axis nobody can offer, not a filter applied where nobody can see it; poc/ui's prototype topic chip is untouched, being a prototype rather than a shipped client.

title: cs show: move the block model to cs-core and emit a conversation as JSON
description: Nothing emits message rows as JSON and cs-core exports no function returning a conversation's messages, so no non-Rust client can render a reader pane. Blocks three surfaces at once: the poc/ui preview, me9.8's reader, and the VS Code client me9.9. Substantially the same work as me9.1.1 (P1, in progress), which is the fold model, tool collapsing and outline mode.
design:
Mostly a MOVE, not a build. Measured against the code 2026-08-03.

WHAT MOVES to cs-core (~200-250 lines of cs-tui/src/preview.rs's 1,363): Block, Fold, Density, drawn(), the SELECT, and the highlight marking pass. Block is already plain data and marks already come from cs_core::highlight.

WHAT STAYS in cs-tui: Row, Fence, LayoutKey, lines(), theming.

THE ONE DESIGN QUESTION: mark_style picks a different style for reasoning because that kind carries no postings (Kind::is_indexed), so highlighting there would claim a match cs search cannot find. That is policy and belongs in core; the COLOUR belongs in the client. Core should return MarkKind::{Ranked, Unranked} and let each client map it — otherwise theming moves into the core.

MUST MOVE INTACT, both bought with measurement:
1. ORDER BY is_sidechain, thread_key, seq — not seq. seq is per-thread, and ordering by it alone made a real 9-thread conversation render as nine opening turns then nine first replies.
2. Marking goes through a scratch table, not the corpus index. On the longest conversation: flat 110-126 ms whatever the query, versus 64 ms for 'borrow checker', 242 ms for 'commits' and 17.9 SECONDS for 'the'.

RISK: 38 tests live in preview.rs and the layout cache is keyed on (conv, query, density, folds). The tui refactor is the schedule risk, not the new code.

CHEAPER FIRST STEP, no Rust: Group already carries match_seqs, user_turns, msg_count, prose_count, cwd, ended_date, title and destinations, so a result ROW is feedable from cs search --json today. Only the preview pane needs cs show.
acceptance_criteria: cs show <id> --json emits message rows with role, kind, seq, on_head_path, is_error, is_sidechain and highlight spans. cs-tui renders from the shared core model rather than its own. The 170-test workspace stays green. The thread-ordering rule and the scratch-table highlighting rationale survive the move as comments.
notes: Filed 2026-08-03 from poc/ui work. See poc/ui/NOTES.md §6.
close_reason: Block, Fold, Density, drawn(), the SELECT and the marking pass now live in cs_core::blocks. mark_style's ratatui Style became MarkKind::{Ranked,Unranked} in core with the colour mapping left in cs-tui. cs show [--json] added; the JSON carries drawn and mark_kind so no client re-derives them, plus a v field and mark_offsets naming the UTF-8 byte basis. Verified end to end against the real index: 923-message conversation, 62 marks all indexing correctly, reasoning marks unranked and everything else ranked. 493 tests green, zero warnings. Follow-ups filed as me9.19 (kind runs for the ribbon) and me9.20 (collapsed forms).

title: Row model: GUI diverges from TUI-DESIGN §3, and the measured basis has changed
description: docs/TUI-DESIGN.md §3 decided one line per conversation with a ten-cell density strip, and rejected a second line because 'a second line would carry the conversation's opening prose, which is roughly what the title already is'. The native-app prototype (poc/ui) deliberately diverges: 2 lines browsing, 3 with a query. Either §3 gains a note that it governs the TUI only, or it is revisited. Letting the two drift silently is the failure preview.rs already demonstrates.
design:
Measured against the live index 2026-08-03, which changes the basis of two §3 claims.

TITLE REDUNDANCY IS CODEX-ONLY, NOT GENERAL.
title_origin distribution: codex 99.4% first_user (651), claude-code 11.0% first_user but 75.9% generated (289), chatgpt-export 99.9% custom (2009). So 'opening prose is roughly the title' holds for ~22% of the corpus, not for it broadly.

ARCHETYPE IS ~87% PREDICTED BY SOURCE.
prose_count/msg_count over conversations >=10 msgs: codex 564/613 under 35% prose; claude-code 274/327 under 35%; chatgpt 265/411 over 60%. Avg msgs 182.1 codex / 132.0 claude-code / 7.2 chatgpt. So a shape encoding that only separates agentic from conversational duplicates the agent badge; it has to encode run structure to earn its space.

MOST HITS ARE IN TOOL TRAFFIC.
Message-level, by query: borrow checker 78% tool, fts5 66%, timezone 85%, schema migration 74%. At conversation level, tool-only matches run 20-73%. Consequence for §8: the 'tool_* that matched fts_tools -> expanded' rule is the common path, not an exception.

FREE SEGMENTATION SIGNALS EXIST.
user_turns gives 2-8 segments typically (claude-code 20.4 msgs/steer, codex 37.0). 1,088 gaps over 4h corpus-wide, ~1 per agent conversation. 4.6% of assistant prose ends in '?' (~1.4/conv). is_error 1.3% of tool_results. is_sidechain 4.2% of messages. All derivable with no inference.db.

PROTOTYPE ROW: line 1 badge + fused shape/match ribbon + dir + msgs + age; line 2 title full width; line 3 (query only) true best match framed with its tool provenance.
acceptance_criteria: Either docs/TUI-DESIGN.md §3 carries a note scoping it to the terminal and naming the GUI divergence, or §3 is revisited against the measurements above. The three corrected figures (title_origin by source, hit distribution by kind, segments per conversation) are recorded wherever §3's reasoning is restated.
notes:

CORRECTION 2026-08-03: this bead's design field, and both published design artifacts, claim 'Blocks::load returns ratatui::Line so no second client can reuse the fold model'. That is WRONG. The only ratatui coupling inside Block is one private mark_style(&Theme) -> Style. The seam is far better than described and cs show is mostly a MOVE, not a build (~200-250 lines of preview.rs's 1,363, plus serde and a subcommand). The two artifacts are still uncorrected.

Related: me9.1.1 already records 'do not privilege user turns'. Full design log with measurements, reversals and open questions: poc/ui/NOTES.md

title: A broad query blocks the event loop on the preview it loads, not on the search
description: Measured under a pty while driving cs tui: typing 'borrow checker' at 50ms per key leaves the app fully caught up 100ms after the last keystroke, while 'there' is still several keystrokes behind 800ms later - though its own search reports 11ms. The gap is sync_preview loading the top-ranked conversation, which for a broad query can be the corpus's longest (9,261 rows). Pre-existing, unrelated to the header total; surfaced while measuring it.
acceptance_criteria: Preview load is off the keystroke path, or bounded, so catching up with typing does not depend on which conversation ranked first.

title: Deferring the header's match total off the keystroke path
description: The count that fills the header's middle number cost 5-36ms on broad prefixes when it ran inline with the search - spent at the one moment the number is worth nothing, since a two-or-three letter prefix is a query on its way somewhere. Move it to a 250ms idle settle on the event loop.
acceptance_criteria: Keystroke overhead measured at zero across the corpus; settle bounded and guarded by a test.
close_reason: search_grouped_counted now answers only from the ranking pass and returns Total::AtLeast otherwise; App::settle_count runs count_matching after a 250ms event::poll timeout. Measured worst keystroke overhead 0.3ms (noise) across the corpus, worst settle 36.6ms charged to the pause.

title: Does unicode61 split identifiers the wrong way for a corpus of engineering talk?
description:
`porter unicode61 remove_diacritics 2` treats `_` and `.` as separators, so `snake_case` indexes as [snake, case] and `foo.bar` as [foo, bar]. For a corpus that is mostly engineering conversation this is worth asking about, and it is not a niche case — measured 2026-08-01 over the 42,919 prose messages:

- **9,082 (21%)** contain a `snake_case` identifier
- **11,944 (28%)** contain a `dotted.name`

## The trade is not one-way, which is why this is a decision and not a task

Adding `tokenchars '_'` looks like a precision win and is mostly a **recall loss**. Today `snake_case` is findable by typing `snake_case`, `snake`, *or* `case`. Make `_` a token character and it becomes a single token, findable only by the whole identifier or a prefix of it. For a corpus whose job is answering 'did I discuss this', losing partial recall is plausibly worse than gaining exact-identifier precision. The same argument applies to `.`.

There is also a second-order effect nobody has looked at: the porter stemmer would then be handed `snake_case` as one token and will do something to it.

## Why it is blocked rather than open

This is the largest quality lever in the system, and chat-search-6eb's own notes ring-fenced quality levers: ranking is declared good-enough and the tuning constants are gated behind an eval set harvested from real searches, *specifically so they stop being moved by intuition*. Changing the tokenizer on a hunch is the exact thing that note forbids.

And there is nothing to measure against today. The logging from chat-search-6eb.22 is built and closed, but `~/.chat-archive/queries.jsonl` does not exist on this machine — no log has accumulated. An A/B run now could only report 'these two rankings differ', with no way to say which is better.

## The adjacent option that does not have this problem

`trigram` tokenization gives true substring search and is purely **additive** — a separate table, no recall change to `fts_prose` — so it does not need the eval set to be safe. It belongs with the fuzzy-fallback work (chat-search-6eb.10) rather than here. Its cost is index size, unmeasured.
design:
Two measurements make this decidable, and the first is cheap enough to do the day the eval set exists:

- **How many vocabulary terms actually merge.** chat-search-6eb.42 adds the `fts5vocab` table that answers this directly, without building a candidate index.
- **How many real queries contain `_` or `.`.** This needs the harvested log. If the answer is 'almost none', the precision gain has no audience and the recall loss decides it on its own.

Run the eval harness over both tokenizations of the same archive; the index is a pure function of the archive (ADR 1), so building both is a rebuild each and nothing else. Note that `highlight` follows the tokenizer automatically — it reads the same declaration and `tokenizer_matches_the_index` fails if the two drift — so marking is not extra work here.
acceptance_criteria: Either the tokenizer declaration changes, with the recall and precision effect measured against the harvested eval set and IMPORTER_VERSION bumped — or the option is rejected against that same evidence and the rejection is written into ADR 6, so the 21%/28% sizing does not invite the question again.

title: Let explain say how broad a prefix is, via fts5vocab
description:
`cs explain` can say a query matched at rank 12, or that no message contains a term. It cannot say the thing that actually explains a slow keystroke: that the prefix being typed expands to hundreds of terms. fts5 exposes exactly this through `fts5vocab`, and the numbers line up with the cost precisely — measured 2026-08-01 on the 180k-message index while doing chat-search-6eb.30:

| prefix | distinct terms | per-row cost to mark |
|---|---:|---:|
| `borrow*` | 1 | ~110 us |
| `commit*` | 6 | 80 us |
| `the*` | 73 | 5427 us |
| `pro*` | 260 | 2558 us |

Declaring it is free. `CREATE VIRTUAL TABLE IF NOT EXISTS vocab_prose USING fts5vocab('fts_prose','row')` adds **0 bytes** to the file — verified by byte-comparing a copy before and after — because it is a view over the index rather than storage. So this needs no reindex and no IMPORTER_VERSION bump: an existing index gains the table on the next `index::open`.

## Scope

`explain` only, plus whatever chat-search-6eb.38 wants for sizing a prefix index — that bead has to know how many terms each candidate prefix length would collapse, and this answers it directly instead of building three indexes and diffing.

**Explicitly not the query path.** It is tempting to probe the vocabulary per keystroke and route `highlight::spans_for` on the answer rather than on 'does a term end in a star' — it would fix the one case that rule gets wrong (`borrow` typeahead, 17.7 ms through the batch where the index would be 7.7 ms). Do not. The probe is a second opinion about an expansion fts5 is about to perform itself, and the two can drift; that is the same failure as the three clients that each derived the local date and the two extractors that each read the query string. It also costs 2-6 ms per keystroke against a 2-17 ms marking budget, so it is not obviously a win even when it agrees.
design:
Three traps, all found by testing on 2026-08-01:

- **Syntax.** In the same database it is the two-argument form, `fts5vocab('fts_prose','row')`. The three-argument `fts5vocab('main','fts_prose','row')` is only for a `temp.` table pointing at another database, and using it in `main` fails with 'wrong number of vtable arguments', which names nothing useful.
- **The vocabulary is stemmed and diacritic-folded**, because that is what was indexed: the table holds `learn` (2454 docs) and not `learning`, `gener` (4732) and not `generated`, `cafe` (46) and not `café`. That is exactly right for 'how broad is this prefix', since stems are what fts5 expands over — and it rules out the other obvious use, driving query autocomplete, which would suggest stems that are not words. The stemmer is lossy, so there is no mapping back.
- **The range constraint is byte arithmetic.** `term >= 'the' AND term < 'thf'` works only because the last byte was hand-incremented as ASCII; a prefix ending in a multibyte character needs a real successor-string function over bytes. Get it wrong and the count is quietly short. The constraint is pushed down and matters enormously: a bounded range is 2-6 ms where an unconstrained scan of the 50,613-term vocabulary is 169 ms.
acceptance_criteria: `cs explain` on a query whose final term is a prefix reports how many distinct index terms that prefix expands to and how many documents they cover, asked of fts5 rather than derived. An index built before this change gains the capability on next open, with no reindex. `highlight::spans_for` routes exactly as it does today.

title: Revise ADR 6: sqlite-vec in its own file, not in index.db
description:
ADR 6 says sqlite-vec goes in the same file when embeddings arrive. chat-search-6eb.40 puts it in a separate one. Both cannot stand and the conflict should be written up rather than papered over.

The argument for splitting: disposability outranks convenience. An index.db that takes an hour to rebuild is not disposable in any sense that matters, and ADR 1 -- the rule everything else rests on -- depends on it staying cheap to delete. SQLite ATTACH makes a cross-file join ordinary SQL, so the cost of the split is close to zero.

Either amend ADR 6 or record the split as a new ADR with ADR 6 amended to point at it.
acceptance_criteria: ADR 6 and chat-search-6eb.40 no longer contradict each other on where embeddings live. Either ADR 6 is amended in place or a new ADR records the split with ADR 6 amended to point at it. The disposability argument is recorded as the reason, so that an index.db which takes an hour to rebuild stops being disposable in the sense ADR 1 depends on, and the question is not re-litigated the next time a store needs a home.

title: message.text_hash, so staleness is a join and not a rehash
description:
chat-search-6eb.40 needs to answer which messages have changed since they were embedded. Without a stored hash that means rehashing 172,000 messages on every check.

text_hash is a pure function of the message text, so it belongs in index.db and strains no rule. The archive manifest already hashes, but at file granularity for change detection -- a different question with the wrong resolution for this one.

Makes the check one indexed join:

  SELECT m.id FROM message m
  LEFT JOIN inf.embedding e ON e.scope='message' AND e.target_id=m.id AND e.model_id=?
  WHERE m.kind='prose' AND (e.target_id IS NULL OR e.input_hash != m.text_hash);

From the 2026-08-01 native-app design discussion.
acceptance_criteria: message carries a text_hash column that is a pure function of the message text, written by the importer, so rm index.db && cs index reproduces it exactly and no authored data enters the index. IMPORTER_VERSION is bumped, since an existing index has no such column. The staleness query in the description runs as one indexed join with no rehashing pass over the corpus, demonstrated against the live index. The column is the archive manifest hash's counterpart at message granularity, and the reason the two exist separately is written where the next reader looks.

title: inference.db: a store for model-derived data that survives a reindex
description:
Embeddings, generated summaries and cluster runs are not pure functions of (archive, importer version) -- change the model and the output changes -- so they cannot be columns in index.db without voiding the rule that makes it disposable. They are also far too expensive to recompute on every 10.6s rebuild. A fourth store holds them.

Invariant: everything in inference.db is the output of a MODEL rather than a parser. cs index must never write to it or delete it. Conversation and message ids are permanent, so the two files rejoin on id after a rebuild and nothing recomputes.

From the 2026-08-01 native-app design discussion.
design:
Key each artefact on a hash of exactly the bytes fed to the model, at the granularity the model consumed them. input_hash is a COLUMN, not part of the primary key -- one current row per (target, model), so staleness is a comparison rather than an accumulating history.

Invalidation policy is per-artefact, not per-file. Two questions decide it: how expensive is recomputing, and how bad is being stale.

  message embedding   key (scope, target_id, model_id)          -> recompute eagerly
  conversation vector pooled from member message vectors        -> not cached at all
  summary             key (conv_id, model_id, prompt_version)   -> keep, mark stale
  cluster assignment  a run_id, not a per-conversation entry    -> assign newcomers to nearest centroid

Message-level granularity is what stops the churn: transcripts GROW, so a whole-conversation hash changes on every capture cycle for anything you are actively using. Messages are append-only, so growth adds rows instead of invalidating them.

Because the key is a hash of the TEXT, an importer improvement invalidates exactly the embeddings whose text actually changed. The importer version never appears in the key.

Clustering is stored as a run, not a per-row cache -- you cannot invalidate one member of a k-means, and topics that reshuffle on every reindex are unusable.

GC is explicit (cs inference gc), never automatic on rebuild: a row whose target is missing from index.db looks like garbage and might be a broken importer. Same instinct as ADR 9.

Embed prose only -- tool traffic is 91% of corpus text and would dominate a pooled vector with file contents. Whether reasoning is embedded is open (see chat-search-8mb).

Size: 384-dim f32 is 1,536 B/vector. 2,963 conversations = 4.5 MB; 172k messages = 264 MB; int8 quantized is 4x smaller. Smaller than the 293 MB index either way -- this is a compute-once problem, not a storage problem.
acceptance_criteria: rm index.db && cs index leaves inference.db untouched and nothing recomputes. Deleting inference.db and rebuilding produces a working index with empty summary/vector columns and no error.

title: Refuse to put the archive in a cloud-synced directory, and say so if it already is
description:
Split out of chat-search-4ar.4 on 2026-08-01. That bead bundled two unrelated things: this check, which is mechanical and doable today, and the redaction decision, which is ADR 15 and still open. 4ar.4 now carries only the redaction half.

ADR 15's context states the minimum plainly: the index concentrates env vars, tokens and file contents into one file, and 'at minimum this must stay out of cloud-synced directories'. That minimum is not enforced anywhere. Nothing in `cs init` or `cs status` looks at where archive_root points, so the only thing keeping the archive off iCloud today is that it happens to be at ~/.chat-archive.

This is not hypothetical on this machine. Measured 2026-08-01, five cloud-synced roots exist here:
  ~/Library/Mobile Documents                                    (iCloud Drive)
  ~/Library/CloudStorage/GoogleDrive-tylerscottcrosse@gmail.com
  ~/Library/CloudStorage/GoogleDrive-... (1-19-26 5:04 PM)
  ~/Library/CloudStorage/OneDrive-GeorgiaInstituteofTechnology
  ~/Library/CloudStorage/OneDrive-SharedLibraries-GeorgiaInstituteofTechnology

The trap worth naming: with iCloud 'Desktop & Documents Folders' enabled, ~/Documents and ~/Desktop are cloud-synced without appearing under any obviously-cloud path. A prefix match on ~/Library alone would miss the most likely accident.

Scope is the archive root and the index that sits in it. Source paths are read-only and are wherever the vendor put them, so they are not this bead's business.
design:
Check the resolved archive_root, not the configured string — a symlink into iCloud is the case a literal prefix match misses. Canonicalise first, then test.

Detection, cheapest first: a path prefix under ~/Library/Mobile Documents or ~/Library/CloudStorage catches iCloud and every CloudStorage provider (Google Drive, OneDrive, Dropbox's newer integration) in one rule. ~/Dropbox and ~/OneDrive as literal home-relative names catch the older layouts. Desktop & Documents is the one needing more than a name: when enabled, ~/Documents is a symlink into ~/Library/Mobile Documents/com~apple~CloudDocs, so canonicalising before the prefix test already handles it — which is the argument for canonicalising rather than a second rule.

Report rather than move. Relocating an archive is destructive and the user may have chosen the location deliberately; the failure this prevents is the silent one.
acceptance_criteria:
`cs status` names the archive root's cloud-sync state as an explicit line, in both directions — a safe location says so rather than staying silent, so the absence of a warning is never mistaken for the absence of a check. A cloud-synced archive root is reported as a warning naming which provider and which path matched.

`cs init` refuses to write a config whose archive_root resolves inside a cloud-synced directory, and its message says why (ADR 15: the index concentrates secrets) and what to do instead. A flag may override it, because a user who has read the reason is allowed to decide otherwise, but the default is refusal.

Detection is on the canonicalised path, with a test proving a symlink pointing into a cloud directory is caught — that is the case a string prefix match on the configured value misses, and the one iCloud's Desktop & Documents Folders setting creates without the user choosing a cloud-looking path.

Nothing is moved, copied or deleted. The check reports; the user relocates.

title: Expose the boolean and proximity operators fts5 already has: phrase, OR, NOT, NEAR
description:
`Query::match_expr` renders every term as `"word"` joined by spaces, which is fts5's implicit AND. That is the only thing the text half of the DSL can express. chat-search-6eb.11 built the facet half (`agent:`, `dir:`, `date:`, and `-` negation on each); this is the other half, and fts5 supports all of it natively at no index cost.

Four gaps, in the order they are likely to be missed:

- **Phrase.** Typing `"deep learning"` today produces `"deep" "learning"` — two required words anywhere in the message. Quotes are the near-universal convention for 'these words, in this order', and a user who types them gets something quietly different from what they asked for.
- **OR.** No way to say `borrow OR ownership`. Everything is ANDed, so a query gets narrower with every word and there is no way to widen it.
- **NOT on text.** `-` negates a facet (`-agent:codex`) but not a word. `borrow -checker` is not expressible.
- **NEAR.** `NEAR(borrow checker, 10)`. For conversational prose, 'discussed together' is often the real question and proximity is a better proxy for it than co-occurrence anywhere in a 100 KB message.

## Why this is not just parser work

The trap is the one `query.rs`'s module doc was written about: the MATCH expression and the marking terms are two renderings of one `Query`, and they must not drift. Every operator here breaks the current rendering in a different way:

- `highlight::any_expr` ORs the marking terms, which is right for AND-of-words and wrong for a phrase — it would mark `deep` and `learning` separately wherever either appeared, including in messages that matched on a different occurrence.
- A NOT term must never be marked at all; it is why a row is absent, not why it is present.
- Under OR, not every term is present in every matching row, so 'the row that ranked has all the terms anyway' — the assumption `any_expr` documents — stops holding.

## Why it is not just correctness either

The typeahead reading has to survive every intermediate state. `chat-search-6eb.11` set the rule: a malformed or half-typed token is searched as literal text rather than erroring, because mid-word is the normal state in a TUI. `NEAR(borrow` and an unclosed `"deep` are both states a user passes through on the way to a valid query, and neither may throw.
design:
One parser, as now: these are more renderings of the same `Query`, not a second reading of the string. The open decisions, none of which should be settled by whoever picks this up without saying so:

- **Precedence.** fts5 binds NOT tighter than AND, and AND tighter than OR. Whether to expose that or to require parentheses is a UX call.
- **Spelling.** Bare uppercase `OR`/`NOT`/`NEAR` is fts5's own syntax and collides with the words themselves; `|` and `-` do not, and `-` already means negation on facets, which argues for reusing it.
- **What `marking_terms` returns.** It is a `Vec<String>` today, which cannot express a phrase or a negation. It probably has to become a structured type, and that is the bulk of the work.

fts5 does the matching either way — the whole of this bead is parsing and marking.
acceptance_criteria: A single input string expresses phrase, OR, NOT and NEAR, and each one changes the result set in the way its syntax claims. Every intermediate state of typing each of them is searched as literal text rather than erroring or returning nothing. `marking_terms` marks what actually made each returned row match — a phrase as a phrase, and never a NOT term — with a test that a row returned under each operator still locates its match, as `every_row_the_ranker_returns_has_something_to_highlight` does for AND today.

title: gemini-cli glob archives 175 MiB of checkpoints for 120 messages
description:
The gemini-cli source uses include = ["**/*.json"] over ~/.gemini/tmp, which matches far more than conversations.

MEASURED 2026-08-01 on the live archive: 34 archived files total — 15 chat sessions, 15 checkpoints, 4 logs.json. The checkpoints are 175.5 MiB of the source's 175.8 MiB, six of them ~29 MiB apiece (e.g. checkpoints/2026-01-31T08-53-53_544Z-tests.py-write_file.json). They contain no conversation content and no importer reads them.

Net: gemini-cli is 7.3% of the entire 2.36 GiB archive and 0.07% of the index (120 of 181,521 messages).

This matters more over time than it looks — ADR 20 puts the archive on a ~14-month runway against 17 GB free, and this is pure waste against that budget.

Likely fix is narrowing the glob to the chats subdirectory, e.g. include = ["**/chats/*.json"]. Worth confirming first whether logs.json carries anything the importer wants; the checkpoints clearly do not.
acceptance_criteria: Glob narrowed so checkpoints are no longer captured; existing captured checkpoints removed from the archive or explicitly kept with a reason; gemini-cli archive size drops to roughly the chat-session bytes; cs index still reports the same 12 conversations / 120 messages.

title: TUI header should say how many conversations matched, not just how many are shown
description: The header reads '100 shown / 3019 indexed'. The shown count is capped by --limit, so nothing on screen says whether the list is the whole answer or the top 100 of two thousand. The corpus total is a fixed number that answers a question nobody is asking mid-search. Add the query's own total: how many conversations the current query selects, uncapped by limit.
acceptance_criteria: Header shows shown/matched/indexed when the query narrows the corpus; per-keystroke cost measured against the real 3k-conversation index and reported.
close_reason: Header now reads 'N of M matched / K indexed'. The total comes off the ranking pass when it saw every match (free) and from a COUNT(DISTINCT conv_id) only when the scan hit its ceiling. Measured at limit 50 on the 3,019-conversation index: 0.0 ms for real queries, +5 to +36 ms for broad two-or-three letter prefixes.

title: Reasoning is searched by nobody and previewed by everybody, and neither surface says so
description:
DECIDED 2026-08-01 by Tyler: do not index reasoning. The measurement on this bead is why — through fts5 with the project tokenizer, the recall gain across 28 real logged queries is exactly zero, because reasoning is about work that also appears in prose. Indexing it would buy nothing findable and would put process boilerplate (preparing 186x, summarizing 169x, verifying 155x) into BM25's way, which is the ADR 5 hazard.

What is left is not an indexing job. It is that two surfaces now disagree about whether reasoning matched, and neither admits it.

DEMONSTRATED on the live index. 'gbdt' appears in chatgpt-export:68c2e851-da90-8327-963f-a1289d7bacaa exactly once, in a reasoning message, and nowhere else in that conversation:

  cs search 'gbdt'   -> does not return it
  cs explain <id> 'gbdt' -> exists: true, best_rank: null, term_hits: [['gbdt', 0]]

term_hits says zero. The text is right there. Zero is true of the INDEX and false of the CONVERSATION, and explain does not distinguish them — so the one command whose entire job is answering 'why did this not come back' gives an answer that reads as 'your word is not in here'.

Meanwhile the preview draws reasoning (Block::drawn is true for everything but a successful tool_result) and marks it with highlight::spans_many, which indexes whatever text it is handed and knows nothing about the corpus index. So open that same conversation and 'gbdt' is highlighted inside the reasoning block — a match the ranker never counted, in a conversation search will not return, that explain reports as zero hits.

That is one fact with two answers, which is the thing this codebase's 'a rule lives in exactly one place' convention exists to prevent.

SCOPE:
1. Say it where the decision is made: the match arm in index::write_one falls through for Kind::Reasoning by accident of structure. Make the exclusion explicit and give the reason.
2. Teach explain the difference between 'not in the text' and 'not indexed'. It already learned that a filter can be why a conversation is missing (4bc8883); an unindexed message kind is the same class of answer. Reporting reasoning_messages beside indexed_prose would be enough.
3. Decide what a preview mark MEANS, and make it consistent. Either the preview stops implying reasoning matches count, or it keeps marking them and says they are unranked. Do not leave it silent.
acceptance_criteria: cs explain can tell 'the word is not in this conversation' from 'the word is in a kind nobody indexes', and says which. The exclusion of Kind::Reasoning is stated at the point it happens rather than being a fallthrough. A highlighted reasoning match in the preview cannot be mistaken for a reason the conversation ranked.
notes:
MEASURED 2026-08-01, against the live index (3,019 convs / 180,564 msgs) and the real query log.

1. Conversation-level recall gain on real queries: ZERO.
   Built an fts5 table over all 14,368 reasoning messages with the project tokenizer
   (porter unicode61 remove_diacritics 2) and ran the 28 distinct queries from
   ~/.chat-archive/queries.jsonl through it. Number of queries that surfaced a conversation
   not already findable via fts_prose/fts_tools: 0. Reasoning is ABOUT work that also appears
   in prose, so at the conversation level it is nearly always redundant.

   A first pass using SQL LIKE said 20 of 30 queries gained 230 conversations. That was wrong
   and is recorded here so it is not repeated: LIKE matched 'rust' inside 'trustworthy' and
   'trusting'. Anything measuring recall here must go through fts5, not LIKE.

2. But reasoning-only vocabulary is real, and it is long-tail.
   Over the 300 most reasoning-heavy conversations, 47.2% of distinct reasoning words
   (45,555 of 96,568) never appear in that conversation's prose or tools. The HEAD of that
   distribution is process boilerplate and worthless to search — preparing 186x, summarizing
   169x, planning 162x, verifying 155x, reviewing 136x. The TAIL is not: umap, gbdt,
   feedforward, latent, descent, modularization, typeerrors, precompile, datasheet. ~2,363
   rare non-process words in a 120-conversation sample.

3. Cost is negligible either way. Reasoning is 2.5 MB of text against prose 44.4 MB,
   tool_result 36.5 MB, tool_call 21.6 MB. The index is 316 MB today.

SO THE DECISION IS NOT 'is reasoning useful' — it is whether long-tail recall is worth a
table. And the process-verb head is exactly the ADR 5 hazard: putting this in fts_prose would
let 'review', 'check', 'verify' rank reasoning noise above prose. If it is indexed at all it
needs its own table, the way tool traffic got one.

Cheapest defensible option: leave it unindexed and make the exclusion legible — say so at the
match arm in index::write_one, and have cs explain report reasoning-message count as a reason
a conversation did not come back, the way it now reports filters.
close_reason: PR #3 (draft), branch worktree-bead-8mb-reasoning-honesty. Kind::is_indexed is now the single home of the rule, matched exhaustively; index::write_one no longer reaches reasoning through a bare _ => {}; cs explain reports unindexed_term_hits and unindexed_messages and leads with a verdict naming the kind; the preview marks unranked kinds in a new match_unranked slot (underline, so it survives NO_COLOR). Verified on the live corpus: chatgpt-export:68c2e851 'gbdt' now explains as 'only in messages of kind reasoning' where it previously claimed no message contained the term. 471 tests, warning-free.

title: Gate: human
description:
Ad-hoc gate blocking chat-search-6eb.30

Reason: Approve this as done, or say which further step you want: the work is committed and green, but the acceptance criterion's '~2 ms of snippet time' is not reachable and I did not close the bead on my own judgement.

WHAT SHIPPED (branch worktree-bead-6eb30-external-content, commit 3baea37, gate green: 439 tests, warning-free --all-targets)

Both fts tables are external content over `message` and IMPORTER_VERSION is 4, as the design said. Marking at limit 50 / nested 3 went from 10.7-29.1 ms to 2.4-17.7 ms, every returned row still locates its match, and `learning` — the query the bead names as crossing the 30 ms budget — is now 21.5 ms end to end.

WHY IT IS NOT THE DESIGN AS WRITTEN

The design expected external content to make marking ~free. It does, but only for a query whose terms are all exact. fts5 answers a prefix term by walking its vocabulary for every term with that prefix, per query, so against the 180k-message index the prescribed per-row route costs 5.4 ms A ROW for `the*` — 753 ms for a keystroke, against 23 ms for the scratch table it was replacing. Measured on the same rows, the only difference being the star: `the` exact 54.6 us/row, `the*` 5427 us/row. The TUI's final token is always a prefix, so shipping the design literally would have been a 30x regression exactly where the bead wants a win.

So highlight::spans_for decides for a result set as a whole — the index when the expression names its terms (2.8-7.8 ms), one scratch-table batch when any term is a prefix (2.4-17.7 ms). Both ask fts5 with the same tokenizer and expression, and a test holds them to the same answer. That second branch is mine, not the bead's, which is the other reason this is a gate.

WHY ~2 MS IS UNREACHABLE, NOT MERELY UNREACHED

Every route has to tokenize each candidate message to say which of its words matched. That floor is ~28 ns/byte, and a 150-message candidate set is 60-680 KB, so 2-18 ms. The bead's '~10-15 us per snippet' came from the 8 us figure for a small already-resident message; real result sets average 2-18 KB per message. 2 ms is only reachable for small sets — `commit` does hit 2.4 ms.

THE THREE READINGS, AND WHICH I WOULD PICK

(a) Done. Marking is off the critical path and no longer the reason any keystroke misses budget; rewrite the criterion to say that. <- I would pick this.
(b) Not done until `pro` and `the` are under 30 ms at nested=3. They are at 38.7 and 71.1 ms, but 29.4 and 59.3 of that is the RANKING, before a snippet exists. That is the same prefix expansion, and it is chat-search-6eb.29 / chat-search-6eb.38 (filed, and 6eb.38 now blocks 6eb.29), not this bead.
(c) Revert the schema change and keep only the batch. It would work — the batch alone is the uniform win — and would spare a forced reindex. I would not: the schema change costs nothing measured (315 MB and 7.4 s rebuild, both unchanged), it is what makes the exact path 3-6x faster, and 6eb.38 may collapse the two branches back into one.

ONE KNOWN IMPERFECTION, DOCUMENTED IN THE CODE: `borrow` typeahead is routed to the batch and would be 7.7 ms through the index instead of 17.7 — 678 KB over 69 messages, where the insert costs more than the expansion it avoids. Deciding on bytes as well would need the texts measured before the route is chosen; I judged that not worth a second input for one query in six. Say if you disagree.

ALSO FIXED, SILENT IF MISSED: external content makes an unconstrained scan of an fts table return every row of `message`, which broke `explain`'s indexed_prose — it reported 937 for a conversation with 175 indexed prose messages. It now counts fts5's _docsize shadow table, with a regression test.

branch: worktree-bead-6eb30-external-content
close_reason: Closed

title: cs explain blames the tokenizer when a filter excluded the conversation
description:
Since chat-search-6eb.11 a query can exclude a conversation by filter, but explain() still knows only two causes of a false negative — never indexed, or ranked too low. Its Explain doc says so in as many words. Three confirmed symptoms, all reproduced against the real index on 2026-07-31:

1. term_hits splits the raw text on whitespace, so a filter token is checked as a word to find: 'cs explain <claude-code conv> "agent:codex rust"' reports [["agent:codex",0],["rust",52]].
2. The verdict blames the wrong subsystem. Same command: the conversation was dropped by agent:codex, and the verdict reads 'terms appear in the text but FTS did not match — likely tokenizer or stemming'.
3. A filter-only query has no terms at all, so the all-zero branch fires: 'cs explain <conv> date:today' reports 'no message contains any query term — this is a recall problem, not ranking'.

6eb.11 added allow_hyphen_values to cs explain specifically so it accepts DSL syntax, which makes this reachable through a documented path. This is the same class as chat-search-6eb.32 — the diagnostic tool answering confidently and wrongly — in the same function.
acceptance_criteria: term_hits is built from Query::terms() rather than raw whitespace splitting, so a filter token is never reported as a missing word. Explain carries whether the filters exclude this conversation, and the verdict names that cause before it blames the tokenizer. A query that is all filters and no terms gets a verdict about filters rather than about recall. The new field is additive, per ADR 12.
