Option A states real advantages rather than a strawman — per-keystroke rather than per-session saving, the only home for cross-query state, and single-writer ownership if incremental indexing lands — and its decisive con is the ADR 1 interaction: a rebuild deletes and recreates index.db, so a daemon holding an open handle reads a deleted inode and serves stale results silently. Also fixes the stale cross-reference under ADR 12 (line 179), which pointed at '(see 13)' when it always meant 14. ADR 15 (redaction) is now the only 'open' entry in the file; ADRs 9-12 remain 'proposed'.

Two corrections applied on review, both unsourced numbers the draft had stated as project constraints: a '~50 ms keystroke-to-paint budget' and a derived '~40 ms of headroom' appeared nowhere else in the repo, and the Context line claimed the figures were measured 'against the real 293 MB index, not the PoC corpus' — a provenance the repo does not record. BACKLOG.md:94 and this bead give the 1.4-6.4 ms / ~3 ms figures without stating where they were taken, and poc/RESULTS.md has different numbers (rust --release 3.8 ms mean, 4.9 ms p95). Softened to 'fits a type-ahead budget' (matching BACKLOG.md:57's existing unquantified phrasing) and to 'the measurements this was decided against, recorded 2026-07-29'. The ~20 ms revisit trigger was rewritten to anchor on today's ~3 ms rather than on the invented budget.

title: Decide redaction: at import or at display (ADR 15)
description:
The location half of this bead was split out on 2026-08-01 as chat-search-4ar.6, which is mechanical and actionable today. What remains here is the decision, and it is ADR 15's, not a task's.

ADR 15 is `open`. Its context: agent transcripts contain env vars, tokens and file contents, and the index concentrates all of it into one file. Not yet decided is whether to redact at import — destructive, and in tension with ADR 1 unless the raw archive is kept intact — or at display, which is safer for reparse but leaves the index holding secrets on disk.

ADR 15's own 'decide by' is the honest trigger: before any surface is shared, or any archive leaves this machine. Neither has happened. It does, however, block real work — a7k.15 (encrypted offsite tier) is gated on it outright, since an offsite copy IS the archive leaving this machine.

Kept open rather than deferred, because unlike the other gated beads this one is not waiting on a threshold or on a second machine. It is waiting on a decision that can be made at any time, and making it early is cheap while making it late is not: every month of transcripts captured under an undecided policy is a month that a redact-at-import answer cannot retroactively apply to without a reparse.
acceptance_criteria:
ADR 15 moves off `open` in docs/DECISIONS.md, with the choice recorded and its consequence for ADR 1 stated explicitly — if redaction happens at import, the doc has to say what 'raw is the source of truth' now means when raw has been altered, or say that raw is kept unredacted and only the derived index is scrubbed.

docs/BACKLOG.md's 'Decisions still open' table drops the ADR 15 row.

Whatever is decided is written down as a rule with one home, not as a policy each importer or client re-implements. If it is redact-at-display, the redactor is in cs-core where every client reaches it; if at import, it is a documented stage in the importer contract, which ADR 1 requires to stay a pure function of (logical_path, bytes).

chat-search-a7k.15 is named in the outcome either way, since it is blocked on this.
notes:
Changed shape on 2026-07-30. Until now everything under archive_root was either re-derivable from the source tools (raw/) or disposable (index.db), so losing the archive cost time rather than data. ~/.chat-archive/queries.jsonl is neither: it records what was searched for and what was opened, and nothing can reconstruct it.

Two consequences for this issue:
- Backup is now load-bearing for one specific file, not merely nice to have.
- Redaction gets a new surface. Query text is a direct record of what was being worked on and worried about, in a way transcripts only imply — arguably the most sensitive per byte of anything here. Any 'sync the archive somewhere' answer has to decide about this file specifically.
- 'log_queries = false' in config is the opt-out if the conclusion is that it should not exist on a synced machine.

title: Native macOS app: a Swift surface over cs-core
description:
The deep surface, now that the language is decided (me9.30) and the reader is defined. me9.8's deferral condition was 'revisit when me9.1 ships and the TUI's limits are known rather than guessed' - me9.1.1 closed on 2026-08-04 and the fold model, collapsed tool traffic and outline mode moved into cs_core::blocks under me9.17, so the reader is a shared rule rather than a thing the TUI is still inventing.

Transport is argv against cs search --json and cs show --json. me9.22 measured keystroke-to-frame at 30-40 ms p50 with one process per character, the seam at 5-13 ms, and fork/exec at 0.3 ms - so cs serve --stdio (me9.21) is an optimisation, not a prerequisite.
design:
THE ORDERING CONSTRAINT: the shell lands before anything else fans out. Five agents told to build the app produce five incompatible skeletons - window, client state, transport and error handling all invented independently. One bead builds the shell, it merges, then the features parallelise on top of it. This is why the children carry dependencies rather than all sitting in bd ready at once.

The shell is a promotion of me9.22's spike code, not a blank page: CsClient.swift already has the transport plus the threading fix that took it from 85 ms to 30 ms p50 (readability handlers rather than waitUntilExit, which parked three threads per invocation and exhausted DispatchQueue.global at four keystrokes in flight).

WHAT poc/ui IS, AND WHAT IT IS NOT: poc/ui/index.html opened with no ?dir= is the VISUAL AND LAYOUT REFERENCE for this phase - pane arrangement, row anatomy, the grouping control, the Library view, the drawer, and the chrome. Open it and build what it shows. It was iterated by hand over many passes and is not itself pixel-perfect, so it is a reference rather than a specification: reproduce its structure and its density, not its pixel values. Three things outrank it, and a worker who hits a disagreement should not resolve it by measuring the mockup. A MEASUREMENT WINS - the row model, the grouping dimension and the kind ramp were argued from the corpus, and NOTES.md holds the numbers. A DEVIATION RECORDED IN A CHILD BEAD WINS, because it was reasoned against something the mockup could not see; the two that exist are me9.8.2's agent badge, forced by a fixed 706px column rather than chosen, and the ribbon, which me9.8.2 deliberately omits until kind_runs lands. AND IT HAS NO AUTHORITY over what it never had, which is what separates a mockup from a client: transport, client state, virtualisation, and empty/error/loading states. NOTES.md and DESIGN-BRIEF.md are the durable prose record.

NO VISUAL DIRECTION IS CHOSEN IN THIS PHASE, and none needs to be. index.html at default renders `terminal`, which directions.css defines as styles.css exactly as it stands, so the reference is fully determined without answering 4ar.12. Applying a chosen direction is me9.8.6 - P3, last, and the only child that touches the question.

WHAT me9.22 SETTLED: SwiftUI List recycles for free (5.2 MB scrolling the whole corpus) where ScrollView+LazyVStack accumulates 65.6 MB in one pass and plain VStack costs 1.6 s and 566 MB. Use List.
notes:
DEFERRED 2026-08-01, direction rather than work. A deep client surface is not startable while the TUI (me9.1) is still defining what a conversation reader looks like — the fold model, collapsed tool traffic and outline mode being built in me9.1.1 ARE the reader, and a second surface would either duplicate that or contradict it. Revisit when me9.1 ships and the TUI's limits are known rather than guessed. No acceptance criteria on purpose: writing them for something that may never be built is the same waste as leaving them blank, moved somewhere harder to see.
2026-08-05, THE VISUAL DIRECTION QUESTION IS SETTLED, and it changed this epic's shape rather than just ticking a box.

Tyler chose poc/ui/index.html as it stands as the target for the initial app. index.html with no ?dir= renders terminal, which directions.css defines as styles.css exactly as it stands, so that is the same answer as choosing the incumbent - but it names the mockup as the artifact rather than a direction off a list. chat-search-4ar.12 is closed on that.

This SUPERSEDES the design section above where it says 'NO VISUAL DIRECTION IS CHOSEN IN THIS PHASE' and 'applying a chosen direction is me9.8.6 - P3, last, and the only child that touches the question'. A direction is chosen, it is chosen by default, and me9.8.6 is no longer the bead that applies it.

The stated requirement behind the choice is what actually reorders the epic: the theme - palette, typography, padding - must be changeable later without a huge lift. A token layer cannot be retrofitted. me9.8.2, .3, .4 and .5 all write views, and if each hardcodes its colours and sizes then theming later means touching all four, which is the same failure this epic's ordering already exists to prevent for the shell. So chat-search-me9.8.8 was filed to put the seam in BEFORE the fan-out: it depends on me9.8.1 and blocks all five remaining children. Wave 0 is now two beads deep rather than one.

me9.8.6 keeps its number and its P3 and stays last, but is now the PROOF rather than the application - port a second direction from directions.css and show the diff touches tokens and no views.

The mechanism for me9.8.8 was probed rather than assumed: @Entry, which is the popular answer everywhere since 2024, does not build against the Command Line Tools SDK this package targets - SwiftUIMacros is an Xcode-only plugin. The explicit EnvironmentKey conformance plus NSColor(name:dynamicProvider:) compiles clean under Swift 6 strict concurrency. Both are written into me9.8.8's design with the error text, so nobody finds it twice.

title: Quick surface — Raycast
description: Raycast first to validate ranking before investing in chrome. ~200 lines of TypeScript shelling out to the binary, whose 4.9 ms p95 cold start fits a type-ahead budget.
acceptance_criteria:
A Raycast extension searches the index and opens a chosen conversation, shelling out to `cs search --json` rather than linking or reimplementing anything. No Rust changes are needed to make it work — if any turn out to be, that is a finding about ADR 12's contract and belongs in its own bead.

It consumes `destinations` as structured data and picks a variant, rather than parsing a rendered string (ADR 12; me9.3 is what made this possible). A result whose destinations list is empty renders as un-openable rather than as a broken command.

Typing stays inside a type-ahead budget end to end, measured through the extension rather than assumed from the binary's 4.9 ms cold start. State the measured p95 for a keystroke, and say which queries were used — broad prefixes are the ones that hurt (6eb.29).

It records picks. `cs pick <conv_id> --query <text>` exists precisely so a client's selection feeds the query log, and a client that opens conversations without recording which one was chosen throws away the ground truth 6eb.21 needs.

The point is validating ranking before investing in chrome, so the outcome includes a judgement: after real use, does the ranking hold up? That answer is the deliverable, not the extension.
notes:
SPEC 2026-08-01. Unblocked as of me9.3 — docs/BACKLOG.md's ordering trap 4 ('query contract before client #2') is recorded as met, because destinations replaced the single pre-rendered resume_cmd string.

Contract as it stands today, verified 2026-08-01 against the real index, so the extension knows what it is consuming:
  top level  count, grouped, ms, query, results, unapplied_filters
  result     conv_id, native_id, source, title, cwd, ended_at, ended_date, user_turns,
             msg_count, prose_count, score, match_count, match_seqs, hits, destinations,
             deleted_upstream
  destination  { kind: "terminal", argv: ["claude", "--resume", "<id>"] }

argv is a vector, not a shell string, which is the detail a TypeScript client most easily gets wrong — spawn it directly rather than joining and passing to a shell, or a cwd with a space in it breaks the open. The bd memory on crossterm and inherited descriptors is the same lesson in the other direction.

Note only kind 'terminal' is emitted at present. The AC's empty-destinations case is therefore about future sources (chatgpt-export has no local resume), not a hypothetical.

title: Never render an empty successful search on failure
description: Keep the previous results and show the error. An empty result list reads as "nothing matched", which is a lie when the real answer is "the reader failed to reload".
acceptance_criteria:
A test proves that a search failure leaves the previous result set on screen and reports the error, rather than rendering an empty list. That is the whole of the remaining work — the behaviour itself already landed.

The test must fail if the Err arm is changed to clear self.groups, which is the specific regression worth guarding: the failure mode is silent and looks exactly like a successful search that matched nothing, so nothing else would catch it.

Cover the two layers separately, since they are two different lies: state.rs must keep the groups, and render.rs must say 'search failed' rather than 'no results'.
notes:
ASSESSED 2026-08-01: the behaviour is implemented, the proof is not.

Already done, and citing this bead by name in the source:
  crates/cs-tui/src/state.rs:110-143 — the Err arm sets self.status and leaves self.groups untouched
  crates/cs-tui/src/render.rs:161  — 'search failed — showing nothing rather than guessing'
  crates/cs-tui/src/render.rs:380  — the same rule one layer down, for an empty message list

Not a concern on the CLI: cs search propagates the error with ? and exits non-zero, so it cannot render an empty success by construction.

What is missing is a test. Nothing in crates/cs-tui pins any of it, so the guarantee currently rests on three comments. Scoped the bead to that rather than closing it, because a rule this easy to regress silently is exactly the kind that needs the test more than the comment.

title: Generation-numbered searches
description: Each keystroke query carries an incrementing number; results from an older generation are dropped on arrival. Without it a slow query that started three keystrokes ago overwrites the fresh results with stale ones. fast-resume tui/state.rs carries both a search_generation and an applied_search_generation so it can also tell "in flight" from "settled". NOTE: the native TUI issue argues the opposite — that at 6 ms the search is synchronous and no generation counter is needed. Resolve the contradiction before building either.
close_reason: Superseded by chat-search-me9.1's design. A generation counter exists to discard results from a query that is still in flight when a newer keystroke arrives. Our search is synchronous in the event loop at 1.4-6.4 ms, so there is never an in-flight query to go stale and the counter guards nothing. fast-resume needs search_generation and applied_search_generation because Tantivy plus a background rescan is genuinely async; we are not. Reinstate trigger recorded on me9.1: if any keystroke path exceeds ~30 ms — most likely via the query DSL (chat-search-6eb.11) or fuzzy-on-failure (chat-search-6eb.10) — the search stops being synchronous and this comes back.

title: CLI search rebuilt against the real schema
description: The PoC has one; it needs rebuilding against the real schema.
close_reason: Already done. cs search is built against the real schema — grouped output, the 6eb.11 filter DSL, me9.3 destinations, and --json as the ADR 12 client contract. The description ('the PoC has one; it needs rebuilding') describes a state that ended when the real CLI landed. Verified 2026-08-01: ./target/release/cs search returns grouped, ranked, dated results off index.db.

title: Tune REPEAT_WEIGHT and the decay constant against a real eval set
description: REPEAT_WEIGHT is currently 0.25.
design:
Now a shell loop rather than a rebuild. REPEAT_WEIGHT and DECAY are per-query fields on cs_core::Query (defaults unchanged), and 'cs eval run' takes --repeat-weight and --decay, so:

  for w in 0.0 0.15 0.25 0.4 1.0; do
    cs eval run --set evals/ranking.toml --repeat-weight $w --json |
      jq -r '"$w \(.report.ndcg) \(.report.mrr)"'
  done

Two traps, both already guarded:
- Judge before sweeping. A sweep over a thin pool measures the pool. 'cs eval run' warns below 80% coverage.
- The judging pool already spans decay=0 and repeat_weight=0 rankers, so a conversation the current constants bury is still a judging candidate. Without that, any sweep would conclude the current values are optimal by construction.
acceptance_criteria: REPEAT_WEIGHT and DECAY are set from a sweep over the harvested eval set rather than left at the current guess of 0.25. The sweep runs only above cs eval run's 80 percent coverage warning, so it measures the ranker and not the judging pool. The swept points and their ndcg/mrr are recorded, so a later corpus change can be rechecked against them rather than re-derived. If the sweep finds the current constants are already best, that is a result and is recorded as one.
notes:
Re-gated 2026-07-30 on chat-search-6eb.21 rather than the deferred chat-search-6eb.9. Removing the old edge briefly left this in 'bd ready' with nothing to tune against, which is precisely the failure the eval exists to prevent — a sweep with no eval set reports numbers that are entirely a function of which results happened to get judged.

Also note the overlap with chat-search-6eb.12: that issue proposes removing the recency decay altogether rather than tuning it, on the grounds that fast-resume applies none. If 6eb.12 wins, half of this issue disappears. Decide 6eb.12 first, or at least measure both in the same sweep.

title: Never let a worse parse overwrite a better one
description: fast-resume classifies a JSONL file as clean / partial / invalid and retains the previously indexed document rather than replacing it from a truncated read. We are insulated from the worst case because the archive holds the bytes, but a mid-write scan still yields a half conversation until the next run.
design: Cheap to adopt: Clean | Partial | Invalid, keyed on whether any valid record follows the last malformed one.
acceptance_criteria:
A scan that reads a file mid-write does not replace a good indexed conversation with a truncated one. The test is the one that reproduces the bug: index a complete transcript, then index a deliberately truncated copy of it, and assert the complete conversation survives.

Each file is classified Clean | Partial | Invalid on the rule already in the design — whether any valid record follows the last malformed one — and the classification is visible in `cs index` output rather than being an internal detail, so a run that read a file mid-write says so.

A Partial read never overwrites a Clean one for the same conversation. A Partial read DOES land when there is nothing indexed for that conversation yet, since half a conversation beats none.

This holds across runs without extra state: the archive holds the bytes (ADR 1), so a later run that reads the same file complete replaces the partial one and the index converges. Nothing needs to remember that a previous read was partial — it only needs to not lose to one.
notes:
SPEC 2026-08-01. The design was already recorded; what was missing is the precedence rule, which is where this class of change goes wrong. 'Retain the previously indexed document' is ambiguous about the first-ever read, and the answer differs: partial-over-nothing is an improvement, partial-over-complete is the bug.

The description is right that the archive insulates us from the worst case — bytes are never lost — so this is about the window between a mid-write capture and the next run, not about permanent corruption. That bounds the priority: the damage is temporary and self-healing, which is why it is P2 and not P1.

title: Codex fork replay dedup
description: A fork copies the parent whole transcript into the child file, so fork-heavy projects flood results with near-identical hits.
acceptance_criteria:
A fork and its parent no longer return as near-identical separate hits for the same query. The measurement is a before/after on a fork-heavy project in the real corpus: state how many duplicate-looking conversations a representative query returned before, and what it returns after.

Replayed content is identified by content, not by file — a fork copies the parent transcript into the child file, so the messages are byte-identical and are detectable as such without trusting any id the format may or may not carry.

Dedup happens at import into the DAG, not in the ranker. ADR 4 makes a conversation a DAG and ADR 7 requires determinism; a ranker-side filter would have to re-derive the relationship on every query and would leave the index still holding the duplicate rows.

Nothing is lost that is not genuinely a replay: the fork's own divergent messages — everything after the branch point — remain searchable and attributed to the fork. The failure to avoid is collapsing a fork whose later content is the thing being searched for.

A test builds a parent and a fork sharing a prefix and asserts one conversation's worth of shared messages, both branches' tails intact.
notes:
SPEC 2026-08-01. Related but distinct from ADR 7's dedup, which handles a conversation spanning several transcript files (the bug that made IndexStats double-count 69 conversations). This is the opposite shape: one logical history copied into two files by a fork.

Check first whether search_grouped's grouping already hides some of this — it collapses a conversation's hits into one row, so the visible symptom may be N sibling conversations rather than N rows of one. That changes what 'flood results' means and therefore what the fix has to do.

title: Claude Code queued_command attachments
description: Real user prompts typed while a tool ran. No uuid/parentUuid, so they must be spliced by timestamp; currently dropped.
acceptance_criteria:
A queued_command attachment reaches the index as a user message with the prose the user actually typed, rather than being dropped.

It is spliced into the DAG by timestamp, and the test that matters covers the ambiguous case: two queued commands typed while the same tool ran must land in typed order, not in an order that depends on HashMap iteration or file order. ADR 7's determinism rule applies — the same bytes must produce the same DAG on every run.

A spliced message is distinguishable from one that carried its own uuid, so a later importer that gains real ids can tell what it inferred from what it was told. Splicing by timestamp is a heuristic and the index should not forget which of its edges were guessed.

The count is stated: how many messages this recovers across the corpus, measured before and after, so the change is justified by what it recovers rather than by the fact that it parses.
notes:
SPEC 2026-08-01. The description already states the mechanism (no uuid/parentUuid, so splice by timestamp) — what it did not state is the determinism constraint, which is the part most likely to be got wrong and the one ADR 7 exists for.

Worth measuring first: 'real user prompts typed while a tool ran' is a claim about how much genuine authored text is being lost, and that number decides the priority. If it is a handful of messages the bead is cosmetic; if it is hundreds it is a recall bug in the most valuable class of message the corpus has, since a user prompt is the thing people search for.

title: Gemini CLI importer
description: 34 files are archived and currently index to zero conversations.
close_reason:
Done, verified. New crates/cs-import/src/gemini.rs, one line in cs-import/src/lib.rs, one match arm in query.rs — scope held exactly. gemini-cli went from 0 conversations to 12, from 15 chats/ files, 120 messages indexed. Re-parenting is implemented correctly against the hazard in Message::parent_native_id: the empty-turn skip happens before prev_native_id advances, so a dropped turn never becomes a parent and no edge dangles.

Corrected two counts in the spec I gave it, both verified against the archive: there are 15 chats/session-*.json files (not 13) and 15 checkpoints (not 17); logs.json at 4 and the 34 total were right. The extra chats files are byte-for-byte duplicates — a personal-site/ directory repeats 3 sessions already present under a hash directory, confirmed by shasum (3 hashes appear exactly twice among the 15).

That duplication drove a design call worth keeping: message native_id is the record's own UUID rather than a per-file ordinal, so the index's INSERT OR IGNORE folds the second copy instead of doubling the conversation. model.rs sanctions this — it asks for file-scoped ids only where the source's own id is file-unique, and Gemini's is a UUID. An ordinal fallback covers a missing or repeated id, which would otherwise be swallowed silently by that same INSERT OR IGNORE.

Also found that 'type' is not only user/gemini — 'info' appears 4 times (auth chatter) and one whole session is nothing but info, so dropping the unknown type would have erased a conversation. Mapped to Role::System and kept. Content is not always a string (2 records are arrays of {text} parts, flattened). Records carry model, now populated last-wins.

13 tests added, all synthetic, covering the four required cases plus unknown type, content-parts flattening, double-archive idempotency, id fallback, model last-wins, and declining logs.json/checkpoints by shape rather than by path. cargo test --workspace: 134 passed, 0 failed, 3 ignored — 119 baseline + 3 (a7k.6) + 12. Follow-ups filed as chat-search-n58.21 (thoughts as Reasoning, 118 of 152 messages carry it) and chat-search-n58.22 (logs.json is not purely redundant — session 74eb0b66 has no chats/ file and survives only there).

title: 8 Codex subagent files cannot be linked to their parent
description: Older rollouts carry neither session_id nor parent_thread_id, so they surface as standalone conversations. Recovering them needs a cross-file pass.
acceptance_criteria:
The 8 orphaned Codex subagent files are linked to their parent conversation, or the bead records why a specific file cannot be and that file is left standalone deliberately. Either outcome is acceptable; a silent partial fix is not — state the count linked out of 8.

Linking survives a full reparse. The cross-file pass runs inside the importer stage over the archive, so `rm index.db && cs index` reproduces the same links (ADR 1, ADR 7). A one-off repair script that mutates the index is the wrong shape — it makes the index no longer a pure function of the archive.

A subagent linked by inference is distinguishable from one linked by an id the file carried, so a later format change that restores session_id does not silently inherit guesses as facts.

A test covers the negative: two unrelated standalone rollouts that merely look similar must NOT be linked. Recovering 8 files is not worth inventing a parent for a 9th.
notes:
SPEC 2026-08-01. The description gives the cause (older rollouts carry neither session_id nor parent_thread_id) but not the recovery signal, which is the actual design question and should be settled before anyone starts: what identifies a parent when both ids are absent? Candidates visible in the corpus are the cwd plus an overlapping time window, and a first-message match against a tool call in the parent.

Worth pricing before doing: 8 files against a 3,003-conversation corpus is 0.27%. The reason to do it anyway is that a subagent surfacing standalone is a wrong answer rather than a missing one — it shows up as a conversation that appears to start mid-task with no context.

title: Codex legacy pre-payload format
description:
18 of the 692 archived Codex files (2.6%) predate the `payload` wrapper, and 121 prose
messages across 17 conversations are silently dropped today.

Verified against the archive on 2026-07-29, not inferred. Every `.jsonl` under `codex/` was
scanned: exactly 18 carry no `payload` key on any line and no `event_msg` anywhere. They are
**one** format, not several — chat-search-n58.16 filed the same 18 files under a
"pre-2025-09-09" boundary and was closed as a duplicate.

Shape:

- Line 1 is a session header: `{id, timestamp, instructions, git{commit_hash, branch, repository_url}}`.
- Every later line is either a bare Responses-API item — `type` of `message` (carrying
  `role` and `content`), `reasoning`, `function_call`, `function_call_output` — or the
  separator line `{"record_type":"state"}`.

The range is 2025-08-07 to 2025-12-07, so this format outlived the date any single cutover
would suggest. Recoverable prose is 58 user + 63 assistant = 121 messages across 17 files.
The 18th (`2025/08/07/rollout-2025-08-07T16-54-05-2df3f3be…jsonl`) is a header-only stub with
no messages at all — a useful edge case for the parser not to choke on.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. `cs index`
2. Query for text known to be in one of the 18 files, e.g. from
   `2025/12/07/rollout-2025-12-07T17-19-51-eff5d92b…jsonl`.
3. Zero hits. The file was read and produced no messages; nothing reports that it was skipped.
design: Needs a disjoint code path gated on 'line has no payload object', which cannot regress the current format. Detect on the header line rather than per-message: line 1 having id+timestamp+git and no payload is an unambiguous format marker, so the file is classified once and dispatched, instead of every line paying a branch. The item shapes are plain Responses-API objects, so the message/reasoning/function_call mapping to Kind is the same table the current parser already has — only the unwrapping differs. Zero event_msg means there is no turn-boundary signal at all: seq comes from line order.
acceptance_criteria: All 18 legacy files import without error. 121 prose messages (58 user, 63 assistant) are indexed across 17 conversations. The header-only 2025-08-07 file yields no conversation rather than an error or an empty-titled row. The 674 payload-format files produce byte-identical index output to before the change, proven by a full reindex diff. Synthetic fixtures only — no real transcripts in the repo (chat-search-4ar.3).

title: Watch vs scan
description: Decides archiver latency and whether a daemon is needed.
close_reason: Answered by shipping. The archiver has run under launchd at 300 s since chat-search-a7k.2 and the latency is fine in practice; no daemon was needed. Nothing in the bead said what would reopen the question, so it was a spike with no live decision behind it. Refile with a concrete trigger (e.g. a source whose writes must be captured in under 300 s) if watch ever becomes worth its complexity.

title: Decompress .zst rollouts in the Codex importer
description: The archiver now captures them verbatim, but nothing can read them yet. Latent until Codex starts compressing here.
acceptance_criteria:
A .zst rollout in the archive imports to the same conversations and messages the equivalent uncompressed rollout produces. A golden test asserts that equivalence directly — same file, compressed and not, must yield byte-identical importer output — since that is the only way to prove decompression is transparent rather than merely non-crashing.

Decompression happens inside the importer, not the archiver. ADR 1 requires the archive to hold source bytes verbatim, and the importer contract is a pure function of (logical_path, bytes), so the bytes it receives are the compressed ones and it decompresses in memory.

A truncated or corrupt .zst is declined the way any unparseable file is declined — it is reported, and it does not abort the run or take the rest of the source down with it.

Selection is by content, not by filename: a rollout that is compressed without a .zst suffix, or named .zst without being compressed, must not silently import as empty.
notes:
SPEC 2026-08-01. Still latent — nothing in the current archive is compressed; the trigger is Codex starting to compress rollouts, at which point every new file silently imports as zero messages if this is not in.

Note the new dependency. The workspace has no zstd crate today (rusqlite, serde, serde_json, toml, thiserror, anyhow, blake3, globset, reflink-copy, uuid, clap, chrono, chrono-tz, ratatui, unicode-width), so this adds one to a deliberately small set. ADR 20 already measured zstd on this corpus at 2.98-3.13x for rollouts, so the format is not in question — only the dependency is.

The silent-empty failure is the one worth designing against: an importer that declines a file it cannot read produces a source that contributes nothing, and cs index already has a row for that case (a7k.22's work). Make sure a compressed file lands in that reporting path rather than in the 'parsed fine, zero messages' path, which looks like an empty transcript.

title: Claude.ai capture
description:
SUPERSEDED — kept for the record because its one-line premise was half wrong.

Original text: 'No local files at all; needs export or API.'

What a survey of this machine on 2026-07-30 actually found:
- 'No local files at all' is false for the Claude DESKTOP app. Cowork and Chat tab transcripts sit in the clear at ~/Library/Application Support/Claude/local-agent-mode-sessions/ — 14 sessions, 30 MB. The earlier conclusion came from inspecting IndexedDB alone, which really does hold no message bodies (React Query cache), but that is the wrong directory. Now chat-search-a7k.23.
- 'Needs export or API' is true for cloud-synced claude.ai conversations, but there is a third route the line did not anticipate: the desktop app's own cookie jar holds a live sessionKey and lastActiveOrg, and its IndexedDB cache reveals the endpoint it calls. ADR 21 took that route. Now chat-search-a7k.24.

The lesson worth keeping: a one-line bead asserting an absence hardened into a fact nobody rechecked for months. Absences need a falsifier, the way docs/ARCHITECTURE.md's 'deliberately absent' table does.

title: bytes captured overstates disk cost
description: An append re-clones the whole file, so the reported figure is file size, not delta. Report allocated blocks instead.
close_reason:
Done, verified — but the bead's prescribed fix turned out not to be what closes the honesty gap, and that is worth recording. scan.rs gained allocated_bytes(&Metadata) (cfg(unix): blocks()*512; cfg(not(unix)): len()) filled from the existing stat call, so no second syscall; FileChange carries it on all paths including the Unchanged fast path. main.rs replaced three loose counters with a Bytes{apparent, allocated, cloned, copied} struct. capture.rs needed no edit — CaptureKind already carried the clone-vs-copy split. JSON contract preserved: 'bytes' and 'bytes_to_capture' keep their exact prior values and meaning; apparent_bytes, allocated_bytes, cloned_bytes, copied_bytes, allocated_to_capture were added alongside. cargo test -p cs-archive 36 passed 0 failed (33 baseline + 3).

FINDING, independently verified: allocated blocks does NOT reduce the figure. Measured over the real 1057-file archive, allocated/apparent is 1.0010 (2268.2 MB vs 2270.4 MB) — these transcripts are neither sparse nor compressed, so blocks()*512 is len() rounded up to 4 KB. Also confirmed by direct experiment that an APFS clonefile destination reports the source's full st_blocks (both 1528 blocks / 782336 bytes for a 780000-byte file), so no stat-based figure can observe the block sharing at all. The clone/copy split from CaptureKind is therefore the only thing that expresses real marginal cost, and on this machine every capture clones, so the report now honestly reads '0.0 MB new on disk' where it used to read '0.7 MB captured'.

The dominant error — an append re-billing the whole file every 300 s — is now visible but not removed. Tracked as a follow-up.

description: Surfaces over the index: CLI, TUI, Raycast, VS Code. cs search --json is the contract they all consume (ADR 12).

title: The bottom drawer has no keyboard reach
description:
Hiding the timeline and dragging a window on it are both mouse-only. The reason is the arrangement this window is built on and it is not a small one: there is exactly one focused view — the query box — and a key this app binds is a key the box stops getting. The fold (chat-search-me9.8.15) got Enter only because Enter was already the list's rather than the field's.

What the drawer would want: a key to hide and show, and some way to move and resize the selection. The second is the hard half. Arrows already move the cursor in the results list, and left/right are how a caret moves through a query that is a grammar (`agent:codex`, a quoted `dir:`), so there is no obvious pair free.

Worth noting the drawer needs it less than the fold did: a fold can hide the row the cursor is standing on, where the drawer can only ever draw. And the window it selects is typeable by hand — `date:2026-07-28..2026-08-02` in the box does everything a drag does, which is the whole point of me9.8.20's round trip. So this is an affordance rather than a gap in what the app can do.
acceptance_criteria: Either the drawer can be hidden and its window moved from the keyboard without taking a key the query box or the results list is using, or apps/macos/README.md says the box is the keyboard route to a date window and this is closed as answered.
notes: 2026-08-06: the analysis above is now one option short. me9.8.21 landed a main menu with Cmd-comma while this was in review, so hiding and showing the drawer no longer needs a free arrow pair — a View item with a key equivalent reaches it without touching what the query box or the results list are using. That is the cheap half; moving and resizing the selection from the keyboard is still the hard half and still has no obvious binding.

title: cs timeline cannot describe a --tools search
description:
`cs timeline` takes `--prefix` and no other search knob, so a query asked against tool traffic has no distribution. That gap is deliberate — a flag on a published command is a promise, and no client draws a timeline under `--tools` today — but it is a gap, and the corpus memory says 66-85% of message-level matches land in tool traffic, so it is the half of the corpus the drawer currently cannot draw at all.

Two candidates. Add `--tools` and `--include-off-path` to `cs timeline` for parity with `cs search`, which is four lines and a contract sentence. Or decide the drawer is prose-only and say so in docs/JSON-CONTRACT.md, which is honest and cheaper. The first is only worth doing when a client offers the toggle; the macOS app has no tools switch (chat-search-me9.8 has no bead for one).
acceptance_criteria: Either `cs timeline --tools` describes the same set `cs search --tools` returns, with the count pinned against it the way the prose one is, or docs/JSON-CONTRACT.md says the timeline is prose-only and why.

title: The rest of the main menu: Edit, and the clipboard in the search field
description:
`chat-search-me9.8.21` built the main menu this executable never had and put three items on it: About, Settings… at Cmd-comma, and Quit at Cmd-Q. Quit was argued in because it was broken and the menu is the only place a key equivalent can live. The same argument reaches further than that bead's design took it, and this is the part it left.

WHAT IS BROKEN. Cmd-C, Cmd-V, Cmd-X, Cmd-A and Cmd-Z do nothing in the search field, and did nothing before me9.8.21 either — a key equivalent is delivered by the main menu, so an app with no Edit menu has no clipboard shortcuts however ordinary the text field is. The search box is where a person pastes a path or a phrase they copied out of a terminal, so this is the one missing menu with a use in the ordinary path.

NOT FOLDED IN ON PURPOSE. me9.8.21's design named three items and pre-empted the question about Quit, so it had thought about what belongs; adding two more menus on the same argument would have been that bead deciding something it was not asked. The mechanism is now built and this is a small file (`MainMenu.swift`) — the work is deciding which menus, not building them.
acceptance_criteria: Cmd-C, Cmd-V, Cmd-X, Cmd-A and Cmd-Z work in the search field and in the reader's selectable text. Whatever other menus are added are argued rather than copied from a template — an item that does nothing in this app is worse than an absent one. Nothing about the settings window or the theme keys changes.
notes:
branch: worktree-me9-8-24-edit-menu (worktree /Users/tylercrosse/dev/projects/.chat-search-worktrees/me9-8-24-edit-menu, branched from origin/main at f03e4a1)

WHAT SHIPPED. Three menus where there was one. Edit carries Undo, Redo, Cut, Copy, Paste and Select All, every action to nil and up the responder chain, which fixes Cmd-C/Cmd-V/Cmd-X/Cmd-A/Cmd-Z in the search field for exactly the reason me9.8.21 fixed Cmd-Q — macOS delivers a key equivalent through a menu and through nothing else, so the field was never broken and the bar was absent. Window carries Close and Minimize, which the app owes the second window me9.8.21 gave it: opened by a key and, until now, dismissable only with the mouse.

THE RULE, since the bead asked for an argument rather than a template. An item is here because a key somebody already presses is dead without it. That excludes Delete (the key already deletes through the field editor), Paste and Match Style (no style in a plain query), Find (this window IS a search and the box takes focus at launch), spelling/substitutions/speech (a query is a grammar, and the machinery that autocorrects prose would rewrite one), Zoom and Bring All to Front (no key equivalent between them), the window list (Cmd-comma already raises the second window), and Hide Others/Show All (both act on other applications).

HIDE WAS ON THE MENU AND CAME OFF, because the pass measured it. AppKit validates hide: as disabled in this process — with an explicit NSApp target and without one — while NSApp.hide(nil) called directly hides the app. So the capability is there and the menu route is what AppKit refuses; the suspect is that this is a plain binary and not a bundle, named as a suspect rather than a cause. A permanently grey item advertises a key that will never fire, which is what the rule excludes. Cmd-H is now the pass's negative control: matched false is what all six keys above it looked like before this bead.

THE BOTTOM OF THE EDIT MENU IS THE SYSTEM'S. Titling a menu Edit makes AppKit insert Writing Tools, AutoFill, Start Dictation and Emoji & Symbols. Two have documented switches (NSDisabledDictationMenuItem, NSDisabledCharacterPaletteMenuItem — both verified to work here), two do not, so throwing them buys a menu still the system's at the bottom while removing two working ways of entering text. Left alone and printed beside the six items this app authored.

--clipboard IS A MODE, NOT A SECTION OF --shot, and the reason is the subject of the check: a key equivalent goes to the key window's first responder, an inactive app has no key window, so this is the one scripted run that must be frontmost — which is what --measure and --shot must not be if their numbers stay comparable with RESULTS.md §1. Measured: under --shot's accessory policy every item validates grey and every press moves nothing while still reporting the menu matched it. So the pass reclaims the front before each press and counts the reclaims, because that failure looks exactly like the bug being checked for.

VERIFIED. --clipboard against the live index: bar read twice (grey with an empty box, live with a selection); ⌘A selects 27 of 27; ⌘C puts the phrase on the pasteboard; ⌘X empties the field AND the query with it; ⌘V brings both back; ⌘Z takes the paste off; ⇧⌘Z redoes it; ⌘H matches nothing while NSApp.hide(nil) hides the app; ⌘M puts the window in the Dock; ⌘W ends the run, which is the evidence for it; the pasteboard comes back holding what a person had left on it; front taken back 3 times. --shot re-run unchanged (58 rows, 563 of 923 drawn, 12/10/2 groups, 0 of 39 rows reachable inside a folded group). --shot --settings re-run unchanged (Settings at 420x273, four appearance probes at the same --bg values, a scripted run wrote none of the four keys, Cmd-Q quits). cargo test --workspace 738 passed 0 failed; cargo build --workspace --all-targets no warnings; swift build -c release no warnings; --verify-theme 6 directions, every one holds.

NOT DEMONSTRATED: the reader's selectable text. With nothing selected copy: correctly resolves nowhere, a selection there is made by dragging, and posting synthetic mouse events would need the Accessibility grant this app has never asked for. That half is reasoned rather than read — the same item on the same chain, and copy: against nil is what SwiftUI's own TextEditingCommands installs — and both the run and the README label it as reasoning.

DOCS: the menu bar was a subsection of the theme seam because Settings… was the only item on it that was this app's; it is now a top-level section of its own, since the rule is load-bearing for whoever adds the next menu. Also corrected a sentence me9.8.21 left stale (the theme seam still listed 'picking one means relaunching' as filed work its own settings window had closed).
pr: https://github.com/tylercrosse/chat-search/pull/41
close_reason: Cmd-C, Cmd-V, Cmd-X, Cmd-A and Cmd-Z work in the search field, through an Edit menu whose absence — not the field — was the bug: macOS delivers a key equivalent through a menu and through nothing else, which is exactly why Cmd-Q was broken before me9.8.21. A Window menu carries Close and Minimize, which the app owes the second window me9.8.21 gave it, opened by a key and until now dismissable only by mouse. Every item is argued from one rule (a key somebody already presses is dead without it) and everything a template would add is named with its own reason. Hide was on the menu and came off because the pass measured it grey: AppKit refuses hide: in this process with or without an explicit target while NSApp.hide(nil) works, so it is now the pass's negative control. --clipboard drives the whole bar through NSMenu.performKeyEquivalent, reads the field editor and the model back after each key, reclaims the front before each press because losing it looks exactly like the bug, and puts the user's pasteboard back before it quits with Cmd-W. The reader's selectable text is the one half not demonstrated — a selection there is made by dragging and synthetic mouse events would want an Accessibility grant this app has never asked for — so it is reasoned from being the same item on the same chain and labelled as reasoning in both the run and the README. Nothing about the settings window or the four theme keys changed; both scripted runs re-verified unchanged. Gate: 738 tests, zero warnings from cargo --all-targets and swift build, --verify-theme 6 of 6.

title: target/debug is 4.2 GB of incremental sediment that cargo never garbage collects
description:
The main checkout's target/debug is 4.2 GB, and almost none of it is the current
build. Measured 2026-08-05 after clearing the merged worktrees:

  deps/         2.9 GB   172,315 .o files
  incremental/  1.2 GB   83 session dirs, oldest 2026-07-28
  build/         40 MB
  rlibs + cs     56 MB

The .o files are rustc codegen units (*.rcgu.o). Debug builds split each crate
into many units, and each cargo build or cargo test writes a new incremental
session keyed by a fresh hash. Cargo never deletes the old ones, so this is
roughly 40 builds of sediment rather than one bloated artifact.

Worth recording because the raw file sizes overstate it: those 172,315 files
map to only 29,571 unique inodes, a 5.8x hard-link amplification, because cargo
hard-links unchanged objects between incremental/ and deps/. Their logical sizes
sum to 5.84 GB; actual disk usage is 2.9 GB. Anything measuring this with
apparent size rather than du will report roughly 3 GB that does not exist.

Also present in the main checkout and not counted above: apps/macos/.build at
594 MB and poc/swift/.build at 206 MB.

Nothing is broken. This is a check-back, not a fix.
design:
Deleting target/debug/incremental reclaims 1.2 GB and loses nothing but the next
build's warm start. cargo clean takes all 4.6 GB including release. Neither was
run on 2026-08-05 because beads were in flight and the rebuild cost was not
worth it.

The question to answer on revisit is whether this needs a policy at all. If
target/debug is still roughly 4 GB, it has plateaued and periodic manual
clearing is fine. If it has kept climbing past what one build needs, then the
incremental session dirs are the growth term and a sweep keyed on session mtime
is the fix.

Note that chat-search-64i covers the per-worktree case and its shared
CARGO_TARGET_DIR option would change this picture completely: a shared target
concentrates all of this into one directory, which makes the sediment question
more urgent, not less.
acceptance_criteria: Re-measure target/debug with du, not apparent size. Either it has plateaued near one build's worth and periodic manual clearing is the documented answer, or it is still growing and a sweep of stale incremental/ sessions is added wherever the 64i cleanup lands.

title: Where a named topic lives: a saved query in library.db, not a facet in the grammar
description:
The other half of chat-search-me9.18, carved off because it is a question about where authored names live rather than a gap in the parser.

The interface prototype narrows by a topic chip. chat-search-me9.18 gave date: an absolute span and deliberately did not give topic: a keyword, because a seeded topic is already expressible as a collection — matches(query) union pinned minus excluded — which makes 'topic:rust-and-cargo' a *named saved query* rather than a facet over an index column. Authored data lives in library.db (ADR 3), so the store is the question and the grammar is at most a consequence of the answer.

It also has no data source. The 26 seeds the prototype draws are a poc/ui/export.py derivation with 37% of the corpus matching none of them; a real one waits on chat-search-6eb.24 (semantic topic labels) or chat-search-6eb.18 (clustering and topic discovery), both of which are open or deferred.

Until this is decided the macOS app draws 'topic' in the GROUP control dashed and unclickable, which is honest: a grouping axis it cannot offer, not a filter it applies where nobody can see it. No client offers a topic *filter*.
design:
Three readings to choose between, in the order they cost.

1. A saved query in library.db with a name, and no grammar at all: a client resolves the name to its query text before searching, so the text in the box is the collection's own query and every existing rule applies unchanged. Nothing new to parse; the whole cost is the authored store and the naming UI.

2. A saved query plus a 'topic:name' keyword that desugars into the saved text at parse time, the way Query::with_source desugars --source. Typeable and copyable, but the text no longer stands alone — a query copied to another machine names a collection that machine may not have, which is the first thing ADR 3's separation makes possible and the first thing this would break.

3. A real facet over a derived column, which is what the prototype's chip looks like. Rejected on its face by ADR 16 and by AGENTS.md: a topic is derived, ids and filters over derived groupings go stale the moment the deriver changes, and 6eb.24's own measurements are why there is no such column.

Recommend 1 unless the saved-query work turns up a reason for 2. Whichever wins, it is a decision about library.db first and about cs_core::query only afterwards.
acceptance_criteria: A written answer to 'what is a topic, where is it stored, and can it be typed', recorded where the project keeps decisions (docs/DECISIONS.md) rather than only in this bead. If the answer gives the grammar a keyword, it comes with the same tests date: got in me9.18: reachable from cs search, copyable out of the box, replayable from a query log. If it does not, the macOS GROUP control's dashed topic chip either points at this bead or goes.

title: A group head counts the rows in hand, and cannot say how many the corpus has
description:
chat-search-me9.8.15 decided the near half of this and left the far half open. The grouped list asks cs for exactly the rows an ungrouped one does — the --limit window, 60 by default — and the fold is what buys the headroom a larger window would otherwise be needed for. Raising the limit for the grouped path spends the answer's latency on rows nobody asked to see, and it would make the key line say less: '12 groups · 500 rows in hand' is a worse sentence than '12 groups · 58 rows in hand'.

What is still not sayable is the prototype's number. poc/ui prints '114 · 30 here' on a project row because it groups an export of the whole index; nothing on cs search --json carries the size of a cwd or of a run, so a head here can only count what arrived. The key line above the list states the set for that reason, which is honest and is not the same as informative — a head reading 39 cannot distinguish a project with 39 conversations from one with 400 that this query touched 39 of.

Two routes, and they are not equivalent. A count on the wire (cs search --json carrying a per-group total for the axis in force) keeps the window at 60 and makes the head corpus-true; a bigger window makes the head sample-true over a bigger sample and settles nothing. The first needs the grammar to know which axis the client grouped by, which is a request the wire does not currently take.
design: cs facets already returns corpus-wide counts per dir: and per agent:, which is the same shape of question one axis at a time. Worth costing whether the grouped head can read the rail's numbers rather than adding a field to the search envelope — that would make project and source corpus-true for free and leave run, whose groups are derived from the rows in hand and have no corpus-wide identity at all.
acceptance_criteria: A group head either states a corpus-true count or states which number it is, with no screen where two numbers of different kinds sit side by side. The run axis has an answer of its own, since its groups do not exist outside the answer that produced them.

title: The two marks a reader cannot compute: a pause and a compaction, on the cs show wire
description:
`poc/ui/app.js` draws two marks on the minimap and the ribbon that nothing on the wire carries: `mm-notch` for a pause and `mm-cut` for a compaction boundary. `chat-search-me9.8.18` shipped the macOS minimap without them and named the hole in `apps/macos/README.md`'s gap table, which is where this bead comes from.

NOTES.md:228 argues the second one hardest, and it is the one worth reading before pricing this: 'a pause says you went away; a compaction says the earlier half stopped being verbatim, so the agent past it knows different things ... at seq 924 of 1,323 you would never find it by scrolling.' A minimap without it is a map missing the one boundary that changes what the conversation means, and it is precisely the boundary you cannot find by reading.

NEITHER IS A CLIENT'S TO DERIVE. Thresholding timestamps in the app is the local-date bug's shape — a rule derived in three places, disagreeing at the edges — and the compaction is not a threshold at all. `Sitting.gapMs` is the closest thing on the wire today and it measures the gap BETWEEN the records folded into a sitting, not within one conversation.

THE COMPACTION IS NOT A HEURISTIC, which is what separates it from the pause. claude-code transcripts carry it explicitly: sampling the first 4,000 lines of one 1,827-message session finds `isCompactSummary` (4), `compactMetadata` (4) and `compact_boundary` (2). So the upstream fact exists and this is an importer-plus-contract question rather than an inference. Whether codex and the other agentic sources carry an equivalent is the first thing to measure, and 'claude-code only' is an acceptable answer as long as the field says so rather than reading as 'this conversation was never compacted'.

THE PAUSE IS A DERIVATION, and it belongs in `cs_core` for the reason the local date does: one renderer, every client reads it. `poc/ui` uses four hours; the corpus has 1,088 gaps over four hours (the corpus-shape memory), so the threshold is not free — it decides how many notches a long session gets.
design:
Both are properties of a MESSAGE rather than of a conversation, which is what makes them fit: `Block` already carries per-message facts a client may not re-derive (`drawn`, `band`, `fold`, `mark_kind`), and this is two more of the same kind. Two nullable-or-false fields on `Block` — something like `gap_ms_before` and `compacted` — cost the Swift and Rust decoders one field each and cost a client that ignores them nothing.

The alternative shape, a separate list of boundaries beside `messages`, is the one to avoid: it would be positions in a second coordinate space, which is `chat-search-me9.25` exactly.

WHAT DEPENDS ON THIS: `apps/macos/README.md`'s minimap gap table, the ribbon (`chat-search-me9.8.19`) which wants the same two marks at row resolution, and the TUI's own reader. Draw order is settled by the prototype and worth keeping: doubled and full-strength for a cut against the notch's single faint line — a pause interrupts, a compaction cuts.
acceptance_criteria: `cs show --json` carries, per message, the silence before it and whether it is a compaction boundary, with the pause threshold rendered once in `cs_core` rather than by each client. What the sources actually carry is measured and written down, including the sources that carry nothing. The macOS minimap draws both and `apps/macos/README.md`'s gap table loses the two rows this bead exists to close.

title: A settings window at Cmd-comma: appearance, and a direction for each side
description:
REWRITTEN 2026-08-05 after Tyler described what the control is actually for. The bead as filed by
me9.8.9's worker assumed the picker offers ONE list — the four directions, one checked. It does not.
`chat-search-me9.8.22` splits appearance from palette into three independent settings, and this is
the surface over those three: an appearance of system / light / dark, a direction for the light
side, and a direction for the dark side, so "GitHub Light by day, Solarized Dark by night" is
something you set rather than something you re-launch into.

That changes what this has to be. A `View > Theme` submenu with one checkmark can express one list;
it cannot express three settings where two of them are lists and the third governs which list you
are currently looking at. So this is a SETTINGS WINDOW at Cmd-comma, which is where macOS puts
exactly this, rather than a menu of directions.

THE BLOCKER IS STILL THE MENU BAR, and it is now load-bearing for a second reason. This executable
creates `NSApplication` by hand and never builds an `NSMenu`, so there is no app menu to hang
`Settings...` on and Cmd-Q does not work either. Building the main menu is a prerequisite for
Cmd-comma rather than an alternative to it, and it fixes Quit on the way past.

WHAT ALREADY WORKS, so this stays a surface and not a mechanism. `Theme.directions` is the list.
`ThemeCheck` prints the class beside the name (`chat-search-me9.8.12`), so a row showing
"solarized-derived · direction" does not have to invent its own vocabulary. Swapping the
environment's theme redraws every view. And me9.8.22 will have already made all three settings
reachable by flag and persisted, so this window is a second way to reach working state rather than
the first and only way.
design:
THE MAIN MENU FIRST, because nothing else can hang anywhere without it. An app menu carrying About,
`Settings...` at Cmd-comma, and Quit at Cmd-Q. Quit is not scope creep: it is currently broken, the
menu is the only place it can live, and shipping a main menu that omits it would be a deliberate
choice to leave it broken.

THE WINDOW holds three controls, and their arrangement should say that appearance governs which of
the other two you are currently seeing:

    Appearance   ( ) System   ( ) Light   ( ) Dark
    Light theme  [ github-light-derived  v ]   direction
    Dark theme   [ solarized-derived     v ]   direction

Each menu lists `Theme.directions` with the class beside the name, for the reason
`chat-search-me9.8.12` already built it: a build can carry a direction off disk
(`chat-search-me9.8.10`) and a picker that shows both without distinguishing them is telling the
user the two are equally fenced when ADR 25 says only one of them is.

Preview on selection, not on confirm. The app redraws under the window, which is the only preview
worth having and costs nothing given the environment override already redraws every view.

WHAT IT MUST NOT BECOME, unchanged from the original bead and worth restating because a settings
window invites it far more than a menu did: `docs/DECISIONS.md` ADR 25 turns on the app not being
the author of a theme. Selecting a direction is selecting. A colour well, a slider on a token, a
"customise..." button that opens the palette — each of those is the app authoring, and each is out
of scope by argument rather than by effort. If a token needs dialling, that is
`chat-search-me9.8.10`'s file-off-disk route, where the authoring happens in a file the user owns
and the result is still measured on load.

THE CHROME ALTERNATIVE STAYS REJECTED and the reason is now stronger, not weaker. `Shell.swift`'s
nav strip has a Spacer where a control would go, but the nav strip is two view switches, three
settings are not a third view, and a strip wide enough for two direction menus is a strip that has
stopped being a nav strip. A settings window is also where the next preference goes, and me9.8.22
having established that this app HAS preferences makes a second one likely rather than hypothetical.

SCOPE BOUNDARY WITH me9.8.22. That bead owns the model, the persistence and the flags; this one owns
the menu and the window. If this bead finds itself deciding what happens to `type` and `geometry`
across an appearance flip, it has crossed the line — that decision belongs to me9.8.22 and should
already be settled and written down by the time this starts.
acceptance_criteria: The app has a main menu, and Cmd-Q works. Cmd-comma opens a settings window carrying three controls: appearance (system/light/dark), a direction for the light side, and a direction for the dark side. Each direction menu lists Theme.directions with the class beside the name. Changing any of the three redraws the running app without relaunching, and the choice persists the same way me9.8.22's flags do — the window and the flags write the same keys. No token value is editable from inside the app. The chrome nav strip is unchanged.
notes:
branch: worktree-me9-8-21-settings (worktree /Users/tylercrosse/dev/projects/.chat-search-worktrees/me9-8-21-settings)

WHAT SHIPPED. A main menu — About, Settings… at Cmd-comma, Quit at Cmd-Q — built by MainMenu.swift and installed in every run, because a hand-made NSApplication has no menu bar at all and a key equivalent is a thing a menu delivers. Cmd-Q worked for the first time. A settings window at Cmd-comma carrying the three settings me9.8.22 made reachable by flag: appearance (system/light/dark) as a horizontal radio group, and a direction per side as two pop-up menus listing Theme.directions with the class beside the name ("paper · direction"). ThemeSettings is the resolved ThemeChoice.Choice held as observed state, Root reads settings.theme into the environment, and that is the whole of preview-on-selection — no OK button, no apply.

THE ONE DECISION THIS BEAD HAD TO MAKE. There are four settings and three controls: nothing on the window stands for where the type scale and the geometry come from. Both side menus naming one direction is read as --theme NAME — that direction whole, side keys cleared — and menus that disagree write theme-light/theme-dark and leave the layout direction alone. Without that rule, picking paper in both menus would draw paper's colours in terminal's metrics while --theme paper draws the serif face, so the same choice said two ways would give two results. A caption under the menus names the layout direction, because a setting that changes the window and appears nowhere on it is worse than a fourth control. This applies me9.8.22's existing rule rather than reopening what a side carries.

THE PANEL IS UNTHEMED ON PURPOSE. Stock AppKit controls, the one view in the app that does not read \.theme. The preview is the window behind it, and a radio group painted in a direction's tokens is a theme authoring a control — the drift ADR 25 exists to prevent. No colour well, no slider, no customise button.

VERIFIED. --shot --settings presses Cmd-comma through NSMenu.performKeyEquivalent (handled true, opened "Settings" at 420x273), prints the menu with its key equivalents, moves all three controls and reads the app's own view tree back through AppearanceProbe after each: --bg #fdfdfc / #f6f1e6 / #f4f7fa / #fbfaf9 for terminal/paper/blueprint/ink light, #1b2123 dark, so a live change reaches the dynamic provider and not only the chrome. Photographs both windows at all three appearances plus the mixed pair on both sides. Confirms a scripted run wrote none of the four keys, exercises the writes against a scratch defaults domain (appearance=dark; differing sides → theme-light/theme-dark; agreeing sides → theme=paper with sides cleared), and quits by pressing Cmd-Q — the run ending there is the evidence, since the line after it only prints when it did not. Reopened with a remembered mixed state and the three controls read it back correctly. --verify-theme 4 directions, every one holds. cargo test --workspace 738 passed 0 failed; cargo build --workspace --all-targets no warnings; swift build -c release no warnings. Plain --shot re-run unchanged. Preferences left as found (domain does not exist).

NOT DONE: Edit, Window and Hide menus — Cmd-C/Cmd-V in the search field are broken for exactly the reason Cmd-Q was, filed as chat-search-me9.8.24 rather than folded in.

close_reason: The app has a main menu — About, Settings… at Cmd-comma, Quit at Cmd-Q — which this hand-made NSApplication never had, so Cmd-Q works for the first time. Cmd-comma opens a settings window over me9.8.22's three settings: an appearance of system/light/dark and a direction per side, each menu naming the class beside the direction, every change redrawing the running app with no OK button and no relaunch, and writing the same four plist keys the flags write. Both side menus on one direction is read as --theme NAME so the window can reach a direction whole; a caption names the layout direction rather than leaving it invisible. The panel is stock AppKit and no token is editable from inside the app. Verified from a script by --shot --settings, which presses Cmd-comma through the menu, drives all three controls, reads the view tree back through AppearanceProbe after each, checks the scripted run wrote nothing, and quits by pressing Cmd-Q. title: The bottom drawer: a timeline of the filtered set, with a scrubber
description:
`poc/ui/DESIGN-BRIEF.md:59` gives the window a fifth region — "**Bottom drawer** — a timeline of
whatever survives the current filters, with a scrubber" — and the app has no bottom drawer at all.
It is the only one of the brief's five regions with no bead, which is why `chat-search-me9.8`'s
children run out at facets: the shell, the row, the reader, grouping and the rail are .1 through
.5, and this was never filed.

WHAT IT IS, from `poc/ui/app.js:850-930`. Its own comment states the claim: "Draws whatever
survives every other filter, with query hits raised above the baseline — so it answers 'when was I
working on this' and 'when did this query land' at once, and scrubbing narrows the same set the
list is showing." Concretely: one mark per conversation at its `ended_at`, hits above the centre
line and everything else below it coloured by source hue, height `log10(n + 1) * 7` clamped to
4-18px, a header reading "<n> in range · <m> with a match · <from> → <to>", 30d/90d/1y/all presets,
and a drag on the track that selects a window — with a drag under 1% of the span clearing the
selection rather than setting a useless one.

The subtlety worth keeping is that it draws `visible(true)` — everything surviving every other
filter EXCEPT the range itself. A timeline that also filtered itself by the range would show a
solid block and nothing else, and would never tell you what widening would get you.

IT IS BLOCKED BY `chat-search-me9.18`, which already names this exact consumer: "The interface
prototype now narrows the list by two things the grammar cannot express: a topic chip and a
timeline range from the scrubber ... a scrubber produces an absolute window, so it needs a range
form, e.g. `date:2026-07-28..2026-08-02`, plus `Older`/`Between` variants in `DateSpec` and the SQL
to match."

THAT DEPENDENCY IS STRUCTURAL, NOT CONVENIENCE, and `poc/ui/NOTES.md` §17 is the record of what
happens when it is treated as convenience. The prototype "let a second filter state back in",
keeping the timeline range in a tuple that never appeared in the query line, and two rounds of the
projects view were written against that state before anyone noticed. `docs/TUI-DESIGN.md` §5 and
`chat-search-me9.16` both settle that query text is the only filter state, and DESIGN-BRIEF states
it as a bug condition: "A filter that narrows the list without appearing here would be a bug." So
the scrubber writes `date:A..B` into the query line and reads its own selection back out of it —
which is only possible once me9.18 lands.
design:
A WIRE QUESTION TO SETTLE BEFORE DRAWING ANYTHING. The drawer's whole claim is that it shows
whatever survives the filters — but the app searches at `--limit 60` (`SearchModel.swift:60`,
`CsClient.swift:94`), so what it has in hand is a page, not the set. A timeline over the top 60
ranked conversations is a different picture from a timeline over the 354 that matched, and it is
misleading in a specific way: ranking is not chronological, so the page is a biased sample of the
axis being drawn.

The app already knows the honest total — `SearchModel.swift:19` carries "how many conversations
match with `--limit` ignored, and whether that number is whole" — so the header's "<n> in range" is
answerable today and the marks are not. `ended_at` is present on 100% of conversations, so the data
exists; what does not exist is a way to ask for the timestamps of everything that matches without
paying for the rows. Options, roughly in cost order: a `--fields` or count-only mode on
`cs search --json` that returns `(conv_id, ended_at)` and nothing else; a second call at a high
limit with the preview and shape off; or draw a histogram of buckets rather than one mark per
conversation, which needs only counts per bucket and scales to any corpus size. The third is
probably the right shape for a native app and is a departure from the prototype, which draws marks
because it only ever had 3,059 of them in memory.

Decide that first. Everything else here is layout.

THE SCRUBBER'S CONTRACT WITH THE QUERY LINE. Dragging writes `date:A..B` into the query text, the
same way clicking a facet does — DESIGN-BRIEF §"Search bar": "The query line is the single source
of truth for filtering; clicking a facet anywhere rewrites it." The selection rectangle is then
derived from the parsed query, not held beside it. That means the round trip has to survive: a user
typing `date:2026-07-28..2026-08-02` by hand should see the scrubber's selection move, and that is
the test that proves there is no second filter state.

The presets (30d/90d/1y/all) are a nicety and can land in the same pass, but note they are relative
windows and `DateSpec` already speaks that language — `<7d`, `<2w` — so they need no new grammar
and could ship before me9.18 if the drawer is wanted early in read-only form.

WHAT NOT TO INHERIT FROM THE PROTOTYPE. Source hue below the line assumes a hue per source, and
`chat-search-g6u` records that the facet rail has no source colour because the mapping is not
written yet, with `chat-search-me9.8.13` open on what google-takeout gets. This bead should consume
that mapping rather than invent a second one.
acceptance_criteria: A bottom drawer draws the time distribution of everything matching the current query, not of the --limit 60 page, and how that is paid for is decided and written down before it is drawn. Dragging the track writes date:A..B into the query line; typing the same range by hand moves the selection. No filter state lives outside the query text, which poc/ui/NOTES.md section 17 records this prototype getting wrong. The drawer's own marks are not narrowed by the selected range, so widening is visible. The drawer hides and shows, and hiding it does not change the result set.
notes:
branch: worktree-me9-8-20-timeline (worktree at ~/dev/projects/.chat-search-worktrees/me9-8-20-timeline, 5 commits off b9080f0)
pr: https://github.com/tylercrosse/chat-search/pull/38
merged into main as d3564de (PR #38, merge commit). Conflicts with me9.8.21's --settings flag and me9.8.17's six directions were three list-append collisions and nothing semantic; --verify-theme measures six and holds, and the drawer draws in solarized-derived with no edit, which is the theme seam paying out.
close_reason: The bottom drawer ships, and the wire question was settled and written down before a bar was drawn: a timeline over the --limit 60 page is a biased sample of its own axis because ranking is not chronological, and it would look exactly like a correct picture. So cs_core::timeline counts over the whole matching set and cs timeline --json returns a fixed-size histogram — a bar per stretch of civil days, the filtered rows stacked by source below a baseline and the query's matches raised above it. The bars are drawn with date: stripped (Query::without_facet), so the window narrows the numbers and never the picture and widening stays visible; --shot prints 'bars unchanged by the window: true' against the real index. The drag is the rail's trade made backwards — a chip can be enumerated and a drag cannot, so cs timeline --drag FROM..UNTIL takes two instants and returns the finished query text, and SearchModel.scrub ends in apply(chip:) so a drag is a keystroke. The rectangle is then derived from the parsed query: --shot clears it and retypes 'date:2025-05-30..2026-06-02' by hand and the selection comes back. Hiding stops the request and leaves the result set alone (58 rows against 58 open). Measured before shipping: the reply costs 1.2x settling the same total warm (56 ms for 'the' against 45) and 140-240 ms through a spawn against the search's 280-340, which is the argument for no debounce; a first draft that joined the sitting per posting cost 760 ms and timeline::cost is what caught it. Log10 and not linear, also measured: the tallest bucket holds 222 and the median non-empty 16, so linear drew three years as a flat line. Departures recorded in apps/macos/README.md, contract pinned by json_contract.rs, TUI-DESIGN §5 closed. Two gaps filed rather than hidden: me9.8.25 (no --tools timeline) and me9.8.26 (no keyboard reach).

title: Draw the row's ribbon, once me9.25 says which coordinate space it lives in
description:
`chat-search-me9.8.2` closed the row with the ribbon's space left and nothing in it, deliberately.
`ResultRow.swift:24-27` records the reason — "There is no ribbon, and nothing stands in its place.
It needs `kind_runs` drawn in the same coordinate space as `match_seqs`, and `chat-search-me9.25`
says those are two spaces today" — and `apps/macos/README.md`'s gap table says the same. What
neither says is which bead eventually draws it. This one does.

EVERYTHING BELOW THE DRAWING IS ALREADY DONE AND MEASURED, which is why this is smaller than it
sounds:

- **Geometry is tokenised.** `Theme.swift:203-209` defines `--rib-h`, `--rib-track` and
  `--rib-top`, at 18/9/6 in `Tokens.swift:110-112`, with the asymmetry documented: `ribbonTop` is
  deliberately not `(ribbonHeight - ribbonTrack) / 2` because the bottom of the cell belongs to the
  failure and question marks and the top to the match ticks, both drawn outside the track.
- **The palette is fenced.** `ThemeCheck.swift:14-21` already holds the four kinds on an even
  ~1.8x luminance ramp against the ribbon track — `kTool` 2.20, `kReason` 4.00, `kUser` 7.20,
  `kAgent` 13.00 — because hue is the channel that degrades fastest at the ~2px the bands are drawn
  at, so kind rides on luminance. Every theme is checked against that today, for a ribbon that does
  not exist yet.
- **The row has already budgeted the width.** `ResultRow.swift:18`: "Even once the ribbon lands the
  directory keeps ~27 of its 44." Adding it does not reopen the column plan.

SO WHAT BLOCKS THIS IS UPSTREAM, AND IT IS A DECISION RATHER THAN A FIX. `chat-search-me9.25` has
to settle whether match positions arrive in the drawn reading order, or as message ids the client
resolves, or not at all — and the third answer changes this bead's scope rather than delaying it,
because a ribbon with kind bands and no match ticks is still worth drawing. Alongside it,
`chat-search-me9.31` (kind_runs is 35% of the response and compresses 1.9x) and
`chat-search-me9.26` (a covering index that would retire `SearchOptions::shape`) decide whether the
shape can be on by default, which decides whether the ribbon is always there or only sometimes.
design:
THE ORDER, and it is not this bead first. `chat-search-me9.25` decides the coordinate space,
`chat-search-me9.26` and `chat-search-me9.31` decide what the shape costs to ask for, and
`chat-search-me9.23` draws it against real `kind_runs` in `poc/ui` where an iteration is a page
reload rather than a build. Doing me9.23 first is not ceremony: the prototype currently synthesises
the band data in `export.py`, so nobody has yet seen a ribbon drawn from the real distribution, and
the row strip is 7px tall over a median of 5 runs and a max of 688. Whether that reads as anything
at all is an open question this bead should not discover in SwiftUI.

THE ALGORITHM IS `poc/ui/app.js:144-176` (`mapBands`), and its two decisions are the ones to keep:
bucket to the available pixel width and let each bucket take its dominant kind, and take height
from `log10(len)` rather than from message count, so a stretch of short tool calls does not draw
the same as a stretch of prose.

DRAW IT ONCE, NOT TWICE. `mapBands` carries the comment "One map renderer, three scales: row strip,
sitting card, big minimap. The TUI spec's rule that the density strip and outline mode are the same
data at two resolutions, extended rather than duplicated." That rule should survive the port: this
bead and the reader-pane minimap bead are the same primitive at two scales, and whichever lands
first should land as something the other consumes. They differ in where their data comes from — the
row from `kind_runs` on the search response, the minimap from the resolved transcript — but not in
what they draw.

THIS IS THE FIRST `Canvas` IN THE APP. `poc/swift/RESULTS.md` §8 records that no `Canvas` drawing
