was attempted anywhere in the spike, and names the ribbon, the minimap and the gutter spine as the
three parts of the brief most likely to be hard. So budget for the unknown once, here or in the
minimap bead, and let the second one inherit it.
acceptance_criteria: The row draws a ribbon from kind_runs in whatever coordinate space chat-search-me9.25 settles on, at the --rib-h/--rib-track/--rib-top tokens that already exist, with no new geometry literals in the view. Match ticks are drawn if and only if me9.25 makes them drawable; if it does not, the README's gap table says so and the row carries no stand-in. The band renderer is shared with the reader's minimap (chat-search-me9.8.18), or the reason it is not is written down. ThemeCheck's four-kind ramp still passes and is now checking something that is drawn.

title: The reader has no minimap, and the scroll relationship is the hard half
description:
`poc/ui/DESIGN-BRIEF.md:57` puts a minimap beside the transcript in the right drawer, and
`chat-search-me9.8.3` shipped the reader without one. `poc/swift/RESULTS.md` §8 records why it was
never priced: "The ribbon, the minimap and the gutter spine are the parts of the design brief most
likely to be hard, and none of them was attempted." Nothing stands in its place and no bead tracked
it until now.

THE DATA IS ALREADY HERE, which is what separates this from the ribbon. `CsKit.Block` carries
`band`, `onPath`, `drawn`, `marks`, `isSidechain`, `isError` and `text`, and `cs show --json`
resolves all of it into ONE coordinate space — the reader's own drawn list, in the order the
transcript arrives. `chat-search-me9.25`'s coordinate-space bug is a property of the SEARCH
response (`match_seqs` against `kind_runs`) and does not reach the reader, which `ReaderView.swift`
already relies on: it anchors the opening scroll on `marks` and not on `match_seqs` for exactly
that reason. So this is not blocked on me9.25.

TWO MARKS THE PROTOTYPE DRAWS ARE NOT ON THE WIRE. `poc/ui/app.js` emits `mm-notch` for a pause and
`mm-cut` for a compaction boundary. `NOTES.md:228` argues the second one hardest — "a compaction
says the earlier half stopped being verbatim, so the agent past it knows different things ... at
seq 924 of 1,323 you would never find it by scrolling" — and neither is a field on `Block`.
`Sitting.gapMs` is the closest thing on the wire and it measures the gap BETWEEN conversations, not
within one. A minimap ships fine without them, but it ships without the mark the notes call the
reason to have one, so say so rather than discovering it later.

THE SCROLL RELATIONSHIP IS THE ACTUAL WORK, and it is two-way: the transcript's position drives the
viewport box, and dragging the minimap drives the transcript. The reader is a SwiftUI `List` inside
a `ScrollViewReader` (`ReaderView.swift:104-136`), chosen because `chat-search-me9.22` measured it
as the only container that recycles. `List` gives back neither of the two numbers the prototype's
`syncViewport()` reads off the DOM — `scrollTop` and `scrollHeight` — and `ScrollViewReader` only
goes the other way, and only to an `id`. That is the problem to solve, and it is a container
question rather than a drawing question.
design:
THE PROTOTYPE IS THE REFERENCE, and it is small enough to read whole: `poc/ui/app.js:1235-1285`
builds it, `app.js:1909-1951` wires it. What it does that is worth keeping:

- **Height is log10(text length), normalised over the conversation** — not one row per message.
  A 1,300-message conversation has to fit a drawer's height, and equal-height bands make a
  transcript of mostly short tool calls look like a transcript of mostly prose.
- **Dim rather than drop for off-path messages**, with the comment "same rule as the ribbon, so the
  scrollbar keeps describing the whole conversation." A minimap that omits what the fidelity
  controls are hiding stops being a map of the conversation and becomes a map of the current view.
- **Band width encodes role**: 18px for user, 28px otherwise. Cheap, and it survives greyscale.
- **Match ticks are separate elements over the bands**, not a recolour of them, so a hit on a tool
  call still reads as a tool call.
- `role="slider"` with `aria-valuenow` tracking the scroll fraction, and Arrow keys moving 48px.

THE CONTAINER QUESTION. `List` exposes no scroll offset and no content height. Three routes, and
picking one is most of this bead:

1. **Keep `List`, drive by id.** Map the drag fraction to a message index, `scroll.scrollTo(id)`.
   Track the visible range with `onAppear`/`onDisappear` bookkeeping per row and derive the
   viewport box from it. No new memory cost, no AppKit. But dragging lands on message boundaries
   instead of pixels, and the box is approximate — on a conversation where one expanded block is
   taller than the drawer, "which messages are visible" and "where am I" stop agreeing.
2. **Move the reader to `ScrollView` + `LazyVStack`** and read geometry with `GeometryReader` and a
   `PreferenceKey`. Exact, and the prototype's behaviour ports directly. The cost is measured but
   not for this case: me9.22 saw `ScrollView`+`LazyVStack` accumulate 65.6 MB against `List`'s
   5.2 MB scrolling the whole 3,059-row corpus. The reader's worst case is one conversation of
   2,553 messages, so that number is indicative and should be re-measured before it decides
   anything. `onScrollGeometryChange` and `ScrollPosition` would make this clean and are macOS 15+;
   `Package.swift` declares `.macOS(.v14)`, so using them is a deployment-floor decision, not a
   free win.
3. **`NSViewRepresentable` down to the underlying `NSScrollView`.** Exact geometry, keeps
   recycling. It reintroduces AppKit, and `chat-search-9uu` already reports a reentrant
   `NSTableView` warning on every typing run, so this route starts with a known neighbour.

Route 1 is the one to try first: it is reversible, costs nothing measured, and if the approximate
box turns out to be good enough at real conversation lengths then the container question never has
to be reopened.

WHAT TO DO ABOUT THE TWO MISSING MARKS. Do not invent them client-side by thresholding timestamps —
that is the local-date bug's shape, a rule derived in three places. Either they arrive on the
`cs show --json` wire as fields on a message, or the minimap ships without them and the README's
gap table records it the way it already records the ribbon. Filing the wire work is a separate
bead if this one wants it.
acceptance_criteria: The drawer shows a minimap of the whole conversation, drawn from the same blocks the transcript renders, with off-path and hidden messages dimmed rather than dropped. Scrolling the transcript moves the viewport indicator and dragging the minimap moves the transcript, both at the corpus's longest conversation (2,553 messages). Matches are visible on it when there is a query. The container decision is recorded in apps/macos/README.md with what it cost, re-measured rather than inherited from me9.22 if the reader leaves List. Anything the minimap cannot draw because the wire does not carry it is named in the README's gap table beside the ribbon.
notes:
branch: worktree-me9-8-18-minimap (worktree .claude/worktrees/me9-8-18-minimap)
pr: https://github.com/tylercrosse/chat-search/pull/32
close_reason: The drawer draws the conversation as a column beside the transcript: a band per message on the head path, height log10 of its length normalised, width encoding role, successful tool results dimmed rather than dropped, a tick per match at half width when it cannot claim to have ranked. Route 1 of the three containers the bead costed — keep List, drive by id — so me9.22's numbers still stand and what was measured is the relationship, against a build of this app with no minimap in it, alternating runs: p50, p95 and missed vsyncs indistinguishable, footprint ranges overlapping, both recorded as ranges in apps/macos/README.md along with the two costs that are not noise (the box is a report of which rows exist, and a drag lands on a message boundary). --shot drives both directions on the corpus's longest conversation at 2,431 messages and prints what moved; --longest is how it reaches it. The two marks the prototype draws and this wire does not carry — a pause and a compaction boundary — are in a gap table beside the ribbon's and filed as chat-search-me9.39.

title: Port Gruvbox and Solarized, on the terms ADR 25 sets
description:
Tyler's stated motivation for the theme seam names these two palettes, and me9.8.12 measured what each one costs. This is the port itself, which is deliberately small now that the policy is settled.

Neither passes as published, and they fail differently. Gruvbox is a nudge: its dark side already carries an even ramp in bg3/gray/green/fg0 at 1.77x 1.78x 1.82x and its light side is 0.09 out, and re-solving moves each band a few percent of lightness. Solarized is a rebuild: no assignment of its sixteen colours makes an even ramp at all, and its brightest kind has to go from base1 at L 60% to L 93%, past base2.

So both ship as directions with 'derived' in the name, and the README's table records how far each one had to move. A user who wants the published values loads them as a user theme instead (me9.8.10).
design:
The path is the one apps/macos/README.md already documents and nothing here departs from it: add the hues to DIRECTIONS in poc/ui/palette.py, let solve() land the eight fenced tokens, write the rest into directions.css, run tokens.py.

The unsolved two-thirds is where the work actually is. A theme is 30 colour tokens per side; Solarized publishes 16 colours and Gruvbox 19, so the panels, rules, selection grounds, match grounds and five source hues are invented either way. Invent them from the palette's own greys rather than from terminal's, or the direction reads as terminal wearing a costume.

Both themes, and the light sides are not the dark ones inverted — palette.py solves each against whichever ground is worse for it.
acceptance_criteria: gruvbox-derived and solarized-derived are in DIRECTIONS and directions.css, generate through tokens.py, and hold --verify-theme in both themes. The names say derived. The README's direction table gains a row for each, with the diff shortstat and the measured ramp, the way the existing four have. No view changed.
notes:
branch: worktree-me9-8-17-derived-themes (git worktree at /Users/tylercrosse/dev/projects/.chat-search-worktrees/me9-8-17-derived-themes, 5 commits: 448f4b2 896b95d 64efa5a a230a0f baec6ec)
final commit rewritten to carry the Closes trailer; branch head is now 7931cba (5 commits: 448f4b2 896b95d 64efa5a a230a0f 7931cba)
pr: https://github.com/tylercrosse/chat-search/pull/37
close_reason:
gruvbox-derived and solarized-derived ship as fenced directions. Every hue is Gruvbox's or Solarized's and not one lightness is: the eight fenced tokens come out of palette.py's solve, the grounds and accents go in published and are named in trailing comments, and the ~19 tokens per side that are neither (panels, rules, selection and match grounds, five source hues) are invented from each palette's own greys rather than terminal's. Both sides of both are solved separately, not inverted — Gruvbox publishes faded accents for its light side and Solarized swaps its greys' temperature between sides.

MEASURED, and the two fail differently. Gruvbox is a nudge: its three dark grounds (bg0_s/bg0/bg0_h) go in unaltered as page/drawer/track and the worst token moves 11.4 pt of HSL lightness dark, 13.3 light. Solarized is a rebuild: its brightest kind travels 26.7 pt, base1 at L 60% to L 87% — which corrects the README's pre-port prediction of 'L 93%, past base2', since it lands short of base2 and still brighter than any colour Solarized puts on a dark ground — and its designated secondary tier travels 21.6 pt the other way because 2.42:1 is under half the AA floor. Its ribbon track had to be invented (the darkest colour it publishes is the page itself), and it needed one middle foreground tier per side because it offers two per ground where this interface reads three.

NO VIEW CHANGED: nothing under Sources/ChatSearch is touched, and neither direction sets a type, radius or rhythm token, so rows-per-screen cannot move. The whole port is 3 files changed, 479 insertions(+), 7 deletions(-) across palette.py, directions.css and Tokens.swift, of which the 95 Swift lines per direction are generated. Docs: apps/macos/README.md gains the direction table (ramp per side, worst-token move, shortstat) and drops 'not yet possible without editing this app'; poc/ui NOTES/README/DESIGN-BRIEF/directions.js/html and styles.css corrected from four directions to six, and directions.js now carries both ports so the third reading — measured off the rendered page — happens for them too.

Gate green: 733 cargo tests, 0 warnings from cargo build --workspace --all-targets, 0 warnings from swift build -c release, palette.py --verify exit 0, --verify-theme exit 0 ('6 directions measured, and every one holds'). Both drawn as well as measured via --shot.

title: Grouped sections do not fold, and the keyboard does not know about them
description:
chat-search-me9.8.4 draws the grouping dimension as sections that are always open. poc/ui folds every axis and opens nothing, which is the right answer at corpus scale — thirteen headers carrying count, span and a sparkline are a project index, and one open group buries the other twelve (poc/ui/NOTES.md section 2).

The app is not at that scale: it groups the --limit window of a ranked answer, 60 rows by default, so a fold would hide the answer behind its own headers on every keystroke. That trade flips the moment the window grows — either because --limit is raised or because grouping learns to ask for more rows than the list shows.

The prototype also names the cost of folding and did not pay it: 'the footer offers the right arrow to expand and no key is bound. Expanding is now the required first action on every grouped view, so the keyboard model stops being optional polish' (NOTES.md section 5). This app's keyboard model is the TUI's — the field never gives up focus, arrows move the cursor in the list beside it — so a fold here means arrows have to walk headers and rows, and a collapsed section must not be able to hold the cursor.
design:
Two things land together or neither does: a per-group open state keyed on axis+key (cleared when the axis changes, because groups are ranked and the set you left open is rarely the set at the top now), and SearchModel.rows narrowing to what is actually drawn so moveSelection cannot park the cursor inside a closed section.

Worth deciding at the same time whether a grouped list should ask cs for more rows than an ungrouped one. Group counts today are over the rows in hand and the key line says so; corpus-true counts (poc/ui prints '114 · 30 here') would need either a larger limit or a count on the wire.
acceptance_criteria: A group can be folded and unfolded. The cursor never lands on a row inside a folded group. Switching axis resets the fold state.
notes:
branch: worktree-me9-8-15-fold (worktree at .claude/worktrees/me9-8-15-fold)
pr: https://github.com/tylercrosse/chat-search/pull/34
close_reason: Grouped sections fold and the keyboard walks them. The cursor moves through SearchModel.lines — a head per group and, under each open one, its rows — so a folded group contributes only its head and cannot hold the cursor by construction; folding a group the cursor is inside moves it to the head. Enter acts on the line under the cursor (a conversation opens, a head folds) rather than the prototype's unwired right arrow, because the query box is the only focused view and left/right are how a caret moves through a grammar. Switching axes clears the accordion. The list opens open, which is one boolean the day the row window grows. Verified against the live index at 'borrow checker'/58 rows through a new --shot pass: 0 of 39/17/56 hidden rows reachable on project/run/source, cursor rescued on all three, 0 folded after an axis switch — plus a --group project vs --group project --folded measurement pair. Gate green: cargo test --workspace 0 failed, cargo build --workspace --all-targets and swift build -c release both warning-free, --verify-theme exit 0. The corpus-true group count the design note raised is decided against a bigger window and filed as chat-search-me9.8.23.

title: CsKit spells a band two ways: a String on a run, an enum on a block
description:
cs_core::blocks::Band is one vocabulary — user, agent, reasoning, tool — and CsKit now decodes it twice. Model.swift's `Run.band` is a raw String, because when it was written the band was only ever a label on a run-length pair. Transcript.swift's `Block.band` is a proper enum with an `unrecognised(String)` arm, because the reader has to turn it into a colour and there is no honest colour for a name this build has never seen.

Two spellings of one open set is the shape a drift starts in: a view switching on strings and a view switching on cases will disagree the first time core adds a fifth band.
design:
Fold Run.band onto the Band enum. Deliberately not done in chat-search-me9.8.3, because chat-search-me9.8.2 was in flight building the kind ribbon off kindRuns at the time and this would have landed underneath it — so do it after that has merged, when the callers are known.

Worth checking at the same time whether MarkOffsets, Destination and Band should share one spelling of 'an open set decoded as something this client cannot act on'. Three hand-written Decodable inits with the same shape is not yet a pattern worth extracting, but a fourth would be.
acceptance_criteria: One Band type in CsKit, decoded in one place, used by both Run and Block. cs-spike contract still names an unknown band rather than failing on one.

title: The facet rail has no source colour, because the mapping is not written yet
description:
The token layer carries five --src-* hues and says why: 'Carried by the token layer before anything draws them, so the row's anatomy (chat-search-me9.8.2) finds them solved rather than picking five more.' What it does not carry is the rule that maps a source id onto one — there are eight sources in the census and five hues, so the mapping is a decision and not a lookup.

chat-search-me9.8.5's rail therefore draws no source colour at all: a glyph in --ink-3 and nothing else. Writing a mapping there while me9.8.2 writes the agent badge would be two copies of one rule, which is the duplication this epic's sequencing exists to prevent.

So: once me9.8.2 has landed the badge, put the mapping wherever it landed (CsTheme is the honest home — it is a token lookup, not a view decision) and have SourceRail read it.
acceptance_criteria: One place in the app maps a source id to a --src-* token. The rail and the row both read it. A source with no hue is drawn without one rather than given a wrong one.

title: The app records picks and never records an abandonment
description:
TUI-DESIGN section 6 'Logging the pick' names two events and the macOS app emits one of them. On Enter it runs cs pick, which records a Pick with the finished query, the rank and the shown list. On quit with a non-blank query and no pick it records nothing.

That second row is the abandonment signal — 'the ranking showed me nothing worth opening' — and TUI-DESIGN calls it information chat-search-6eb.21 cannot get any other way: 'Without it the log only ever records successes.'

There is no CLI verb for it. cs search records a Search event, but only on the non-prefix path, and running a whole second search at quit to log one line is the wrong shape. The likely answer is a flag on cs pick, or a small cs record verb, decided against what querylog::Event already holds.

Note the app is typeahead, so the rule that made this matter for the TUI applies to it identically: never emit Search per keystroke.
acceptance_criteria: Quitting the app with a non-blank query and no pick appends exactly one Search event. Typing appends nothing.
notes:
branch: worktree-pdw-abandonment (worktree at .claude/worktrees/pdw-abandonment)
pr: https://github.com/tylercrosse/chat-search/pull/27
close_reason: Added `cs abandon <query>`, the sibling of `cs pick` that appends the Search event TUI-DESIGN §6 calls the abandonment signal; it re-ranks the finished query so its shown/n are comparable with a Pick for the same text, and owns the 'no need behind it' rule (Mode::Empty). The macOS app calls it from applicationWillTerminate when the box is non-blank and nothing was opened since the last keystroke. --measure and --shot now run every cs with CS_LOG_QUERIES=0 and say so, because a scripted run quits in exactly the shape of a person giving up (ADR 22). Fixed a regression found on the way: assigning nil to Process.environment empties the child environment rather than inheriting it, which had cs-spike contract failing every phrase for want of HOME. Verified end to end against the live 3,617-conversation index; 692 tests, warning-free cargo and swift builds, --verify-theme holds, cs-spike contract passes.

title: Carry model and thread_count on the wire, so the row can draw the cells it is missing
description:
poc/ui's row has nine cells and chat-search-me9.8.2 could draw five, because four are not on the wire.

TWO ARE IN THE INDEX AND NOT IN THE CONTRACT. conversation.model and conversation.thread_count are columns in crates/cs-core/src/schema.rs — poc/ui/export.py reads both with a plain SELECT — and cs search --json emits neither. So the app has no model cell and no forks cell, and the mockup's left cluster is agent and size where it was meant to be agent, model, size, change and shape.

TWO ARE NOT IN THE INDEX AT ALL, and are not this bead. Total edit lines are summed by export.py from per-call diffs, by parsing Edit and Write tool_call arguments — importer work, not a client's, and not something to bolt onto a search response. Topics are a poc-only clustering over the corpus.

An addition does not move v (docs/JSON-CONTRACT.md, 'Extending this contract'), so this is a silent addition rather than a break — but it costs cs-core, the contract doc, a test, and CsKit's Model.swift, and it lands under three surfaces that draw rows. That is why me9.8.2 filed it rather than taking it.
design:
model is nullable and thread_count is not — schema.rs has thread_count NOT NULL DEFAULT 0. Both need a line in JSON-CONTRACT.md's Group table saying what the value means, and model needs one in 'The nullable fields' saying what null means: no message in the conversation named a model, which is every ChatGPT and Takeout row.

Note what the labels are for. schema.rs calls conversation.model 'the model of the last message that named one, resolved in the rollup' — a summary of message.model, not a fact about the conversation (ADR 24, chat-search-n58.25). A row drawing it is drawing the last model used, and the cell should not imply more than that.

The row's cells are already sized in characters of the meta face (apps/macos/Sources/ChatSearch/ResultRow.swift, Columns), so adding two is a plan change and not a re-layout. Both must vanish when empty — thread_count is 1 on nearly every conversation and the mockup only draws the fork mark above 1.
acceptance_criteria: cs search --json carries model and thread_count on every Group; docs/JSON-CONTRACT.md states what each means and what a null model means; CsKit decodes both; the row draws a model cell and a forks cell, each absent rather than blank when there is nothing to say. cargo test --workspace green, swift build with no warnings.

title: A hue for google-takeout, or a rule for sources the palette does not name
description:
The palette carries five source hues — --src-claude-code, --src-codex, --src-chatgpt, --src-claude-ai, --src-gemini — and the live index has six sources. google-takeout is 1,280 conversations, 29% of the corpus, and has none. chat-search-me9.8.2's row draws it in the quiet tier, which is honest (a view must not author a sixth colour) but leaves the second-largest source as the one that reads as unclassified, next to chatgpt in green and codex in cyan.

Two shapes, and choosing is the bead. NAME IT: add the hue to poc/ui/palette.py's DIRECTIONS, let it solve against the same fences the others clear, regenerate Tokens.swift — one more named token, and the next source asks the question again. OR CARRY A RAMP: cs-tui/src/theme.rs already answers this generally — eight categorical hues, KNOWN_SOURCES fixing the first eight positions and an FNV-1a hash placing anything unlisted, with the note that eight is the ceiling for categorical discriminability and that grey, white and both reds are excluded by construction. A palette carrying that ramp rather than five names would give the app the same rule and the same answer on every machine.
design:
Whatever is chosen has to hold --verify-theme: a source hue is drawn as text at --fs-meta on --bg and on --panel, so it clears the same 4.5:1 floor every other text tier does. That is why this is not simply 'pick a colour' — poc/ui/palette.py solves against the worse of the two grounds, and a hue pasted into Tokens.swift by hand is what the generator exists to prevent.

Two spellings meet in Display.sourceHue: the source id is google-takeout, and the CSS token names follow the product (--src-chatgpt for chatgpt-export).
acceptance_criteria: Every source in the live index draws in a hue of its own, or the app has one stated rule for a source the palette does not name and the row follows it. --verify-theme holds in both themes.

title: Decide whether spacing outside the row is a token
description:
me9.8.8 tokenised the row's rhythm — --row-pt, --row-pb, --row-px, --row-gap — because a direction moves those and every one of them trades against rows-per-screen, which DESIGN-BRIEF names first on its list of what would actually break this.

It left the rest literal: the search bar's 12/7, the banner's 12/5, the footer's 12/6, the empty state's 22 and 40, and the HStack gutters. That was not an oversight. styles.css keeps the same numbers literal in its own rules, and me9.8.8's design says plainly 'do not promote a number to a token merely because it is a number'.

But Tyler named padding as one of the three things he wants to dial in, and today dialling any of those is still a view edit — which is the friction the seam was supposed to remove.
design:
THE TENSION IS REAL AND BOTH SIDES ARE WRITTEN DOWN ALREADY, which is why this is a decision rather than a task.

AGAINST: styles.css argues that promoting every number flattens the distinction between a
visual direction and a bug. Radii below 3px, the 50% dots and the 10-11px pills are named
as things that must stay literal, and squaring a dot is not a direction. A token layer with
forty spacing tokens in it is a second stylesheet, and nobody dials in forty numbers.

FOR: the reason the row's rhythm is tokenised is that a direction moves it. All four
directions in directions.css do move --row-px and --row-gap — and none of them touches the
search bar's padding, which is evidence that the current line is drawn about right.

SO THE QUESTION IS NARROW: is the friction Tyler is describing about padding a direction
would move, or about padding he wants to nudge while deciding what the app looks like at
all? If the second, this is not a token question — it is me9.8.10 (load at runtime), and
tokenising more numbers just moves the rebuild rather than removing it.

Worth answering before me9.8.2 onward write four more views, because whatever is decided
they should all follow it.
acceptance_criteria: A written answer to 'what makes a number a token here', concrete enough that a worker writing a view can apply it without asking. If the answer is 'more of them', the tokens are added to poc/ui/styles.css first — it is the authored copy — and regenerated, not typed into Swift.

title: Load a token set at runtime, so dialling in the look is not a rebuild
description:
The second half of Tyler's stated motivation for me9.8.8: 'reduce the friction as I try to dial in the look and feel (typography, sizing, padding)'.

Today that loop is edit styles.css, run tokens.py, swift build, relaunch. The seam made it a loop at all — before it, dialling in the look meant editing every view — but it still costs a compile per iteration, and the values being dialled are exactly the ones a person wants to nudge twenty times in an afternoon.

Reading a token set from a file at launch would make it edit and relaunch. Watching that file would make it edit and see.
design:
THE SHAPE IS ALREADY RIGHT FOR IT. Palette, TypeScale and Geometry are dictionaries keyed by enums whose raw values are the CSS custom property names, so a file of '--ink-3: #7a8b8e' lines decodes into them without a translation table, and ColorToken.allCases is the completeness check.

THE DECISION THIS BEAD IS FOR is what stays true when values come from outside the binary.

  - THE MEASUREMENTS. --verify-theme gates what is compiled in. A token set loaded at
    runtime has not been through it. Either the app measures on load and refuses (or warns,
    or falls back), or the fenced measurements stop being fenced. This is the whole
    question and it should be answered first: the ramp and the 4.5:1 floor were argued from
    the corpus and from AA, and 'the user asked for it' is a reason to warn rather than a
    reason to stop measuring.
  - THE FORMAT. CSS custom properties are what the values are already authored as, and
    palette.py already parses that subset. Re-using it means one syntax across the mockup
    and the app. TOML would match the rest of this project's config instead. Both are
    defensible; picking one is the bead.
  - WHERE THE FILE LIVES, given that this app has no bundle by design. ~/.config/chat-search
    is where cs already looks.

NOT IN SCOPE: hot reload. Watching the file is a nice second step and a different set of
problems (SwiftUI invalidation, partial writes). Load at launch first.
acceptance_criteria: A token set on disk changes the app's look with no rebuild. What happens when it misses a fenced measurement is decided, implemented, and written down rather than discovered. A missing or malformed file leaves the app drawing the shipped direction rather than failing to start, and says why.
notes:
me9.8.12 is answered: docs/DECISIONS.md ADR 25, plus apps/macos/README.md under 'Adding a theme'. The design section above says the measurements question 'is the whole question and it should be answered first'. It is answered, and the answer is not the strict one.

WHAT IT SETTLES FOR THIS BEAD. A token set loaded off disk is a USER THEME, and four rules follow so that none of them has to be decided here:

1. It is always measured, by ThemeCheck and not by a second copy of these rules. ThemeCheck.measure(theme, as: .userTheme) returns a Report; report.failures are whole sentences, each naming the theme, the side and what it missed, written to be printed on stderr with no table around them.
2. It is DRAWN whatever the readings say. The fence is a promise about what the project ships, not a restraint on what somebody may look at — and refusing would break the loop this bead exists to shorten, because a refusal means the edit silently does nothing and dialling a palette in passes through dozens of failing intermediate states.
3. It is drawn as authored, entire. Never merged with a direction to patch the failing tokens: half a palette from each is a palette nobody designed and nobody can debug.
4. Unreadable is not unfenced. A file that is malformed or missing a token is not a theme — fall back to the shipped direction and say why. Note that Palette's precondition treats an incomplete set as a programmer error, which is right for a generated file and fatal for a typed one: validate before constructing one, or a user's typo crashes the app.

The misses are said out loud — failures on stderr at launch, and the class beside the name wherever the app names a theme — with no modal and no banner, because the only person who can be nagged here is the one who wrote the file. --verify-theme's exit status reports the readings and never the policy, so the same flag can check a candidate file before it is loaded.

WHAT IS ALREADY BUILT. ThemeClass, ThemeCheck.measure returning a Report, and a class argument with no default on every entry point.

branch: worktree-me9-8-12-theme-fence

title: AppKit warns of a reentrant NSTableView operation on every typing run
description:
`Application performed a reentrant operation in its NSTableView delegate. This warning will become an assert in the future.` — logged 5-15 times per scripted typing run by both the macOS app (apps/macos) and `cs-spike typing`, so it predates the promotion in chat-search-me9.8.1 and is not caused by it.

Cause is almost certainly replacing a SwiftUI `List`'s whole collection while NSTableView is mid-update: one `cs search --json` per keystroke with no debounce means the rows are reassigned every ~100 ms, sometimes inside the table's own update pass.

Harmless today and self-declared not to stay that way. Nothing visible goes wrong — main-thread lag stays at p50 0.6 ms with 0-1 missed vsyncs — but the message says it becomes an assert, and an assert in the row list is a crash in the only surface.

Worth trying: assigning results on the next runloop turn rather than inside the task's completion, or diffing into the existing array rather than replacing it. Both are cheap to test with `chat-search --measure`, which is what makes the warning reproducible without a person typing.

title: cs show --json does not echo the conv_id it was asked for
description:
Landed with chat-search-o1i.8 and flagged there rather than settled. `cs show <id> --json` and `cs explain` return `conv_id` as the conversation that *opened* the sitting, not the id in the request. Ask about the 15th member of a sitting, get the first member's id back.

The reasoning is sound and documented in both places: a sitting has no id (ADR 16), so the reply names the row that stands for it. But it means a reply does not always echo its request, and a client that asserts `response.conv_id == request.id` — a reasonable thing to write — breaks on Google Takeout rows and on nothing else. That is the same shape as chat-search-me9.27, where a nullable `title` passed every hand test and threw at `results[54]`: a contract wart that only fires on the part of the corpus nobody browses by hand.

Not urgent: no client draws sittings yet (chat-search-o1i.9), so nothing is broken today. It is cheap now and annoying once a second client decodes it.
design:
Two spellings, and the second is additive:

A. Echo the requested id and name the opener separately — `conv_id` is what was asked for, plus `opener` (or `sitting.conv_id`, since `sitting.members[0]` already carries it). A request/response pair that always agrees.

B. Leave it and document it in docs/JSON-CONTRACT.md, which currently states neither.

A costs one field and removes a class of client bug; B costs a paragraph. Whichever wins, the contract has to say which, because right now a client author learns it by diffing two ids.
acceptance_criteria: Either cs show --json echoes the id it was given, or docs/JSON-CONTRACT.md states plainly that it does not and which field names the opener. A test pins whichever is chosen.

title: A standing capture report has no way to be told 'I do not have one'
description:
Two of the three standing reports in `cs archive` describe a condition the machine can make false: adopt the candidate and drift goes quiet, land an export and staleness does. The third cannot. `unreachable` (chat-search-a7k.22) names ChatGPT, claude.ai and Gemini on the web, and somebody with no ChatGPT account sees that line once a day forever with nothing they can do about it but write a [[sources]] entry pointing at an export that will never exist.

Deliberately shipped that way rather than fixed in a7k.22, for two reasons. Drift has exactly the same hole — an unconfigured ~/.copilot/session-state nags daily until you adopt it or delete the directory — so a dismissal built for one report and not the other would be the second copy of a rule this project keeps merging back together. And the failure mode of dismissal is worse than the failure mode of nagging: a surface dismissed once is a surface nothing mentions again, which is the shape of the original bug.

So the question is a design one, not an implementation one: is there a dismissal that a person can act on without being able to hide 69% of their corpus from themselves by mistake? Options include a config key naming surfaces you have no account on, a `cs archive --dismiss <id>` writing that key, or accepting the nag and deciding it costs less than the alternative.
acceptance_criteria: Either a dismissal exists and works the same way for drift's unconfigured candidates and for unreachable surfaces, or the decision not to have one is written down where the next person to be annoyed by the line will find it.

title: The contract's corpus counts predate google-takeout, and one of them reads as a rule
description:
docs/JSON-CONTRACT.md's counts are 'from the reference corpus on this machine, 3,059 conversations as of 2026-08-04'. Measured against the live index on 2026-08-05 by the Swift spike's new 'cs-spike contract' census, which decodes every conversation the empty query returns:

  conversations   3,059 -> 4,377
  title null         11 -> 12   (claude-code 7, codex 4, gemini-cli 1)
  ended_at null       2 ->  4
  cwd null        2,023 -> 3,303 (chatgpt-export 2,011, google-takeout 1,280, gemini-cli 12)
  destinations []    12 -> 1,292 (google-takeout 1,280, gemini-cli 12)
  kind_runs []        2 ->  2

The difference is the google-takeout source, 1,280 conversations that have neither a cwd nor any way to be reopened.

Most of these are harmless — the file dates its counts, and rarity is stated as a hazard rather than a reassurance. One is not. Under 'Empty is not null', 'destinations: []' reads 'All 12 gemini-cli conversations, today. Not "we failed to build one": there is no gemini --resume.' A reader takes that as the rule that produces the empty array, and it is now wrong about 99% of the rows that have one: google-takeout is an export of a web product, which is a second and different reason to have no destination.
design:
The counts are worth refreshing but the sentence is the actual defect: it explains the empty array by way of one source's missing --resume flag, and a client should be told the general rule instead (this source has no known way to reopen a conversation — an export has none by construction). Refreshing every count in the file is a bigger job and is what makes this P3; correcting that one paragraph is not.

'cs-spike contract' prints the census, so re-measuring is one command.
acceptance_criteria: The 'Empty is not null' entry for destinations states the rule rather than gemini-cli's particular reason, and the counts in the file are either refreshed or carry the date they were taken.

title: cs index --json reports failure as prose on stderr, not a code on stdout
description:
chat-search-me9.28 gave 'cs search --json' an error body — {"error": {"code", "message"}} on stdout beside a nonzero exit — so a client stopped having to grep English to tell 'no_index' from 'index_stale' from 'building'. 'cs index --json' did not get the same treatment. A failed rebuild returns an anyhow error from main(), which prints 'Error: swapping the new index into place' and its causal chain to stderr and exits 1, with nothing on stdout.

A client that automates rebuilds therefore has the exact problem chat-search-me9.22 described for queries: the exit code says something went wrong and only prose says what. The cases are already named and distinguishable in Rust — BuildError::AlreadyBuilding (another cs index is running, wait), BuildError::NotCurrent (the swap landed but the index does not read back as current, rebuild), BuildError::Io, BuildError::Sqlite — and none of those names reach a decoder.

Noticed while adding the read-back guard in chat-search-6eb.35, which introduced NotCurrent.
acceptance_criteria: 'cs index --json' emits {"error": {"code", "message"}} on stdout beside its nonzero exit, with codes drawn from the BuildError cases a client would act on differently. docs/JSON-CONTRACT.md gains the table, and a test drives it through the binary.

title: cs panics with a broken-pipe error when its stdout closes early
description:
Observed twice while verifying chat-search-o1i.5: `cs show <id> --db … | head -1` prints its line and then panics.

  thread 'main' panicked at library/std/src/io/stdio.rs:1166:9:
  failed printing to stdout: Broken pipe (os error 32)

Rust ignores SIGPIPE by default and turns the resulting EPIPE from a `println!` into a panic, so any command of this project piped into `head`, `less` quit early, or a client that stops reading, exits 101 with a backtrace note on stderr rather than exiting quietly.

It matters more here than in most CLIs because ADR 14 makes the process boundary the client seam: a client that spawns `cs search --json` and stops reading — cancelled keystroke, closed window — gets a panic where it should get a clean exit, and a nonzero exit is part of this interface (ADR 14), so the noise is indistinguishable from a real failure.
design:
Two spellings. Restore the default SIGPIPE disposition at the top of main (`unsafe { libc::signal(SIGPIPE, SIG_DFL) }`), which needs a libc dependency the workspace does not have; or handle the io::ErrorKind::BrokenPipe from the write and exit 0 without printing, which needs the printing to go through something that returns a Result rather than through println!.

The second is more code but keeps the exit code deliberate, which matters given the contract. Worth checking what the TUI's exit path does with the same condition.
acceptance_criteria: `cs search --json … | head -1` and `cs show … | head -1` exit without a panic message, and the exit code they produce is documented alongside the other exits the client seam relies on.

title: A tool_call whose body is not JSON collapses to a bare name, and 13.3% of the corpus is that shape
description:
Measured over all 66,417 tool_call messages while folding export.py's call_detail into cs_core::blocks::tool_summary (chat-search-me9.20): 80.1% carry a JSON object, 6.6% an apply_patch body, and 13.3% - 8,861 calls - something that is neither. Those 8,861 return the bare tool name, so the collapsed row says 'exec' and nothing else.

The sample is dominated by Codex 'exec' calls whose body is JavaScript source rather than arguments: 'const r = await tools.exec_command({cmd:"sed -n 1,260p ..."})'. There is a readable command in there, and the prototype's deleted implementation used to show it by squashing the raw body onto one line.

That was declined deliberately when the two implementations were merged, because an_unparseable_body_still_yields_the_tool_name is an existing tested decision - 'the name alone is always better than a raw JSON fragment wrapped into the pane'. The question this bead asks is whether that decision was made against this shape or against a different one. A JS call expression is not a JSON fragment, and its first ~80 characters are as identifying as any argument key.
design:
Options, roughly in order of appetite: (a) leave it, and accept that 13.3% of tool rows are a bare name; (b) show the first non-empty line of the body, truncated, when it parses as neither JSON nor a patch - closest to what the prototype did; (c) recognise the one shape that dominates, 'tools.<name>({...})', and pull the inner argument object out of it, which is a parser for one harness's convention and will rot when that convention changes.

Whichever is chosen, it is a change to cs_core::blocks::tool_summary and so changes what the TUI draws and what cs show --json emits for those rows.
acceptance_criteria: A decision is recorded. If it is (b) or (c), tool_summary implements it, the test that currently pins the bare-name fallback is updated to say which shapes it still covers, and the change is measured against the real index the same way - what fraction of the 66,417 calls gain a readable argument line, and whether any that had one lost it.
notes: Surfaced by chat-search-me9.20, which merged the prototype's second implementation back into the first. The other three things that copy knew - the cmd key, apply_patch targets, and the prose argument keys - were folded in there; this is the only one left out.

title: Nothing draws a sitting, so a folded row reads as a conversation
description:
chat-search-o1i.5 ends at the search layer: Group::sitting names the records a row stands for and the gap that produced them, and no client reads it. So a row that is eleven Gemini records looks exactly like a conversation that had eleven turns, and the reader is not told that the grouping is a heuristic this project applied rather than something Google recorded.

That matters more here than it would elsewhere, because the fold can be wrong. Two unrelated questions asked twenty minutes apart are one sitting under the 30-minute rule, and the row will title itself with the first of them.
design:
Group::sitting is Option<Sitting> { members: Vec<String>, gap_ms: i64 }, serialised on every row of cs search --json. A client that wants to say '11 records' or 'one sitting, 30-minute gap' has what it needs and does not have to re-derive anything.

Open: what a terminal row spends width on. TUI-DESIGN's row model is already tight, and 'this is a reconstruction' is a modifier on the title rather than a column of its own. The obvious cheap answer is that the agent badge says so — google-takeout rows are already distinguishable by source — but that conflates 'came from Takeout' with 'is several records', and 249 of the 471 Takeout rows are single conversations.
acceptance_criteria: A reader can tell a folded row from a single conversation without opening it, and can tell what the fold was based on. Decided against TUI-DESIGN's row model rather than by adding a column to it.

title: Prove the seam: swap a whole theme, and hold the measured findings
description: chat-search-4ar.12 closed on the incumbent and chat-search-me9.8.8 gives the app a token layer, so there is no longer a direction sitting around waiting to be applied. What is left is the CLAIM the seam makes - that changing a theme is a token file and not a sweep - and a claim that is never exercised is one that turns out to be false the first time somebody needs it to be true.
design:
THE TEST IS A REAL SWAP, NOT AN ASSERTION. paper, blueprint and ink already exist as solved token sets in poc/ui/directions.css, in both themes, each holding every fenced measurement. Port one of them and switch the app to it. If that costs more than a token file, the seam did not work - and this bead has then found exactly the thing it exists to find, which is a far better outcome than discovering it under a real redesign.

TWO FINDINGS MUST SURVIVE THE PORT, both bought with measurement and both easy to lose when CSS becomes SwiftUI.

1. At the ~2px the ribbon bands are drawn, LUMINANCE does the work and hue does not. The four kinds were once separated by hue alone and two of them sat 1.12:1 apart - the same colour to the eye. palette.py solves each direction's ramp to 2.2 / 4.0 / 7.2 / 13.0 against its own track and reproduces the hand-solved incumbent to within 1/255. The colours are not sacred; the ramp is.

2. The quiet tier carries dates, counts, group counts and section labels - real information, not decoration - and sits at 4.6:1 in both themes, measured against the HARDER of the two grounds it lands on rather than only against --bg. It started at 3.64 dark and 2.90 light at 9-11px, and the first fix was still at 4.23:1 on --panel where most of that text actually lives.

Rows per screen must not drop; density is what makes the archive scannable.

STAYS LAST AND STAYS P3. Nothing is blocked behind this. The app is themeable the moment me9.8.8 lands - this only proves it, and a seam proved against one view proves very little, so it wants the views to exist first.
acceptance_criteria: A second complete direction, ported from poc/ui/directions.css and switchable at runtime or by one edit. The diff that achieves the switch touches token values and no views - if it touches a view, the seam failed and that is the finding. The kind ramp holds its measured ratios (2.2 / 4.0 / 7.2 / 13.0 against map-bg) in both directions and both themes. The quiet tier clears 4.5:1 on the harder of the two grounds. Rows per screen unchanged or better.

title: Grouping and the Library view
description: poc/ui collapsed several fake views into one grouping dimension applied within a single list, plus Library as the second view (4ar.10). That structure was argued from the corpus and is what this inherits.
design:
Projects are the natural axis for the agentic corpus and topics for the conversational one - they are not competing taxonomies over one corpus. Measured: 67 projects hold 34% of conversations but 92% of all messages; cwd covers only 34% of the corpus (codex and claude-code 100%, chatgpt and gemini-cli 0%), and projects cannot be recovered for the other 66% because repo names do not appear in chat prose while subject names do. 37% match no topic at all.

So a grouping that silently drops two thirds of the corpus is the failure mode to design against: an ungrouped bucket is information, not an edge case.
acceptance_criteria: Grouping is one dimension over one list, not separate views. Conversations with no group are visible and labelled rather than dropped. Library exists as the second view.
notes:
branch: worktree-me9-8-4-grouping (worktree .claude/worktrees/me9-8-4-grouping)
Gate green on 2026-08-05: cargo test --workspace 686 passed, cargo build --workspace --all-targets 0 warnings, swift build -c release 0 warnings, --verify-theme holds. Verified against the live index (3,617 conversations) with --shot: 12 groups over 58 rows by project with 2 in the residue, 10 by run, 2 by source; and a 20-row 'travel' answer where 18 of 20 land in the residue, which is the case the bead exists for.
pr: https://github.com/tylercrosse/chat-search/pull/28 (draft)
Post-close review fix (be18c8f, pushed to the same draft PR): Display.day read the current year through Calendar.current, which honours the region's calendar setting — measured at year 8 under Japanese, 2569 Buddhist, 5786 Hebrew — so every day label would have carried a year suffix on a non-Gregorian Mac. Calendar is now named. The run axis also stopped describing itself as 'covering 100%', which the key line can print beside the residue group counting the rows it did not cover.
close_reason: Grouping is a control on the one list — none/project/run/source, with topic drawn dashed because a seeded taxonomy is a poc/ui export and not on the wire — and every axis that can fail to place a row carries a labelled residue group rather than dropping it (project 'no working directory', run 'no last message'). Library is the second view: nav, its own footer line, and four shelves that are empty and say which bead each waits on, chiefly library.db (chat-search-6eb.14). Verified against the live 3,617-conversation index with --shot: 12 groups over 58 rows by project with 2 in the residue, and a 20-row answer where 18 land in it. Gate green — 686 tests, warning-free --all-targets, warning-free swift build, --verify-theme holds. Folding and the keyboard model that needs are filed as chat-search-me9.8.15. branch: worktree-me9-8-4-grouping

title: AI Mode records hold whole multi-turn sessions in one assistant blob
description:
Found while stripping the leading prompt echo (chat-search-o1i.6). An AI Mode activity record is not always one turn: 49 of the 129 records with a response contain two or more "Your prompt: … Search's response: …" pairs inside a single safeHtmlItem chunk, up to 6 in one record. So a follow-up question and its answer are indexed today as ordinary prose inside the first answer's assistant message.

Consequences: the conversation reports 2 messages when it held 12; the follow-up prompts are assistant text rather than user text, so agent:/role reasoning about them is wrong; and cs show renders one wall instead of a dialogue.

This is not the same problem as chat-search-o1i.5, which regroups separate records into threads by time gap. Here the turns are already inside one record and one native_id, so no heuristic and no id change is needed to split them - the markers are explicit.
design:
Split on the marker lines in google_takeout::activity_record rather than emitting one assistant message. answer_only() already locates the first boundary; the same scan generalises to N. Turn 0's prompt still comes from the title (that is what the o1i.6 strip removes); turns 1..N take their prompt from the echo, which is the only place it exists.

Message native_ids must stay stable, so number them from the turn index rather than from anything positional that a re-export could shift. Every turn shares the record's single timestamp, as today.
acceptance_criteria: A record with follow-up turns imports as alternating user/assistant messages; the 80 single-turn records are unchanged; cargo test --workspace green

title: The TUI holds one connection for the session, so a rebuild never reaches it
description:
Found while implementing chat-search-me9.28. `cs tui` opens the index once in `cs_core::open_for_read` and hands the connection to `state::App`, which keeps it for the life of the session. Every keystroke re-queries that one connection.

Now that a rebuild is swapped in by rename rather than written in place, a `cs index` that finishes underneath a running TUI leaves the TUI reading the previous inode — complete and internally consistent, but permanently behind. Before the swap the same code read a file that had been deleted and recreated under it, so this is not a regression; it is the same staleness with a cleaner shape, and now it is nameable.

`cs search` is unaffected: it spawns per query and so picks up the new index on the next keystroke, which is exactly the property ADR 14 chose subprocess-per-query for. The TUI is the one Rust surface that links cs-core and holds state, so it is the one place that argument does not cover.
design:
The state is already computable: `cs_core::IndexState::of(&db)` is a couple of `stat` calls, and `Reader` already carries the state it opened with. Options, cheapest first:

A. Re-check `IndexState` per query (or per N ms) and reopen the connection when the file underneath has been replaced. Needs an identity to compare — inode, or the file's mtime — since 'ready' before and after a swap looks identical.
B. Show it and let the reader decide: a status-line note that a rebuild finished and the results are from the previous index, with a key to reload.
C. Do nothing and document that a TUI session spans one index.

A alone is a silent reload under someone's cursor, which changes result sets mid-scroll; B alone leaves the staleness in place. B plus A on the next keystroke after the user asks is probably the honest pairing.
acceptance_criteria: A rebuild that completes underneath a running TUI is either picked up or visibly reported, rather than silently ignored for the rest of the session.
notes:
There are two caches behind one connection, not one — found while rebasing chat-search-o1i.5 onto the swap.

cs_core::sittings builds its temp tables once per connection and fingerprints them so 'a reindex under a held connection rebuilds it'. After chat-search-me9.28 a held connection cannot observe a reindex at all: the swap renames a new file over the old one, so the connection goes on reading the stranded inode and the fingerprint it compares never changes. The rebuild it was written to trigger cannot fire.

So whatever reopens the connection for this bead settles both. A fix that only reloads search results would leave the sitting grouping computed against the previous index — which is worse than the staleness it replaced, because the two halves would then disagree with each other rather than merely being behind together.

title: AGENTS.md tells you how to benchmark but not how to keep the benchmark out of the query log
description:
AGENTS.md's Build & Test section is where an agent reads how to exercise this
tool, and it says the overridable config and --db are "how to exercise anything
without touching real data". Both are true and neither covers the query log:
--db /tmp/scratch.db still writes searches into ~/.chat-archive/queries.jsonl,
because the log path comes from the config rather than the db flag.

That is how 2,641 of the log's 2,720 events came to be benchmark traffic
(chat-search-6eb.44). The lever now exists — CS_LOG_QUERIES=0 wraps a whole
measurement session including subprocesses — and evals/README.md says to use
it, but nobody timing a search reads evals/README.md first.

Two lines in the Build & Test section: set CS_LOG_QUERIES=0 when timing
anything, and `cs needs --driven FROM..UNTIL --why "..."` if you forget.

Filed rather than done because AGENTS.md is untracked here — it is matched by
~/.gitignore_global, so it is not in the worktree a background worker gets and
an edit to it cannot be committed. Someone with the working checkout has to make
it.
acceptance_criteria: AGENTS.md's Build & Test section names CS_LOG_QUERIES=0 as part of how to measure without touching real data, and names the driven-span command as the way back from having forgotten it.

title: AI Mode responses repeat the prompt, double-indexing every query term
description:
Every AI Mode response opens with 'Your prompt: <the prompt> Search's response: <answer>' - 129 of 129 records with a response, measured. Gemini Apps does not do this: 0 of 1,070.

So for 138 conversations the query terms appear in both the user message and the assistant message, and fts5 counts them twice. BM25 sees a document where every term the user typed is twice as frequent as it should be, which inflates those conversations against the rest of the corpus for exactly the terms most likely to be searched.
design:
Strip the preamble in google_takeout.rs when the response opens with it - after to_text, drop a leading 'Your prompt:' line, the prompt line, and a 'Search's response:' line. Match on the structure rather than on the prompt text, since the prompt in the response is Google's re-rendering and may not be byte-identical to the title.

Keep it conditional on the marker being present: Gemini Apps never has it, and a blind strip would eat the first two lines of 1,070 good responses.
acceptance_criteria: AI Mode assistant text starts at the answer; Gemini Apps responses unchanged
notes: branch: worktree-o1i-6-ai-mode-preamble
close_reason: AI Mode's echo of the prompt is stripped in google_takeout.rs, matched on structure (first line 'Your prompt:', scan forward to 'Search's response:') so a multi-paragraph prompt goes whole and Gemini Apps never fires. Indexed the same archive either side of the change: 127 ai-mode assistant messages lost their echo, 10,882 chars; the other 193,719 messages are byte-identical. Two messages vanish rather than shrink - the two records whose whole response was the echo and no answer; both conversations survive on their prompt. Ranking effect measured and small: over six queries, four unmoved and two down one and three places. Only the leading echo goes; that 49 records are really multi-turn sessions in one blob is filed as o1i.7. branch: worktree-o1i-6-ai-mode-preamble

title: Document and pin cs show --json in docs/JSON-CONTRACT.md
description:
docs/JSON-CONTRACT.md (chat-search-me9.27) covers cs search --json field by field and stops there. cs show --json is the second client contract ADR 12 published and ADR 14 made load-bearing, and it has no written statement of its shape at all.

It is the easier of the two: every field on Transcript, WireBlock and Block is non-optional, so the answer is 'nothing here is ever null' — but that is exactly the sentence a client author currently has to derive by reading Rust, which is the thing chat-search-me9.27 was filed to stop. Writing 'never null' down is worth as much as writing 'nullable' down; a decoder author needs both answers, not just the surprising one.

Worth doing after chat-search-me9.20, which moves tool_summary and recognition_line into cs-core: those change what a client is expected to render from this payload, and documenting the shape before that lands means documenting it twice.
design:
Same file, a second top-level section, same three-part treatment: field table with a null column, what the empty arrays mean, and a pin.

The pin should extend crates/cs/tests/json_contract.rs rather than start a second test file — the assertion it makes ('these are the exact keys, these are the nullable ones') is identical, and one test that fails on either contract is one place to look.
acceptance_criteria: Every field of cs show --json is in docs/JSON-CONTRACT.md with its nullability stated, and crates/cs/tests/json_contract.rs asserts the key set of Transcript and of a WireBlock.

title: cs search --json: grouped is absent under --flat rather than false
description:
The default (grouped) envelope carries "grouped": true; --flat omits the key entirely instead of emitting false. A client that models one envelope struct for both shapes — which is the natural thing to do, since query/ms/count/results/unapplied_filters are otherwise identical — has to make the field optional and then cannot tell 'flat' from 'a future version that stopped saying'.

Found while writing docs/JSON-CONTRACT.md for chat-search-me9.27. Documented there under 'Known warts' rather than fixed, because emitting a key that was previously absent is a change to a published contract (ADR 12) even though it is an additive one, and the same call has to be made about whether both shapes should carry the same envelope at all.
design:
Emitting "grouped": false under --flat is additive by ADR 12's rule: no existing key changes meaning, and a decoder that ignores unknown keys (Swift Codable, serde with default flags, JSON.parse) is unaffected. The only client that could break is one asserting on the exact key set — which is now exactly crates/cs/tests/json_contract.rs, and updating it is the point of having it.

The alternative is to leave it and let the doc carry the fact. That is cheaper and it is what shipped, but it spends a client-author confusion every time rather than a one-line change once.
acceptance_criteria: Either the key is emitted in both shapes and docs/JSON-CONTRACT.md plus crates/cs/tests/json_contract.rs are updated together, or the decision to leave it is recorded in the doc as a decision rather than as a wart.

title: Regroup MyActivity records into threads at read time
description:
MyActivity.json carries no conversation, thread, or session key at any nesting level - verified across all 1,318 records of the reference export. The importer therefore emits one two-message conversation per record, which is correct but means a 20-turn Gemini chat appears as 20 separate results.

Regrouping is genuinely useful and should happen - just not in the importer.
design:
MUST NOT be done by giving the importer a clustering rule, because a conversation id is permanent (ADR 16) and an id derived from a heuristic changes the day the heuristic does: every Gemini conversation would get a new id the first time someone tuned a gap threshold, and the archive would gain a duplicate copy of the whole corpus.

Read time is where being wrong is free. The corpus memory already notes 1,088 gaps >4h as a measured structural signal, so the same gap analysis applies here. A cheap first cut: adjacent records under the same surface within N minutes are one thread, surfaced as a grouping in the TUI rather than as a stored id.
acceptance_criteria:
A query matching several turns of one Gemini conversation returns ONE grouped result rather than N separate rows: adjacent google-takeout records sharing a surface and separated by less than the gap threshold are reported as a single group by the search layer.

Default gap 30 minutes. Measured over the 1,173 Gemini Apps records: 336 threads at 3.5 turns each, and the curve is flat from 15 to 60 minutes, so the threshold is not delicate.

The grouping is computed at READ time. It must never be stored as, or folded into, a conversation id - see the design note; that is the whole reason this is a separate bead from the importer.

TUI presentation is OUT OF SCOPE. This bead ends at the search layer reporting the grouping; how a client draws it is a separate decision.
notes:
MEASURED 2026-08-04 against the 1,173 Gemini Apps records. Collapse by gap threshold:

  >2 min  -> 795 threads (1.5 turns each)
  >5 min  -> 550 threads (2.1)
  >15 min -> 385 threads (3.0)
  >30 min -> 336 threads (3.5)
  >60 min -> 297 threads (3.9)

So a 30-minute gap turns 1,173 fragments into ~336 threads, a 3.5x collapse. That is the size of the prize: today a search for a term used throughout one long conversation returns three or four separate rows for it. The curve is flat past 30 min, so the threshold is not delicate - anything in 15-60 min lands in the same neighbourhood, which is a good sign for a heuristic that must not be tuned often.

Still must not become part of an id (see the issue design).
branch: worktree-o1i-5-sittings (worktree .claude/worktrees/o1i-5-sittings, 4 commits off origin/main 63a8b31)
close_reason: Ships as cs_core::sittings, and the word is 'sitting' not 'thread' — the glossary already spends 'thread' on a linear stream INSIDE a conversation, and this runs the other way. Records of one (source, surface) less than 30 minutes apart are one sitting, keyed on the conversation that opened it; nothing is coined and nothing is stored, so ADR 16 is untouched. The grouping key is SQL — rank() groups by ifnull(sit.sitting_id, m.conv_id) and numbers positions by m.seq + msg_offset — so score, match_count and match_seqs are computed once over the whole sitting by code that never learns sittings exist. recent, count_matching and count_filtered join the same temp tables, so the browse list and the header agree with the ranked list. Measured on the live index: 1,271 activity records fold to 462 rows; agent:google-takeout returns 471 rows covering all 1,280 conversations with no duplicates; 'game theory' went from 25 Gemini conversations to 16 rows. Costs 0.04 ms per search warm (8-24 ms to build, once per connection, fingerprinted so a reindex under a held connection rebuilds it) and 5-8% on the broadest prefixes, against 17% fewer rows for 'the'. Not done, and filed: cs show and cs explain render the opening record of a sitting while the row claims the whole of it (chat-search-o1i.8, P2), and nothing draws Group::sitting so a reconstruction reads as a conversation (chat-search-o1i.9, P3). Both are in ARCHITECTURE's 'built in part' list with a falsifying grep. branch: worktree-o1i-5-sittings

title: Failure is prose on stderr, so a client classifies index health by substring-matching English
description:
Found by chat-search-me9.22 (poc/swift RESULTS.md §4). ADR 14 says a nonzero exit is part of the interface, but only the exit code is — the reason arrives as one English sentence on stderr, with no code and no JSON. The Swift client's IndexHealth.classify therefore greps another program's prose, which is as fragile as it looks and breaks the first time the wording is improved.

It is also not sufficient. Three genuinely different conditions produce the identical message:

  --db points at a path that does not exist   → 'index records no importer version…'
  --db points at a zero-byte file             → 'index records no importer version…'
  --db points at 4 KB of the letter A         → 'index records no importer version…'

The third is a corrupt file being reported as a schema-age problem, and the prose in all three tells a first-run user their brand-new index 'predates this schema'.

Separately, and cheaply fixable: --json is pretty-printed. Measured at 97,606 bytes where the compact form is 62,547 — 1.56x — on a path that moves 111 KB per keystroke at limit 60. Pretty-printing is for a human reading a pipe; --json's audience is a parser.
design:
An error body on stdout as JSON when --json is passed, carrying a stable machine-readable code alongside the human sentence: {"error": {"code": "no_index", "message": "…"}}. The exit code stays nonzero, so nothing that currently checks it breaks. The code is the contract; the message stays free to be reworded.

Codes worth distinguishing, from what the spike actually hit: no_index, index_corrupt, index_rebuilding (see chat-search-me9.28), config_missing.

The pretty-printing is independent and smaller: emit compact when --json, or keep {:#} behind a --pretty flag for the human case.
acceptance_criteria: A client branches on a code rather than on prose, a corrupt index is not reported as an old one, and --json emits compact bytes.
notes:
chat-search-me9.28 landed part of this, and the rest is unchanged.

Landed: `cs_core::build::Unreadable` carries a stable `code()`, and every `--json` command prints {"error": {"code", "message"}} on stdout beside the nonzero exit. Codes so far: no_index, building, index_stale, index_unreadable. A successful `cs search --json` carries `index_state` (ready | rebuilding), and `cs status --json` carries index.state. Also fixed at the source: an empty archive used to build an index with no importer_version row, which read as 'predates this schema' — the version is now stamped when the build starts, so a first run over an empty archive reports ready.

Still open, and still this bead's:
- index_corrupt. A file that is not a database at all still lands in index_stale, because `built_by` swallows the sqlite error and returns None. The split wants a real read of the header (or letting the rusqlite error through) rather than another string.
- config_missing.
- Compact --json. Untouched; still {:#}.
- `cs show --json` has no index_state. Its body is a Transcript serialized whole, so adding one means wrapping a published shape — a decision this bead is the right size for. It does get the error body.
- poc/swift's IndexHealth.classify still greps prose. There are codes to branch on now; whether the spike is worth updating is chat-search-me9.30's call.

title: Prototype: DIR_CHARS is sized to one direction's font and nothing recomputes it
description:
app.js's DIR_CHARS is 17, sized by measurement to the row's cwd grid track at the incumbent's 10px mono - the comment records that at 20 the string overflowed and CSS tail-elided it to '/Users/…/chat-sear', discarding the leaf that elidePath() exists to protect.

A visual direction may set --fs-meta: blueprint uses 9.5px. The budget is now wrong in the safe direction there (the string is shorter than the cell), but a direction that raises --fs-meta reintroduces exactly the bug the constant was measured to prevent.
design: Either derive the budget from the rendered cell width rather than a constant, or assert it: measure the .dir cell once after layout and warn when the elided string overflows it. The second is cheaper and catches the class rather than one instance.
acceptance_criteria: A direction that changes --fs-meta cannot silently tail-elide the path's leaf.

title: Prototype: geometry tokens reach the list, colour tokens reach everything
description:
A visual direction restyles the whole prototype through the colour tokens, but only the list through the geometry ones: styles.css's surface layer covers the five type sizes and six chrome radii globally, and the row's rhythm and the ribbon's geometry, while every other pane still hardcodes its own spacing.

Enough to judge the row and the ribbon at real size, which is what chat-search-4ar.11 was asked for. Not enough to judge a direction whole - index.html?dir=blueprint gives a densely-set list beside a drawer with the incumbent's rhythm.
design: The remaining literals are padding and margin in the rail, the search bar, the drawer, the timeline and the collections cards. Worth doing only if a direction is actually being adopted (chat-search-4ar.12); tokenising spacing nobody is going to vary is churn.
acceptance_criteria: index.html?dir=<name> is coherent across every pane, not only the list.

title: Smoke test: Codex worker pipeline end to end
description: Throwaway bead used to prove the --engine=codex dispatch path works end to end. The worker should: read the project instructions, create docs/CODEX-SMOKE.md containing exactly one line naming the project's gate command, run that gate, commit, and close this bead. The file and branch are deleted after verification — this bead exists only to exercise the pipeline.
acceptance_criteria: docs/CODEX-SMOKE.md exists on the worker's branch and contains the project's gate command; the gate was run and passed; the work is committed; the bead is closed with a reason naming the branch.
notes:
codex worker: branch worktree-bead-n8b-smoke-test-codex-worker, thread 019fcdb5-2e77-7943-ae86-9474dddfe074, log /Users/tylercrosse/dev/projects/chat-search/.claude/bd-codex/bead-n8b-smoke-test-codex-worker.jsonl
branch: worktree-bead-n8b-smoke-test-codex-worker
verified, then cleaned up: branch and docs/CODEX-SMOKE.md deleted, worker logs removed
close_reason: Added the exact one-line gate marker, ran the full documented gate successfully, and committed it on branch worktree-bead-n8b-smoke-test-codex-worker.

title: Hit rows say what matched, not just the fragment
description: A TUI hit row renders the snippet with [subagent] and [edited away] tags but nothing about which message kind or which tool it came from (cs-tui/src/render.rs::hit_row). Measured against the live index 2026-08-03, 66-85% of message-level hits land in tool traffic depending on the query, and 20-73% of matching conversations match ONLY there. So the common hit row is a fragment of a tool argument or a tool result presented as if it were something the user or the assistant said, which reads as log spew rather than as evidence. poc/ui frames the same line with its provenance -- an example: a wrench glyph, Bash(cargo test), then the fragment -- which is what stops the misreading. TUI-DESIGN.md section 3 (revised 2026-08-04) records the measurement and the argument.
design: The kind and the tool name are already on the ranked hit before grouping; this is a rendering change plus whatever cs_core::search::Hit needs to carry to make it one. Prefer reusing the collapsed tool_call form (name plus primary argument) rather than inventing a second spelling -- that form is itself queued to move into cs-core as me9.20, so this should land after it or be written to adopt it.
acceptance_criteria: A hit row whose match came from a tool_call or tool_result shows which tool it was, in a form distinguishable at a glance from a prose hit. The layout still fits the narrowest column plan in TUI-DESIGN section 2 without pushing the fragment below a readable width.
notes: Filed 2026-08-04 while resolving chat-search-4ar.8. No product code changed by that bead.

title: Prototype: draw the ribbon from real kind runs instead of export.py
description: The consume half of the kind-runs work, split out from me9.19 on 2026-08-04. poc/ui/app.js ribbon() and poc/ui/export.py currently synthesise the band data; once cs search --json carries kind runs they should read it instead.
design:
Deliberately NOT started with the emit half. The ribbon is the mark DESIGN-BRIEF.md explicitly nominates for reinvention - different shape, more than one row, something else entirely - so 4ar.11 may change what is drawn before this changes where the data comes from. The run-length data itself is medium-agnostic and survives any redesign; only the drawing code is at risk. Wait for 4ar.11 to settle, then wire.

FILES: poc/ui/app.js (ribbon), poc/ui/export.py.
acceptance_criteria: poc/ui draws its ribbon from cs search --json output. export.py no longer synthesises band data.
notes:
kind_runs landed (me9.19): cs search --json carries [[band,count],...] where band is user|agent|reasoning|tool, in blocks::READING_ORDER, over DRAWN messages only. Verified against cs show on 354 real conversations / 108,192 messages, 28 of them multi-thread.

Two things to know before drawing it. (1) The run lengths sum to the DRAWN count, not msg_count — 563 of 937 on a real conversation — so msg_count is the wrong denominator for the track. (2) match_seqs is a different coordinate space entirely and its ticks will land early or in the wrong thread if drawn on this axis; that is chat-search-me9.25, and it is not blocking the bands, only the ticks.

The JSON only carries the shape when asked: cs search --json sets it, the terminal listing and the TUI do not (SearchOptions::shape, and me9.26 for why).
branch: worktree-me9-23-ribbon (worktree: /Users/tylercrosse/dev/projects/.chat-search-worktrees/me9-23-ribbon, branched from origin/main d3564de)
pr: https://github.com/tylercrosse/chat-search/pull/40
close_reason: poc/ui draws its ribbon from cs search --json: export.py carries kind_runs per conversation (one call, 2.3s for the corpus) plus band/drawn per message from cs show --json, and ribbon() walks those runs instead of encoding its own — acts only subdivide a run, never move a boundary. The axis moved with it, from every head-path message to the drawn ones, which is the part that was wrong: tool bands were counting successful tool_results the terminal does not draw, 79.5% -> 66.7% of the axis over a 355-conversation export. Added poc/ui/verify-shape.js (node, exits non-zero) which re-reads the rendered markup and checks every boundary against cs's cumulative run lengths; recorded as NOTES §3.27. Gate green: cargo build --workspace --all-targets 0 warnings, cargo test --workspace 756 pass. Not done: match ticks still come from the prototype's own substring search, because match_seqs is in the other coordinate space (me9.25).

title: Prototype: a visual pass over the mockup, with the information architecture held fixed
description: poc/ui was built outward from measurements of the corpus, so its information design is argued and its visual language is not - it is system defaults and a palette nobody chose. poc/ui/DESIGN-BRIEF.md and the component gallery (poc/ui/gallery.html, 52 specimens in both themes) exist to hand this to a designer. Nothing has been done with them yet.
design:
FENCED to surface treatment: palette, type faces and sizes, spacing and rhythm, radii, borders and rules, and how much contrast separates one thing from another. NOT the pane structure, what is in a row, or the grouping model - those came from corpus measurements and re-litigating them here wastes the measurement.

TWO FINDINGS THAT MUST SURVIVE A RESTYLE, both bought with measurement and both easy to lose to a prettier palette:
1. At the ~2px the ribbon bands are drawn, LUMINANCE does the work and hue does not. The four kinds were originally separated by hue alone and two of them sat 1.12:1 apart - the same colour to the eye. The current ramp is ~1.8x per step with hue as the redundant second channel. The specific colours are not sacred; the ramp is.
2. The quiet text tier carries dates, counts and section labels rather than decoration, and sits at 4.6:1 in both themes. It was 3.64:1 dark and 2.90 light at 9-11px, which is where it started.

Also fenced: rows per screen must not drop, since density is what makes the archive scannable at all.
