Ask for several distinct directions rather than one refinement, and for the row and the ribbon shown at real size in each - those are where a purely visual pass breaks without noticing.
acceptance_criteria: Several named visual directions, each shown at real size on the row and the ribbon, in both themes. The two measured findings above still hold in whichever is chosen. Rows per screen unchanged or better.
notes:
Filed 2026-08-04. Runs in parallel with the Swift spike rather than after it - the visual questions are the one class the mockup is still the cheapest tool for, and they are independent of which toolkit ships.
branch: worktree-poc-ui-directions (three commits, branched from poc-ui-prototype @ c688a6b). The baseline commit c688a6b — the component gallery and DESIGN-BRIEF.md, which this bead's description names as its input — was committed on poc-ui-prototype itself, because it was sitting uncommitted in the shared checkout and this pass edits the same files. The Rust changes beside it belong to another bead and were left alone.

Verified headless: cargo test --workspace 487 passed / 0 failed, cargo build --workspace --all-targets 0 warnings. poc/ is outside the cargo workspace, so the substance was checked with Chrome headless against directions.html, gallery.html and index.html?dir=<name> over the real 354-conversation sample, plus python3 poc/ui/palette.py --verify.
close_reason:
Four named visual directions — terminal (the incumbent, declaring nothing so the control stays one), paper, blueprint, ink — shown on the row and the ribbon at real size in both themes by poc/ui/directions.html, which renders the app's own components and measures itself. Both fenced findings hold in all four: the kind ramp stays on an even ~1.8x luminance step (2.2/4.0/7.2/13.0 against each direction's own track, solved by palette.py rather than picked), and the quiet tier clears 4.5:1. Rows per screen is equal or better everywhere — terminal 66.3px/12, paper 64.9/12, blueprint 60.6/13, ink 65.3/12. Information architecture untouched.

Two things beyond the ask. styles.css gained a surface token layer so a direction is ~40 declarations rather than a fork, and palette.py --verify found that the quiet tier's earlier 2.90-to-4.60 fix was measured against --bg when --panel is the harder ground in the light theme: it was still at 4.23:1 in the drawer, where most of that text lives. Fixed in all four and in the incumbent.

Choosing between them is judgement rather than measurement and is filed as chat-search-4ar.12, with 4ar.13 (geometry tokens reach only the list) and 4ar.14 (DIR_CHARS assumes one direction's font size) behind it.

title: cs serve --stdio: one long-lived process per client, same JSON contract
description: Today every non-Rust client spawns cs per query and pays process startup. Measured 2026-08-04: cs search --json is ~10ms end to end warm, which ADR 14 accepted as the price for having no daemon. --stdio removes the spawn without becoming one: requests on stdin, responses on stdout, one process per client, the client owning its lifetime and its death.
design:
ADR 14 names this as the cheap middle step and says to try it before anything resident. It is an envelope over the existing payload, not a new format - a cs show or cs search body becomes the result field of a JSON-RPC 2.0 response - so migrating a client is wrapping rather than rewriting.

WHAT IT BUYS, in order of how much it matters:
1. Cancellation. The user types another character and the in-flight query is abandoned. argv cannot express this at all, and it is the one thing a real typeahead surface needs that the current transport structurally cannot give.
2. Push, via notifications - a message with no id, expecting no reply. This is the third axis: request-response cannot say the archiver just captured something. Only the ambient features need it.
3. The ~3ms spawn-and-open, which is the least of the three and the one it is tempting to lead with.

WHAT IT COSTS: framing (where a message ends on a stream), id correlation, and a version handshake. NOT daemon lifecycle - the client owns the process, which is the whole reason this is cheaper than a socket.

WHY NOT YET: nothing on the roadmap needs cancellation until a client is doing live typeahead, and ADR 14 sets the revisit trigger at spawn-plus-open p95 passing ~20ms. Today it is ~10ms total. Do this when a real client is typing into it, not before.
acceptance_criteria: cs serve --stdio answers search and show over the same JSON the CLI emits. A client can cancel an in-flight request. Startup cost per query is gone. ADR 12 and ADR 14 are updated with the transport actually in use.
notes:
Filed 2026-08-04 while sequencing the native-app work. Deliberately below the Swift spike in priority - see that bead for why the transport should follow the direction rather than lead it.
MEASURED by chat-search-me9.22 (poc/swift/RESULTS.md §1), 2026-08-04, from a real Swift client against the live 324 MB index: the seam --stdio would remove — everything outside sqlite, differenced per sample — is min 5.2 / p50 8.0 / p95 12.5 ms. fork/exec alone is 0.3 ms p50. Against a keystroke-to-frame p50 of 29-40 ms, and against a total p95 of 87 ms that is almost entirely sqlite (80.5 ms). So --stdio buys the smallest and steadiest term in the round trip and leaves the tail untouched. ADR 14's revisit trigger for this is spawn-plus-open p95 past ~20 ms; it is at 12.5. Two client-side levers are each worth more than this bead: --limit moves sqlite p50 from 6.9 to 29.4, and --prefix costs 2-3x at every limit. Not an argument to close it, but it should not be picked up on latency grounds until those are spent.
DEFERRED 2026-08-06 by triage sweep, on the bead's own argument rather than a new one. Its design section already says 'Do this when a real client is typing into it, not before', and ADR 14 sets the revisit trigger at spawn-plus-open p95 past ~20 ms against a measured 12.5 ms. That reasoning was in the prose and not in the status, so bd ready kept offering it as startable work — the same gap chat-search-4ar.2 names for ADR triggers generally. Undefer when a client does live typeahead and needs cancellation, which is the thing argv structurally cannot express.

title: Prototype: collapse the fake views into a grouping dimension, add Library
description:
IA pass on poc/ui. Two of the three top-level views were GROUP BY over the same set wearing the costume of destinations - Search, Projects and Sittings drew the same rows from the same filters into the same drawer, and nothing was in one and not the others. Meanwhile a run of work was a divider inside Projects and a whole tab as Sittings: the same primitive (clustering ended_at) at two parameterisations.

Grouping is now a control on one list - none | project | run | topic | source - and the freed tab goes to Library, the only surface that is not derived from the index.
design:
Nav: [Search] [Library]. Group control sits in the search bar beside the query it modifies, not in the title bar with the views, because grouping is a property of the list rather than a place.

Two axes came free that nobody had built: topic, which was filterable but never browsable, and source, which matters because archetype is ~87% predicted by it. Topic grouping carries an explicit 'no topic matched' residue group - a grouping that silently drops 24% of the rows is lying about the set. Run grouping drops the old sittings requirement that a run cross two tools, which was a display filter masquerading as a definition; cross-tool runs are tagged instead.

One filter state: state.query = {free, agents, date, dirs, topics, range}, and drawQuery renders all six with a per-token clear. topics and range have no grammar in cs_core::query, so they are drawn dashed and filed as chat-search-me9.18 rather than given invented syntax.

Library: collections (a rule, not a list), proposals with accept/dismiss, project merges, pinned. Mostly empty, with the first real empty states in the prototype - which is the true state of an app where nothing has been authored yet. The merge section finds the one genuinely non-derivable project fact by itself: /dev/career (89) + /dev/projects/career (65) = 154.
notes:
Verified headless: all four groupings render, every filter round-trips through a token, the drawer links back to its project, and accepting a proposal promotes it to a collection.

Also fixed from the same review: rail reordered by coverage (When 100%, Sources 100%, Projects 34%, Topics 76% - Sources and When had been below the fold); dir: gained the rail section it was missing, so it is no longer the only facet unreachable without clicking through another view; the drawer's cwd became a link, so the one navigable relation is no longer half-wired; and Library hides the rail and query bar rather than drawing them inert, which is the defect Sittings had.
close_reason: Shipped in poc/ui: the fake views collapsed into a GROUPINGS dimension applied within one list, and Library exists as the second view alongside Search. Verified in the merged tree 2026-08-04.

title: Prototype: projects view as an accordion with lineage runs
description:
The projects view in poc/ui groups by exact cwd, sorts by count, and shows a two-pane master/detail. Measured against the real index that is wrong in five ways: worktrees fragment their parent (chat-search = 11 rows), nesting is invisible (spar-gd = 54 convs across 7 dirs), 30 Codex scratch dirs and 2 temp dirs are listed as projects, sorting by count buries live work, and 38 of 69 projects hold <=3 conversations so half the list is noise.

Replace with an accordion: project rows expand in place to reveal their conversations using the same row component the search view uses, with a project summary band and non-collapsible lineage dividers between runs of work.
design:
V1 + V2 + V4 from the design conversation.

V1 accordion: expanding a project inserts search rows (ribbon, meta grid, best-match line) indented under it. Clicking a conversation opens the existing preview column, so the two views share both the row and the drawer.

V2 summary band: on expand, one band above the rows carrying the project's topic fingerprint, top files scoped to the directory, tools, and error/question counts.

V4 lineage dividers: conversations inside a project are separated by run dividers (>3 day gap, matching export.py lineages()), NOT collapsible - they are labels, not controls.

Cap 20 rows then 'show all N' which hands off to the search view with dir: set, so there is one list implementation.

MEASURED, and why topics go on the project row and not the conversation rows: with the shipped seed rule over all message text, a chat-search conversation matches 7.3 topics (median 7); the top topic is 'Rust and cargo' on 10 of the 12 largest; density normalisation gives an identical 69/114 distinct top-3 signatures; lift-within-project returns 'Money and finance', 'Travel', 'Health and fitness' - the same failure NOTES section 2 records for term mining. At project level the fingerprints are sharp and differ: chat-search = Rust/SQLite/Agents, personal-site = Prose/Web/Image, rl-assignments = RL/DL.

Corpus numbers behind the folds: 1,036 of 3,059 conversations carry a cwd (34%) but they hold 169,589 of 184,099 messages (92%). After folding worktrees and dropping scratch dirs: 69 projects, 991 conversations; 11 projects hold 719 of them (73%); 38 hold <=3.
notes:
Built and verified headless (Chrome, file://). Landed: accordion with corpus-true counts, project summary band (topics as subject-first chips, files scoped and relative, messages/dirs/questions/failures/pauses), 12h run dividers, 20-row cap handing off to Search with dir: set, small-project tail fold, sittings sharing the same preview drawer.

Two refactors fell out and are the durable part: conversationRow(c, slot) is now one component used by search and projects (slot picks path vs clock for the shared meta cell), and the drawer's zoom/fidelity/minimap wiring keys on the presence of .col.preview rather than on view === 'search' — which is what had left those controls dead the moment the drawer appeared anywhere else.

export.py gained project_of() (worktree fold, Codex-scratch and temp-dir drop), corpus_projects() (rollup over the whole index, not the sample), and a third sampling stratum by project. Sample is now 354 conversations / 8.8 MB, 284 across 33 projects.

Six things measured wrong on the way and fixed, recorded as NOTES.md items 11-16: cap applied after dividers so a divider announced 26 rows above 20; project topics ranked by term frequency (length bias, every fingerprint read 'Rust and cargo 1392'); 'screen'/'offer' seeds putting Interviews and hiring on chat-search at 50; sparkline over a fixed 26-week window drawing a 5-day project as a dotted rule; drawer controls wired by view name; and sampling only the ten largest projects so the small-project fold had nothing to fold.

Not done, by decision: git_branch as an axis (deprioritised by the user), project nesting (V3), authored path merges for /dev/career + /dev/projects/career.
close_reason: Shipped in poc/ui: the projects view is an accordion (state.expanded keyed group:key) and lineage runs are runsOf(), which the project rows render. Verified in the merged tree 2026-08-04.

title: TUI has no copy-the-resume-command key
description:
The retired scripts/cs-fzf bound ctrl-y to 'copy the resume command to the clipboard, then abort' — the one thing it did that cs tui does not. The TUI's only non-launch exit is the print path (cs tui --print, or stdout not being a terminal), which hands the line to a shell rather than to the pasteboard, so 'get me that command without opening the session here' now takes a pipeline.

docs/TUI-DESIGN.md already anticipates this: PendingAction is specced as an enum over {Resume, Copy} sharing one destination modal, so this is the Copy arm of a design that exists rather than a new concept.
acceptance_criteria: A key in cs tui puts the resume line (cd <dir> && <cmd> form, same renderer as Destination::shell_line) on the system clipboard without launching anything, and says so. Works for a Web destination by copying the URL.
notes: Filed 2026-08-01 while deleting scripts/cs-fzf. Not a regression anyone reported — recorded so the one capability the script had is not lost silently.

title: dir: case-folding relies on two different lowercase implementations agreeing
description:
filter_sql compares 'ifnull(lower(c.cwd),'') LIKE ?' against a pattern built by like_contains from a value the parser already lowercased with Rust's to_lowercase(). The two do not agree: SQLite's lower() is ASCII-only without ICU, Rust's is full Unicode.

Verified 2026-07-31: sqlite3 'SELECT lower("/tmp/CAFÉ")' returns /tmp/cafÉ, while Rust returns /tmp/café. So dir:café would not match a cwd of /tmp/CAFÉ, and neither would dir:CAFÉ — case-insensitivity silently stops at the first non-ASCII letter.

LATENT, not live: zero of the 3,003 conversations currently have a non-ASCII character in cwd (checked with length(cwd) <> length(cast(cwd AS blob))). The 980 rows with uppercase in cwd are all ASCII and do fold correctly — dir:CHAT-SEARCH and dir:chat-search both return 43.

Also worth noting as a shape: like_contains() does not lowercase its own input, it relies on Query::parse having lowercased the whole query string. That is a cross-module invariant with nothing asserting it, so a Selection built by any other route would silently stop matching.
acceptance_criteria: Either the pattern and the column are folded by the same implementation, or the invariant that filter values arrive pre-lowercased is asserted where like_contains can see it. A test with a non-ASCII uppercase directory name proves the fold.

title: Quoted filter values, for a path with a space in it
description:
The DSL splits on whitespace, so a filter value containing a space becomes two tokens: `dir:"my project"` parses as the filter `dir:"my` plus the free-text term `project`. It neither errors nor filters as asked — it silently searches for the second word.

docs/TUI-DESIGN.md §5 lists `dir:"my project"` among the fast-resume forms it calls 'worth lifting wholesale'. It was the one form chat-search-6eb.11 did not implement; the acceptance criteria there named `dir:!web-app` and not the quoted case, so it was left rather than half-done.

Measured 2026-07-31 against the 2,976-conversation index: 100 distinct cwd values, none of which currently contains a space, so nothing in today's corpus needs it. That is why this is P3 and not P2 — it is a correctness gap with no live victim yet.
acceptance_criteria: A filter value may be quoted, and a quoted value containing a space selects on the whole value rather than splitting. An unterminated quote is treated as ordinary text rather than an error, because mid-word is the normal state in a typeahead — the same rule the rest of the DSL follows. A test covers every prefix of `dir:\"my project\"` being typed.

title: Tab after a held query builds rows under a different rule than the search
description:
App::search blanks the query text when holding, then passes is_blank(&text) = true to rows::build. App::rebuild_rows, reached by Tab, passes self.is_blank() = false for the same on-screen state, because it asks the raw query rather than the rewritten text.

So expanding a conversation after a half-typed query builds its rows under a different rule than the search that produced them. Two consumers computing am I browsing from different inputs.

Fixed by Query::mode being one value that both read.
close_reason: Removed by chat-search-6eb.31.5, but the original framing was wrong and is worth correcting rather than closing quietly. The two derivations were real — search() blanked its query text before asking is_blank, rebuild_rows asked the raw query — but the effect was NOT observable. rows::build only adds hit rows for groups that have hits, and the browse path comes from recent(), which returns groups with hits: Vec::new(). So both row vectors came out identical either way. Latent inconsistency, not a user-visible bug. Fixed as one value read in both places, and pinned by one_query_decides_whether_the_list_is_matches_or_recent so it stays one.

title: cs archive --adopt <id> to write the config entry
description: a7k.12 reports unconfigured candidates and prints the exact [[sources]] block to paste, but adopting still means opening config.toml and pasting. A flag would make the explicit act one command while keeping it explicit — ADR 16 only requires that cs never chooses a permanent source id on its own, not that the user retype it.
design: Refuse without an explicit id: --adopt takes the candidate id, so nothing is ever adopted by a bare cs archive. Append to the config rather than rewriting it, so hand-written comments (the chatgpt-export note) survive. Probably belongs on a config subcommand rather than on archive, which otherwise never writes the config.
acceptance_criteria: cs archive --adopt copilot-cli appends the candidate's [[sources]] block to the config, preserves existing comments, refuses an id that is not a present candidate, and refuses one already configured.

title: Segment awareness: score and display by episode, keep the conversation as the unit
description:
Long conversations cover several topics, so a match count against the whole conversation cannot say what it is about. Measured 2026-07-30: 303 conversations (10%) contain an internal gap over 4 hours, which would make 757 extra segments, ~3.5 per split conversation. It lands where it should — 190 of the 303 have 6+ user turns, only 22 have 2 or fewer — and it is spread across all three sources (chatgpt 162, codex 80, claude-code 61).

The tempting move is to make the segment the retrieval unit. That should NOT be done, for a reason specific to this codebase, and this issue is the smaller thing to do instead.
design:
DECIDED: segments change scoring and display. They do not become results, and they never get ids.

Why not the retrieval unit — ADR 16 says a source id is permanent because it is embedded in every conversation id, and conv_id is source:native_id, derived from an id the source itself minted. A segment id would have to be source:native_id:n, where n comes from a boundary rule we chose and will want to tune. Change 4h to 6h and every segment id after the first altered boundary shifts. That would break eval judgements keyed on them and anything authored in library.db, and it means segment ids cannot satisfy ADR 16 while the rule stays tunable.

Two further costs of the full version: resume_cmd resumes a session, not a slice of one, so the thing shown and the thing opened would be different objects; and judgements collected against conversations become ambiguous the day the unit changes.

The smaller version keeps conv_id as identity and adds a derived message.segment column. Derived from (archive, importer version) provided the boundary rule is versioned as part of the importer, so ADR 1 holds and a rule change is an ordinary reindex.

What it buys:
- Ranking: apply REPEAT_WEIGHT within a segment instead of across the whole conversation, so a long session stops accumulating repeat-match credit from topics it is not about. This is the actual ranking defect, and it is exactly what REPEAT_WEIGHT was set by intuition to paper over.
- Display: report the matching segment's date range and turn count instead of the whole conversation's, which is what makes the match-position strip (chat-search-6eb.23) actionable rather than merely suggestive.
- Resume stays the conversation, so nothing about opening changes.

Boundary signals, best first: a cwd or git_branch change (unambiguous, but only present for the 940 agent conversations); a time gap over ~4h; lexical shift as a last resort. The gap rule is a proxy in both directions — an overnight break mid-task is not a topic change, and a mid-session pivot has no gap — which is another reason to keep it out of identity.
acceptance_criteria: Measured against the eval before adoption, not assumed. Specifically: does within-segment REPEAT_WEIGHT beat across-conversation REPEAT_WEIGHT on nDCG and success@1? If it does not, the segmentation is display-only and should say so.

title: Generated conversation summaries, and where they are allowed to live
description:
From the 2026-07-30 design discussion. A summary would help both search recall (index it alongside prose) and recognition (show it in a result row), and it is the obvious answer to 'this 40-turn conversation covers four topics and its title mentions one'.

Checked first, so nobody re-derives it: there are no free summaries to harvest. Claude Code writes 'ai-title' but the importer already uses it and it never changes within a conversation. Codex 'summary' fields are per-reasoning-block internal monologue, not conversation-level. ChatGPT export gives a title only. Anything here has to be generated.
design:
The blocking question is not how to generate them, it is where they are allowed to live.

schema.rs states the invariant: every column must be a pure function of (archive, importer version). That is what makes 'rm index.db && cs index' a valid response to any schema change, and it is why there are no migrations. An LLM summary is not a pure function — a different model, or the same model resampled, gives different text — so it cannot simply become a column without quietly voiding the rule that makes the index disposable.

Three ways out, in increasing cost:
1. library.db (chat-search-6eb.14). Correct by construction: authored, precious, backed up, and already the designated home for anything that is not derivable. Costs building library.db first.
2. A cache in index.db keyed on (conversation content hash, model id, prompt version), where a key miss means stale rather than wrong. Keeps the rebuild honest — a rebuild simply finds nothing and the column is empty until regenerated — at the cost of an explicit staleness notion the schema does not have today.
3. Regenerate on every rebuild. Purity preserved, but a full rebuild is currently ~7s and this would make it minutes and cost money, which breaks ADR 1's premise that the index is cheap to throw away.

Recommendation is (1), which makes this depend on library.db rather than race it.
acceptance_criteria: A decision recorded in DECISIONS.md about where generated text may live relative to the ADR 1 purity rule, before any summary is generated.
notes:
ANSWERED 2026-08-01, by the native-app design discussion. The blocking question was where a generated summary is allowed to live. Answer: chat-search-6eb.40, inference.db -- the store for anything a MODEL produced rather than a parser. That is option 2 from this issue's design field, promoted out of index.db into its own file so a rebuild neither destroys summaries nor is slowed by them.

Keyed on (conv_id, model_id, prompt_version) with input_hash as a column, where input_hash is a hash-of-hashes over the head-path messages. On change the summary is KEPT and marked stale rather than recomputed: generation is expensive and possibly metered, and a slightly out-of-date summary beats none.

Searchable via fold-on-rebuild -- cs index reads summaries out of inference.db and writes them alongside prose, the same mechanism ADR 3 already specifies for library.db. Purity survives because the fold is optional: delete inference.db, rebuild, and you get a working index with an empty summary column and no error.

Note the redaction coupling: a LOCAL generator keeps ADR 15 dormant. A hosted model wakes it up and makes it blocking.

title: Semantic topic labels for recognising a conversation
description:
From the 2026-07-30 design discussion. The hardest part of judging a result, and of using search at all, is quickly understanding what a conversation was about. Titles help but are one line and fixed at the first turn; a long conversation that moved on is mislabelled by its own title.

Cluster-derived topic labels are one answer. Note the framing that makes this cheap to justify: wanting embeddings for DISPLAY (help me recognise this conversation) clears a much lower bar than wanting them for RANKING (chat-search-6eb.17), because a wrong label costs a glance while a wrong ranking costs the result. Do the display version first if either.
design:
Explicitly deferred until the ranking can be measured. Adding semantic retrieval before the eval works means you cannot tell whether it helped, which is the trap chat-search-6eb.9 exists to avoid.

Cheaper things to exhaust first, all of which attack the same recognition problem with no model involved: the match-position strip (chat-search-6eb.23, done), the collapsed user-message spine (see docs/TUI-DESIGN.md), and cwd-derived project names.

If it does get built, labels are derived data and cannot be a plain index.db column under ADR 1 — same purity problem as chat-search-6eb.24.
notes: Checked 2026-07-30 for free labels already in the archive: Claude Code writes 'ai-title' records, but the importer already consumes them and no conversation carries more than one distinct value, so there is no free topic-drift signal there. Codex 'summary' hits are per-reasoning-block, not conversation-level.

title: Gemini CLI: index assistant 'thoughts' as Reasoning
description:
The gemini-cli importer (crates/cs-import/src/gemini.rs) currently maps only the 'content' field of each record. Every 'gemini' record also carries a 'thoughts' array of {subject, description} objects -- 118 of 152 messages in the reference archive. That is genuine reasoning prose and is dropped today.

Decide whether to emit it as a separate Kind::Reasoning message per turn (like codex.rs does for response_item/reasoning) or to leave it out. If emitted, it needs its own native_id derived from the parent record's id, and it must be chained so parents stay non-dangling.
acceptance_criteria:
Assistant 'thoughts' from gemini-cli records are indexed rather than dropped. The reference measurement is the target: 118 of 152 messages in the reference archive carry them, and after this the corpus reports how many Reasoning messages gemini-cli contributes.

They are emitted as a separate message per turn with the reasoning kind, following what codex.rs already does — one importer inventing its own shape for the same concept is the thing to avoid, so match the existing precedent rather than adding a thoughts column.

The {subject, description} pair is preserved as prose that reads correctly when it is a search result, not concatenated into something that reads as one run-on message.

Reasoning is separable at search time. Whether it is searched by default is a ranking question, not this bead's — but it must be possible to tell a Reasoning hit from a prose hit in the result, since reasoning is the model talking to itself and a user searching their own words should not be flooded by it.
notes:
SPEC 2026-08-01. The description asks the implementer to 'decide whether to emit it as a separate Kind::Reasoning message per turn (like codex.rs does)'. That decision is now made in the acceptance criteria — follow codex.rs — because it is the convention question and not a per-source judgement call, and the repo's own rule is that a rule lives in exactly one place.

Check against the 8mb reasoning work in flight (worktree-bead-8mb-reasoning-honesty, 'say that reasoning is unindexed, in the two places that implied otherwise'), which suggests reasoning indexing is being actively reconsidered right now. This bead should not contradict whatever that concludes.

title: Gemini CLI: decide whether logs.json is worth importing
description:
The gemini-cli source globs **/*.json, so <projectHash>/logs.json reaches the importer and is declined by shape. It is a JSON array of {sessionId, messageId, type, message, timestamp} -- a thin prompt log, 5 records across 4 files in the reference archive, all type 'user', largely redundant with the chats/ files.

It names 2 sessions. One (d84cb634) also has a chats/ file, so those records are redundant. The other (74eb0b66, a '/theme' command from 2025-07-02) has no chats/ file at all, so logs.json is the only surviving trace of it. Volume is trivial either way. Decide and document.
acceptance_criteria:
A decision, written down, either way. 'Decide and document' is the description's own instruction and the deliverable is the documented decision — docs/FORMAT-NOTES.md is where the gemini-cli format findings already live.

If logs.json is imported: the one session it uniquely preserves (74eb0b66) appears in the corpus, and records for sessions that also have a chats/ file do NOT produce a duplicate conversation — dedup by sessionId against the chats/ import, since the redundancy is known in advance rather than discovered.

If it is declined: the reason is recorded in FORMAT-NOTES.md, and the shape-based decline is deliberate rather than incidental, so a future reader can tell 'we looked at this and said no' from 'nothing ever handled it'. Say explicitly that one session is being given up, and that it is a /theme command.

Either way the importer stops declining it silently. A file the glob delivers on every run and the importer rejects by shape is indistinguishable from a file that failed to parse.
notes:
SPEC 2026-08-01. My recommendation is DECLINE and document. The whole population is 5 records across 4 files, of which the unique content is a single '/theme' command from 2025-07-02 — a slash command with no conversational value, and 9qj is separately tracking bare slash commands reaching title_candidate as a defect. Importing a code path plus a dedup rule to preserve that is a poor trade.

The part worth keeping regardless is the last acceptance clause. This is a live example of the pattern a7k.11 and n58.15 also touch: a file arrives, is declined by shape, and nothing says so. Whichever way the decision goes, the silent decline should stop.

title: cs-archive still carries two private now_ms() copies
description: machine.rs:105 and manifest.rs:159 each define now_ms() -> u64. The shared clock landed in cs-core::time as part of chat-search-me9.12, but cs-archive cannot use it: capture must not depend on the index crate (ADR 16), and these return u64 because manifest Event.ts is serialized as u64. Cheap fix within the crate: machine.rs uses manifest::now_ms() instead of its own.
design: Do not reach for cs-core here — the dependency would run capture -> index, which is exactly the direction ADR 16 keeps open for retroactive reparse. Collapsing the two inside cs-archive is the whole job.
close_reason: Done, verified. The two now_ms() bodies were byte-identical (same UNIX_EPOCH base, same truncating as_millis() as u64, same unwrap_or(0) on a pre-1970 clock), so the collapse arbitrated nothing. machine.rs:105 deleted; machine.rs now imports crate::manifest::now_ms. manifest.rs unchanged and still pub — it has two other consumers at cs/src/main.rs:165 and :178. cs-archive/Cargo.toml confirmed to have no cs-core dependency, so ADR 16's capture-must-not-depend-on-index direction is intact. The why-comment sits on the import (the line someone would edit to 'fix' this) and both its claims check out: cs_core::time::now_ms returns i64 while the manifest Event.ts wire format needs u64. cargo test -p cs-archive: 33 passed, 0 failed.

title: Mechanise the Revisit when triggers
description: 17 ADRs carry one, and nothing checks any of them — a trigger with no monitor is a wish. Four are mechanisable today because the tools already measure the inputs: ADR 1 (rebuild exceeds ~60 s, indexer); ADR 6 (corpus exceeds ~50 GB, archiver); ADR 20 (free space < 10 GB or growth > 1.5 GB/month, archiver); ADR 19 (a source mutates in place without changing size, --verify pass).
acceptance_criteria:
The four mechanisable triggers named in the description fire on their own, from the tool that already measures the input, and say which ADR they belong to when they do:
  ADR 1  — rebuild exceeds ~60 s (indexer)
  ADR 6  — corpus exceeds ~50 GB (archiver)
  ADR 20 — free space under 10 GB, or growth over 1.5 GB/month (archiver)
  ADR 19 — a source mutates in place without changing size (--verify pass)

A trigger that fires produces something durable, not a log line that scrolls past — the archiver runs unattended every 300 s under launchd, so a warning nobody is present to read is the same as no warning. Filing or reopening a bead is the natural form, since that is where work lives.

A trigger that has not fired is visible as not-fired. `cs status` reporting the current value against the threshold is what turns 17 wishes into a dashboard, and it is what makes the check trustworthy: silence has to mean 'measured and fine', never 'never ran'.

The remaining 13 ADR triggers are enumerated with one line each on why they are not mechanisable yet, so the next pass starts from a list rather than from a re-read of all 17.
notes:
SPEC 2026-08-01. This bead is worth more than its P3 suggests, and this session is the evidence: six beads were deferred today whose only blocker is a threshold nobody measures — 6eb.16 waits on ADR 10's rebuild-duration trigger, a7k.14 on ADR 20's growth trigger, a7k.16 on ADR 19's mutate-in-place trigger. Those are precisely the triggers this mechanises. Until it exists, a deferred bead stays deferred because nobody happened to check, not because the condition is false.

Two of the four are close to free. The indexer already times a rebuild and prints it; the archiver already computes sizes per source. ADR 20's growth number needs a month-over-month comparison, which the manifest's append-only event log (ADR 19) can answer without new state.

title: exec() the resume command on Unix
description: Rather than printing it, so the agent inherits the terminal and there is no orphaned parent. Windows spawns and waits instead. Printing a copyable string stays right for --json and Raycast.
close_reason: Enter now execs the resume command with all three descriptors inherited (never redirected, which is what breaks crossterm). URLs go to the platform opener; cwd is set via current_dir rather than a composed 'cd &&'; Windows spawns and waits. Printing is kept for --print and whenever stdin/stdout is not a terminal, so eval "$(cs tui)" still works. Verified end-to-end under a pty against real codex.

title: Title resolution fold, including the authored override
acceptance_criteria:
Titles resolve as ADR 8's fold: authored override > custom-title > ai-title > first user message, evaluated at read time rather than stored. A test covers each rung and, importantly, each FALLTHROUGH — an empty custom-title must not beat a good ai-title, which is the way a fold like this usually breaks.

The both-renamed case is settled per the 2026-08-01 decision: authored always wins. A test pins it with a conversation renamed in-app and upstream, asserting the authored name survives regardless of which timestamp is later.

Claude Code re-emits custom-title on every save — observed up to 44 times in one session — so the fold takes the last one and a test covers a session carrying many. Rename history stays recoverable from the archive, per ADR 8's own reasoning.

An authored override is authored data, so per ADR 3 it does not live in index.db. This bead may therefore not be completable without 6eb.14 (library.db); if so, say that and wire the dependency rather than writing an authored column into the index.
notes:
UNBLOCKED 2026-08-01. ADR 8's open sub-question — 'if a conversation is renamed both in-app and upstream, authored currently wins; last-write-wins by timestamp is the alternative' — was decided in favour of AUTHORED ALWAYS WINS.

Reasoning recorded with the decision: an in-app rename is a deliberate act by the user, while an upstream rename is usually the vendor regenerating a title. It needs no cross-source clock comparison, and it matches the fold order ADR 8 already states. Last-write-wins was rejected as depending on two sources' timestamps being comparable, which is not established.

docs/DECISIONS.md ADR 8 needs updating to record this — it still reads 'Open sub-question'.

The ADR 3 tension in the last acceptance clause is the real risk in this bead: 35 sessions carry a custom-title today, which is derived and fine, but the 'authored override' rung is authored data and index.db is a pure function of (archive, importer version). Check that boundary before writing any schema.

title: Incremental / tail indexing for the live session
notes:
DEFERRED 2026-08-01: threshold-gated by ADR 10, not underspecified.

GATE: ADR 10 ('No incremental indexing yet') already decided this, including the design — build change DETECTION but respond with a full rebuild, and tail-append only files touched in the last few minutes, so the tail path only ever handles pure append. Its reasoning is that a 7 s rebuild makes incremental indexing pure complexity, and that patching an FTS index through deletes is where the bugs live.

UNBLOCKS WHEN: ADR 10's own revisit trigger fires — rebuild exceeds ~60 s, or live-session latency becomes a felt problem. Rebuild was ~7 s at 2,963 conversations and the corpus is now 3,003, so the trigger is nowhere close.

This is the clearest case of the class: the bead is empty because the ADR holds the whole design, and the only thing missing is permission to start, which is a measurement rather than a decision. 4ar.2 is what would make that measurement automatic — ADR 1's rebuild-duration trigger is one of the four it names as mechanisable today.

title: library.db and the authored event log
description: Skipping library.db is safe only while nothing authored is written into index.db; that invariant is easy to hold and expensive to unwind.
acceptance_criteria:
library.db exists as the home for authored data, separate from index.db, per ADR 3. The invariant it protects is stated as a test, not only as prose: a rebuild — `rm index.db && cs index` — loses nothing the user authored.

Every index.db column stays a pure function of (archive, importer version). Anything authored or generated lives in library.db, which is never rebuilt from the archive and is the thing that would need backing up.

It is an append-only event log rather than a mutable row per conversation, so an authored title has history and a rename can be undone — the same shape ADR 19 uses for the manifest and the same shape Claude Code's own custom-title events already have.

The first consumer is named and works end to end, since a store with no reader cannot be shown to be correct. 6eb.15's authored title override is the obvious candidate.
notes:
SPEC 2026-08-01. The description states the invariant ('skipping library.db is safe only while nothing authored is written into index.db; that invariant is easy to hold and expensive to unwind') but not the trigger, which is what makes it actionable: this becomes required the moment any bead needs to store something the user wrote.

Two beads are already pressing on it. 6eb.15 (title fold) needs somewhere to put an authored override. 6eb.25 (generated conversation summaries) is titled 'and where they are allowed to live', which is this question for generated rather than authored data.

So the sequencing is real: 6eb.15 and 6eb.25 both either wait for this, or quietly breach ADR 3. Worth deciding which before either starts.
Third bead pressing on this: chat-search-me9.8.4 shipped the macOS app's Library view, whose four shelves (collections, proposals, project merges, pins) are all empty because there is nowhere to author into. It draws each empty state naming this bead rather than a feature promise, so nothing is blocked — but the view exists now and stays empty until library.db does.

title: Recency as a mode, not a weight
description: fast-resume applies no time decay to scored queries at all: an empty query sorts by timestamp, a text query sorts by pure relevance. That has no constant to tune and no direction to get backwards. Worth A/B-ing against our multiplicative decay when the eval set exists.
acceptance_criteria:
An A/B against the current multiplicative decay, scored on the eval set, with a number for each arm. The outcome is a decision recorded in DECISIONS.md — either recency becomes a mode and DECAY is deleted, or the weight is kept and the alternative is written down as rejected so it is not re-litigated.

Both arms are run on the same judged queries. SearchOptions.decay already exists so the eval harness can pool candidates from a recency-blind ranker as well as this one, which is the mechanism this needs and it is already there.

If the mode wins, the change is that a text query sorts by pure relevance and an empty query sorts by timestamp — with no constant to tune. State what that does to the queries where decay currently helps, because 'no constant' is only an improvement if nothing regresses behind it.
notes:
SPEC 2026-08-01, and a missing dependency wired the same day: this now depends on 6eb.21 (harvest the eval set), which its own description implied — 'worth A/B-ing when the eval set exists' — but nothing encoded. 6eb.13 (tune REPEAT_WEIGHT and the decay constant) already had that dependency; this one did not, so it was being offered by bd ready as though it were startable. It is not: an A/B with nothing to score against is two numbers nobody can compare.

6eb.21 is currently deferred pending the judging pass, so this is gated behind that.

title: Fuzzy-on-failure typo tolerance
description: fts5vocab exposes the term list (49,538 terms); bounded edit distance with a first-char and length prefilter corrects to the stemmed form the index actually holds. Only run when the exact query returns nothing, so correctly-spelled queries pay nothing. Prototype corrected borrwo->borrow, tailwidn->tailwind, reciprocol->reciproc.
acceptance_criteria:
A misspelled query that currently returns nothing returns the results of the corrected spelling. The three the prototype already corrected are the floor — borrwo->borrow, tailwidn->tailwind, reciprocol->reciproc — and the test uses the real term list rather than a fixture, since correcting to 'the stemmed form the index actually holds' is the entire point and a fixture cannot exercise it.

A correctly-spelled query pays nothing measurable. Fuzzy runs only after the exact query returns zero rows, so the common path never reaches it — assert that, do not assume it, because a prefilter that runs eagerly would put an edit-distance scan on every keystroke.

The correction is visible to the user. A result set silently produced by a different query than the one typed is a lie in the same family as me9.5's empty-search-on-failure — say what it searched for instead.

Cost is stated for the worst case that will actually happen: a misspelling with a common first character and a common length, which is where the prefilter does least work. The zero-result path is already the slowest one to reach, so this adds to a query that has already scanned everything.
notes:
SPEC 2026-08-01. The description carries the design and a working prototype — 49,538 terms out of fts5vocab, bounded edit distance behind a first-char and length prefilter — so what was missing was the shape of proof, not the approach.

Interaction worth checking before starting: 6eb.11's DSL means a query can now return zero rows because a FILTER excluded everything, not because a term was misspelled. Correcting the spelling of a query that failed on 'agent:codex' would produce a second empty result set and a confusing message. 6eb.36 fixed exactly this confusion in cs explain; the same trap applies here, and the fuzzy path should not fire when a filter is what emptied the set.

title: Read ~/.claude/projects/<project>/sessions-index.json
description: New sidecar, present in 2 of 27 project dirs here. Carries isSidechain, gitBranch, messageCount, firstPrompt, created/modified per session — gitBranch in particular is a filter facet reachable no other way. Note it does not carry the summary field fast-resume reads from it, so their Claude rename support is dead code on this machine.
acceptance_criteria:
gitBranch reaches the conversation table from sessions-index.json, and is reachable as a filter — it is a facet available no other way, which is the reason this bead exists rather than the sidecar being interesting in itself.

The sidecar is optional and absent more often than present (2 of 27 project dirs here), so a project without one imports exactly as it does today. Its absence is never an error and never a reason to skip the project's transcripts.

The sidecar never overrides what the transcripts themselves say. Where both carry a fact — isSidechain, messageCount — the transcript wins and the sidecar is corroboration, because the transcript is the thing ADR 1 guarantees and the sidecar is a cache the vendor maintains.

Coverage is stated: how many conversations gain a gitBranch, out of how many. A facet that covers 7% of the corpus is a different feature from one that covers most of it, and 6eb.11's dir: filter is the precedent — it shipped knowing cwd was 100% on agent sources and 0% on chatgpt-export.

Once gitBranch exists as a column, adding a branch: filter is 6eb.11's DSL work and belongs in its own bead, not this one.
notes:
SPEC 2026-08-01. The description already records the useful negative — the sidecar does NOT carry the summary field fast-resume reads from it, so their Claude rename support is dead code on this machine. Keep that: it is the kind of finding that stops someone re-deriving the same disappointment.

Sequencing note: this is capture-adjacent but the sidecar is inside ~/.claude/projects, which is already an archived source, so the bytes may already be in the archive. Check before assuming any archiver change is needed — if the glob already catches it, this is importer-only work.

title: Codex pre-2025-09-09 format
description: 18 files here, no parser anywhere handles it. NOTE: possibly the same 18 files as the pre-payload issue — confirm before working either.
close_reason: Duplicate of chat-search-n58.6 — verified against the archive, not assumed. All 692 archived Codex .jsonl files were scanned: exactly 18 lack a payload wrapper, and they are the same 18 files n58.6 describes. They are a single format, not two: line 1 is a session header {id, timestamp, instructions, git} and subsequent lines are bare Responses-API items (type = message | reasoning | function_call | function_call_output) interleaved with {"record_type":"state"} separators. Zero lines carry event_msg. The 'pre-2025-09-09' boundary in this issue's title is wrong: the format runs 2025-08-07 to 2025-12-07, and only 4 of the 18 predate 2025-09-09. No separate older shape exists in this corpus. Verified facts folded into n58.6.

title: Separate role from authoredness
description: Kind currently conflates what a message is with who wrote it; environment_context and isMeta are exactly that collision. See the material_origin idea in docs/FORMAT-NOTES.md.
acceptance_criteria:
Role and authoredness are separate fields. A message can be 'assistant-role, machine-authored' and 'user-role, machine-authored' independently, so environment_context and isMeta stop being encoded as a Kind.

The two collisions named in the description are the tests: environment_context is user-role but not user-authored, and isMeta is likewise. Both must be distinguishable from a real user prompt after the change, and a search for authored user prose must not return either.

Every existing Kind maps onto the new pair explicitly. No message becomes unclassifiable, and the mapping is written down — this is a schema change, so per ADR 1 it is an IMPORTER_VERSION bump and a rebuild rather than a migration.

The payoff is stated in numbers: how many messages currently classified as user prose are machine-authored, corpus-wide. That figure is what justifies the change, since it is the amount of noise currently competing with real user prompts in ranking.
notes:
SPEC 2026-08-01. docs/FORMAT-NOTES.md holds the material_origin idea the description points at; read that before designing, since the vocabulary should not be invented twice.

This is more valuable than P3 suggests and the measurement in the last acceptance clause would prove it either way: a user prompt is the highest-signal thing in the corpus for search, and anything machine-generated wearing a user role dilutes exactly that. 6eb.11's agent: filter and n58.21's Reasoning kind are both in this neighbourhood — the general question is what a message IS, as distinct from who said it.

title: Codex paginated history mode
description: Not present in this corpus, but a legacy-only parser extracts zero messages from such files if it appears.
acceptance_criteria:
A Codex paginated-history file imports its messages instead of yielding zero. The fixture is synthetic (ordering trap 3) and shaped from the documented format rather than from a real rollout, since the corpus contains no example.

Detection is by shape, not by filename or by assuming a version — the same rule n58.6 applies to the legacy pre-payload format.

The failure mode this prevents is stated as a test: a legacy-only parser extracts zero messages from such a file, and zero messages is indistinguishable from an empty conversation. It must instead be declined loudly, or parsed.

A file that is neither format is still declined without taking the rest of the source down.
notes:
SPEC 2026-08-01. Not present in this corpus — this is insurance against a format Codex may emit, in the same family as a7k.11 (.zst rollouts). Both share the dangerous property that the failure is silent: the file parses to nothing rather than erroring, so a source quietly loses conversations while cs index reports success.

Worth doing together with n58.6 (Codex legacy pre-payload format, P2, already specced) since both are format-detection in codex.rs and both want the same declined-loudly path.

title: Derived surface and account columns
notes:
DEFERRED 2026-08-01: gated on ADR 16, not on missing detail.

GATE: ADR 16 ('Source identifier is the watched location, not the surface') settles that a source id is permanent and that surface must never be part of an id. What it does NOT settle is the work/personal account question, which docs/BACKLOG.md lists as open and describes as 'nothing now — effectively forced to one source'. Derived surface and account columns cannot be specified until that is decided, because the whole question is what an account column would key on when one machine has one account per tool.

UNBLOCKS WHEN: a second account exists on any source, or ADR 16's account sub-question is decided. Either makes the column's contents definable; today it would be a column with one value.

Note the constraint any future spec inherits: surface and account are DERIVED, so per the index-is-disposable rule they must be a pure function of (archive, importer version) and must never become part of an id (ADR 16).

title: OpenCode importer
Lift the duplicated RFC3339 -> epoch-millis parser into a shared module
description: Currently duplicated in codex.rs and claude_code.rs.
acceptance_criteria:
One RFC3339 -> epoch-millis parser, in one module, used by every importer that needs it. cs_core::time is the established home for exactly this kind of rule — it already owns the local-day fold and the civil-time arithmetic — and 'a rule lives in exactly one place' is the convention being applied.

The existing tests move with the function rather than being rewritten, and the union of what the copies covered is preserved: leap day, pre-epoch dates, and fractional seconds at 1, 2, 3 and 9 digits all still have a case.

Byte-identical import output before and after, proven by the golden tests. This is a refactor; if any conversation or timestamp changes, one of the copies had a bug and that is a separate finding to record rather than to absorb silently.

The private digits() helper collapses too, or the bead says why each copy differs.
notes:
MEASURED 2026-08-01, and the description understates it. It says 'codex.rs and claude_code.rs'. Actual state: epoch_millis(&str) in codex.rs:436, claude_code.rs:460, gemini.rs:198; digits() in codex.rs:508, claude_code.rs:525, gemini.rs:270; and chatgpt_export.rs:385 has a genuinely different function that shares the name but takes a serde_json::Value and reads float seconds - NOT part of this migration.

UPDATE 2026-08-04 (chat-search-o1i): the shared home now EXISTS at crates/cs-import/src/timestamp.rs, with tests. google_takeout.rs would have been the fourth copy and uses the shared module instead. What remains is migrating the three existing copies into it and deleting them, which means moving their tests too - deliberately not done alongside a new importer.

title: forget operation
description: Remove from raw + index, write a tombstone so a rescan cannot resurrect it.
acceptance_criteria:
`cs forget` removes a conversation from the raw archive and the index, and writes a tombstone that survives both, so a later `cs archive` cannot re-capture the file and a later `cs index` cannot resurrect the rows.

A rescan after a forget is the test: archive, forget, archive again, index, and assert the conversation is still absent. That is the whole point of the tombstone and the only way to prove it works.

Forgetting is explicit and distinct from deletion-upstream, per ADR 9 — a conversation deleted in the source tool keeps its data and is flagged deleted_upstream; a forgotten one is gone. The two must not be conflated in the schema or the UI.

The tombstone records enough to block re-capture and no more: it is the one artifact that outlives the thing it describes, so it must not become a copy of what was forgotten.

It is authored data — a decision the user made — so per ADR 3 it does not live in index.db, which is rebuilt from the archive. Where it does live is this bead's design question and may make it depend on 6eb.14.
notes:
SPEC 2026-08-01. Directly relevant to n58.23 ('Tombstones are read in five places and written in none'), which is P2 and open — that bead reports the readers already exist. Check whether this bead is the writer n58.23 is missing, in which case one of the two should absorb the other rather than both inventing a format.

ADR 9 ('Deletion keeps data; forgetting is explicit') is accepted and holds the policy, so this is implementation rather than decision — with the exception of where the tombstone lives, which runs into ADR 3 the same way 6eb.15 does.

title: --verify full-hash pass for periodic paranoia
notes:
DEFERRED 2026-08-01: gated on ADR 19, not on missing detail.

GATE: ADR 19 (manifest as an append-only event log) is accepted, but docs/BACKLOG.md lists the hash-strength question as still open, and marks it 'blocks nothing now'. A --verify pass is a choice of what to verify against: today's capture records a hash of the first 64 KB (ADR 10's change-detection tuple), so a full-hash pass means deciding whether the manifest stores a full-content hash going forward, and what to do about every entry already written without one.

UNBLOCKS WHEN: ADR 19's hash strength is decided. Note ADR 19 also carries a revisit trigger that 4ar.2 would mechanise — 'a source mutates in place without changing size' — and that trigger firing is the event that would make this urgent rather than paranoid.

Its own title says 'periodic paranoia', which is the honest priority: there is no observed corruption, only the absence of a check.

title: Encrypted offsite tier
description: ADR 20 option D. Solves disaster, which cloning does not.
notes:
DEFERRED 2026-08-01: gated on ADR 20 option D and on there being somewhere to send it.

GATE: ADR 20 option D. Its value is stated correctly in the description — it solves DISASTER, which cloning does not: an APFS clone lives on the same 96%-full internal disk as the thing it protects, so it survives deletion but not the disk.

Two things must be decided before this is specifiable, and neither is a detail. ADR 15 (redaction) is open and gates 'any archive leaving this machine' in as many words, so an offsite copy is blocked on it outright. ADR 18 (sync transport) is also open and would decide what offsite even means here.

UNBLOCKS WHEN: ADR 15 and ADR 18 are both decided. 4ar.4 now carries the redaction half of that.

Worth stating plainly since this is the only bead that covers it: there is currently NO disaster recovery for the archive. The archive is the source of truth per ADR 1 and the index is disposable, so the archive is the only thing whose loss is unrecoverable — and it exists in exactly one place.

title: Compression, when clone divergence starts costing real space
notes:
DEFERRED 2026-08-01: threshold-gated by ADR 20, not underspecified.

GATE: ADR 20 is accepted and chose option A (APFS clone on the internal disk) for v1, measured at ~3.2 MB consumed for a 1.5 GB source — effectively free, with growth costing only diverged blocks. Compression is the next option, and this bead's own title states the trigger: 'when clone divergence starts costing real space'.

ADR 20 already did the pricing, so a future spec inherits its numbers rather than re-measuring: zstd -3 is the level to use (-19 buys 5% for far more CPU); per-file zstd on opencode is 4.7x; bundling first then zstd is 10.3x; capping tool_result does not pay (p50 718 B, p99 40 KB — a fat middle, not a few giants) and would breach ADR 1 anyway.

UNBLOCKS WHEN: measured divergence makes the archive's real allocated size approach the ~1 GB/month growth curve rather than tracking clone-shared blocks. ADR 20's own trigger — free space under 10 GB, or growth over 1.5 GB/month — is one of the four 4ar.2 names as mechanisable today, and is the right monitor for this.

Still open inside ADR 20 per BACKLOG.md: compress per-file or per-bundle. That is a genuine decision and would have to be settled first.

title: OpenCode bundling
description: 170k files. layout = "bundle" is reserved in config but unimplemented, so OpenCode is currently not archived at all. Dormant since 2026-02, which is why it was deferred — not because it is unimportant.
acceptance_criteria:
OpenCode is archived. layout = "bundle" stops being a reserved-but-unimplemented config value and does what ADR 18 specifies for fragmented sources, and `cs status` shows opencode as ok rather than as a configured source contributing nothing.

The 170k files land as bundles, not as 170k archived files. ADR 18's whole reason for the bundle layout is file count, and ADR 20 measured the payoff: per-file zstd on opencode is 4.7x, bundled-then-zstd is 10.3x, so bundling more than doubles the compression available later.

A bundle is still reparseable per ADR 1 — the importer receives (logical_path, bytes) for each member, so the bundle format is a capture detail the importer stage does not have to know about.

Incremental capture works: a second `cs archive` after new OpenCode activity does not rewrite every bundle. State what it does write.

The n58.9 importer is unblocked by this and can then be scheduled — this bead is capture only, and archiving without an importer is the correct intermediate state per ADR 1.
notes:
SPEC 2026-08-01. Note this is the only source configured on this machine that is capturing NOTHING — cs status lists opencode as Bundle with the layout unimplemented, so it reports ok while archiving zero files. That is the exact failure the Capture epic forbids ('a source that is skipped says so'), and it is worth checking whether cs status is currently telling the truth about it.

Deferred because OpenCode has been dormant since 2026-02, not because it is unimportant — the description is explicit about that. The risk in waiting is asymmetric though: transcripts that are pruned before capture are gone permanently (that is why claude-code's corpus floor is 2026-06-19), so a dormant source is only safe while it stays dormant.

n58.9 (OpenCode importer) is already wired to depend on this.

title: Judge the hand-authored eval set
description:
The 24 hand-written queries in evals/ranking.toml, judged. Sheets are emitted and waiting: 263 candidates across 24 queries.

Deferred, not abandoned. Judging these would produce numbers, but numbers about invented needs — see the notes for why that stalled. Kept because it is a usable stopgap if a ranking change needs measuring before the query log has filled up, and because the seed queries were checked to return at least four conversations each, so every one poses a real ranking decision.

Prefer chat-search-6eb.21. Come back to this only if something needs measuring sooner than the log allows.
acceptance_criteria: Enough of the 24 queries judged that 'cs eval run' reports coverage above 80% and a non-zero scorable count. The harness itself is chat-search-6eb.28 and is already done.
notes:
Harness landed 2026-07-30; what remains is the judging pass, which only Tyler can do.

Built:
- cs-core/src/eval.rs — graded relevance (0 irrelevant / 1 related / 2 useful / 3 exact) and the metrics: nDCG@k with exponential gain, MRR, success@1/@5, exact@1, plus pool coverage. Pure arithmetic, 11 synthetic tests, no I/O.
- crates/cs/src/eval.rs — 'cs eval judge' and 'cs eval run', 8 tests.
- evals/ranking.toml — 24 seed queries, each verified to return >= 4 conversations so it poses a ranking decision rather than a recall test. Gitignored; evals/example.toml and evals/README.md are committed.

Design decisions worth keeping:
- Two files, two lifecycles. The set is hand-written TOML the tool never rewrites, so its comments survive. Judgements are append-only JSONL, last-wins per (query id, conv id) — the same fold the archive manifest uses. Quitting a session mid-way keeps every answer already given.
- Judging pools across three rankers (default, decay=0, repeat_weight=0), not just the shipping one. Judging only what the current constants return is how a tuning run proves the current constants optimal: a conversation they bury is never seen, never judged, and counts as irrelevant for every configuration tried afterwards.
- A query with no positive judgement reports as unscorable, not as zero. Averaging a zero would make the score fall every time a query was added to the set.
- Grade 1 (related) deliberately does not count as a hit for MRR/success@k. A search that returns things about the right subject and never the conversation itself looks defensible result by result and has still failed.

Prerequisite work done to make the measurement honest: REPEAT_WEIGHT and DECAY are now per-query fields on Query rather than compile-time constants, with tests proving each actually moves the ranking — a sweep over a dead knob would report a flat line and read as 'the current value is fine'. This makes chat-search-6eb.13 a shell loop over 'cs eval run --repeat-weight'.

Known friction for the judging pass: chat-search-202 (Codex IDE context blocks in titles) makes some pooled candidates hard to read in the judge prompt. Worth fixing first if judging feels slow.

--- 2026-07-30 follow-up: judging is revisable ---
Two gaps closed after a first walkthrough of the judge loop.

'b' steps back one conversation and re-asks, showing the grade just given so it can be replaced. Mistyping a grade on the candidate you just passed was otherwise only fixable by hand-editing the JSONL mid-session.

'cs eval judge --review' walks the whole pool including already-graded conversations, showing each existing grade in the prompt; enter keeps it, a number replaces it, and nothing is appended unless the value actually changes. Default behaviour still offers only ungraded candidates, because otherwise every session after the first begins by pressing enter through all your earlier work.

Both rely on the append-only last-wins fold that was already there, so a correction is a new line and the original judgement stays visible in the file.

Testability: ask() now takes &mut dyn BufRead rather than Stdin, and candidate selection is a free function, so the key mapping and the review/default split are unit-tested rather than only smoke-tested. A mistyped key re-prompts and is never taken as a grade — 'x' silently becoming irrelevant would put a judgement in the log nobody made.

--- 2026-07-30: interactive loop dropped, replaced by sheets ---
The prompt loop was the wrong interface and is gone (183 lines). 'cs eval sheet' writes one gradeable file per query into evals/sheets/; you fill in the first column in an editor; 'cs eval collect' reads them back and appends to the same JSONL log.

Why, in order of weight:
1. Relevance is a comparative judgement. Whether a result is a 2 or a 1 depends on what else came back, and a one-at-a-time prompt makes you calibrate against memory of what already scrolled past. Seeing the whole pool at once is how the call actually gets made.
2. The prompt showed the conversation's FIRST USER MESSAGE, not the query-matched snippet — so you judged relevance against text chosen without reference to the query. Sheets carry Group.hits[0].snippet, i.e. what a real result row shows. This was a genuine defect, not just ergonomics.
3. 'b' and '--review' were ~120 lines reimplementing what a text editor does for free.

Format: a row is a grade char in column one, whitespace, then a pre-filled conv id. Everything else on the line is ignored, so notes to yourself are safe anywhere in the file. Candidates are ordered newest-first and carry NO rank — rank order would anchor the judgement to the ranking being measured (the bias pooling exists to remove) and would reshuffle a half-graded file on every re-emit.

Three guards, all tested: a grade char outside 0-3/_ is fatal rather than skipped (silently dropping it would lose a judgement actually made); a conv id the index does not hold aborts the whole collect without writing (hand-edited ids are nearly always typos, --allow-unknown escapes); and 'sheet' refuses to overwrite a file holding grades not yet collected, which is the one way this flow could lose work.

Re-emitting pre-fills every grade already in the log, so sheets/ is disposable and 'sheet' is safe to re-run after a ranking change.

Seeded state: 24 sheets, 263 candidates total. Notes in ranking.toml no longer repeat the candidate count now that the sheet header prints it.

--- 2026-07-30: deferred, and no longer blocking anything ---
Decision: the ranking is good enough to live with, so stop hand-authoring queries and collect real ones instead. Blocking edges to chat-search-6eb.13 and chat-search-6eb.12 removed; both are now free to proceed on judgement rather than waiting on a set nobody can finish honestly.

What stalled it, stated plainly so it is not rediscovered: a query invented by reading the corpus has no information need behind it. Asked which result is 'the one I meant', the honest answer is that several are fine and none is the one, because there was no one. The judging was measuring the queries, not the ranking.

The harness itself is finished and stays useful — sheets, pooled candidates, metrics, and the append-only judgement log are all what a harvested set will be scored with. What is deferred is the hand-judging pass over the 24 invented queries.

Succeeded by chat-search-6eb.21 (harvest the set from the query log). Revisit when 'cs needs' shows roughly 50-100 picks across 20+ distinct queries.

title: ChatGPT desktop store: closed, the key is not derivable
description:
Filed so this is not investigated a third time. It is a NEGATIVE result, and the right outcome is to close it as wontfix with the reason attached.

~/Library/Application Support/com.openai.chat/conversations-v3-<uuid>/*.data holds 204 conversations / 18 MB on this machine. AES-256-GCM: 12-byte nonce, ciphertext, 16-byte tag. Confirmed high-entropy with no magic bytes.

The key sits behind a Keychain ACCESS GROUP (2DC432GLL2.com.openai.shared), not behind a Safe Storage password. That distinction is the whole thing. Chrome's cookie key is a password any process can read and stretch with PBKDF2 - which is why chat-search-a7k.24 is feasible. An access-group item is readable only by a binary code-signed with OpenAI's Team ID. There is nothing to reimplement.

cass is sometimes described as reading this store. It does not: it requires the user to supply CHATGPT_ENCRYPTION_KEY themselves.

The 2026-07-09 Codex merge did not change this. The merged app writes artifacts to ~/Documents/Codex/<date>/<title-slug>/ - outputs/, work/, research/ - with no transcript among them (71 files here, verified). The slug and date leak that a conversation happened and nothing else. ChatGPT Atlas is discontinued 2026-08-09, so its Chromium profile is not worth targeting either.

ADR 21 therefore routes ChatGPT through the manual export, and chat-search-a7k.10's staleness nag is what bounds the gap.
acceptance_criteria: Closed as wontfix, with the access-group reason recorded where the next person to look at those .data files will find it (docs/FORMAT-NOTES.md, 'ChatGPT desktop - why the local store is out of reach').
close_reason: Negative result, not abandoned work. The v3 key is behind Keychain access group 2DC432GLL2.com.openai.shared, readable only by an OpenAI-signed binary — there is no derivable password to reimplement, unlike Chrome's Safe Storage. Reason recorded in docs/FORMAT-NOTES.md so the .data files do not invite a third investigation. ChatGPT stays on the manual export per ADR 21.

title: Bare slash command reaches title_candidate on the claude-code side
description:
A slash command typed with no wrapping markup (observed: '/usage/usage', 2 threads, from the cc-usage tool) is not filtered on the claude-code path. Codex now has is_command_line for exactly this (added in chat-search-n58.3); claude_code has no equivalent.

Currently masked by an ai-title on both threads, so 0 conversations are affected today. Filed only so it is not rediscovered from scratch — it becomes visible the moment a bare-command thread has no AI title.

title: Theming
description: A config-file colour system for clients. Stays P4 on purpose: docs/TUI-DESIGN.md §6 decides that layer-1 structural colour comes from the terminal's indexed palette (0-15), so the user's existing terminal theme IS the theme and a bespoke system is a nicety rather than a fix. Only becomes real work if a client needs colours the 16-colour palette cannot express, or if source-identity assignments need to be user-overridable.
design: Three-layer model from docs/TUI-DESIGN.md §6: (1) structure — selection, borders, dim text, warning, accent — from the terminal's indexed palette, never hardcoded RGB, and never a full-screen background; (2) source identity from a discriminable categorical palette assigned stably per sorted source id, NOT brand colours (fast-resume proves brand colours collide: cursor and grok are both pure white, opencode and copilot near-white, in the one column whose job is telling sources apart); (3) match highlighting as the loudest thing on screen, the one place a hardcoded high-contrast pair is justified. Hard rules: nothing encoded in colour alone, respect NO_COLOR, no truecolor without COLORTERM, test on a light background before shipping.
acceptance_criteria:
A client can be themed from the config file without recompiling, and the three-layer model in the design is preserved rather than flattened: structural colour still comes from the terminal's indexed palette (0-15), source identity from a discriminable categorical set, and neither becomes a hardcoded RGB value or a full-screen background.

The default with no theme config is exactly today's appearance, so the terminal's own theme remains the theme and this adds a capability rather than a look.

An invalid or partial theme file degrades to the default and says so, rather than rendering an unreadable screen — a colour system that can lock a user out of the UI that would let them fix it is worse than none.

Contrast is checked, not assumed. docs/TUI-DESIGN.md §7's hard rules are the acceptance bar, and a theme that violates them is rejected at load with the rule it broke.
notes:
SPEC 2026-08-01, and it stays P4 deliberately — the description already argues why, and the argument is sound: TUI-DESIGN §6 decides that layer-1 colour comes from the terminal's indexed palette, so the user's existing terminal theme IS the theme.

Left open rather than deferred, unlike the other P4s, because it has a real design recorded and a concrete trigger stated in its own description: it becomes real work if a client needs colours the 16-colour palette cannot express, or if source-identity assignments need to be user-controlled. That is a specific condition, not 'someday'.

title: VS Code extension
notes: DEFERRED 2026-08-01. Blocked on nothing technical — ADR 12's JSON contract and me9.3's destinations already make an editor client a thin shell over 'cs search --json'. It is deferred because the client effort is going into the TUI, and because an extension is the surface that most needs the ranking to be good first. Revisit alongside me9.7 (Raycast), which is the cheaper validation of the same contract and should go first.

title: Embeddings and hybrid ranking
description: BM25 + vector, reciprocal rank fusion.
notes: DEFERRED 2026-08-01. Not a spec problem — a sequencing one. Hybrid ranking can only be justified against a measurement, and the eval set that would provide it (6eb.21) is itself deferred pending the judging pass. Adding embeddings before the eval set exists means tuning two rankers with no way to tell whether either got better, which is the failure ADR 6's 'revisit when' language exists to prevent. Revisit when 6eb.21 lands and BM25 has a measured recall ceiling to beat.

title: Cursor and Antigravity importers
description: protobuf, 52 conversations, poor value/effort ratio.
notes: DEFERRED 2026-08-01, kept rather than closed. Its own note prices it: protobuf parsing for 52 conversations, a poor value/effort ratio against the 3,003 already indexed. Not closed as won't-do because the judgement is about today's corpus — if Cursor or Antigravity becomes a tool that is actually used here, the 52 becomes a live number and the ratio changes. Revisit on that signal, not on a date.

title: Machine re-key detection after a clone or restore
notes:
DEFERRED 2026-08-01: gated on ADR 17, not on missing detail.

GATE: ADR 17 fixes machine identity as a generated UUID with a human alias. The clone/restore re-key POLICY is the open part, and docs/BACKLOG.md records it as blocking 'second machine'. Detecting a re-key is only definable once it is decided what a re-key means — whether a restored backup is the same machine continuing or a new machine forking, which is the whole question.

UNBLOCKS WHEN: ADR 17's re-key policy is decided, which BACKLOG.md ties to a second machine actually existing. There is one machine (tylers-macbook-air) today, so the detection has nothing to detect.

Related and also gated: a7k.15 (encrypted offsite tier) and ADR 18 (sync transport) are the other two that only become real on a second machine.
